ELOY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona family is grieving after a mother of eight was hit and killed by a train while on a morning run.

Thelma Candelaria, 47, was a caregiver and mother of eight children. She had been baptized less than a week before her death in what was supposed to be the start of a new beginning.

She went out for a routine run Thursday morning in Eloy. She was recording the run on social media, and her daughter, Alaisha Candelaria, provided videos showing her smiling and in good spirits.

“She was singing along to Jessie Reyez, which is her favorite artist. She was laughing,” said Alaisha Candelaria of her mother.

Alaisha Candelaria would later use her mother’s videos, along with surveillance footage, to piece together what happened next.

During her run, Thelma Candelaria stopped at a railroad crossing around 6 a.m. As she was recording one train, a separate train on another track approached her from the opposite direction, according to her daughter.

The mother didn’t see the second train, and any sound it made was muffled by her earbuds and the train she was already recording. Eloy Police say both trains sounded their horns before she was hit.

“She had her noise-canceling Beat headphones on. She was in her own world,” Alaisha Candelaria said.

Eloy Police say the train that hit Thelma Candelaria applied its emergency brake but couldn’t avoid the collision. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

“It’s a lot. It’s a lot,” Alaisha Candelaria said.

She says she wants the community to know her mother’s death was a horrible accident.

“People, continuously, they’ve always told me my whole life, ‘You are so, so lucky to have the mother that you have,’” Alaisha Candelaria said. “She was an angel.”

The family has created a GoFundMe to help with funeral costs and support for Thelma Candelaria’s children.

The Eloy Police Department’s Vehicular Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.

Topic:Gender Discrimination

Sex discrimination commissioner Anna Cody says legislation is "not keeping up". (Four Corners: Ron Foley)

A new report from the Australian Human Rights Commission recommends stronger laws to protect pregnant women and mothers from discrimination at work.

Sex discrimination commissioner Anna Cody says current legislation is "not keeping up with modern families", which often rely on two incomes.

The government has not yet committed to the report's recommendations.

Australia's sex discrimination laws must be overhauled to stop workplaces "penalising" pregnant women and mothers, a new report urges.

More than 100 women have told Four Corners they experienced discrimination at work after falling pregnant, revealing it can occur regardless of industry, seniority, pay or where you live.

It comes as Australia's fertility rate plummets to historic lows and more women choose to have fewer children later in life.

Now, a new report from the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC), obtained exclusively by Four Corners, has found pregnancy discrimination remains a major barrier to gender equality and workforce participation.

Four Corners has uncovered the tactics used to push mothers out of the workforce.

It recommends wide-ranging changes to the Sex Discrimination Act, such as making it illegal for an employer to indirectly discriminate against a worker due to family responsibilities.

That is when a company rule that applies to all workers, such as requiring a day's notice to work from home, unfairly disadvantages someone who is pregnant or a parent.

"Many workplaces treat family responsibilities as an inconvenience or disruption and penalise people with care responsibilities," the report said.

"This disproportionately impacts women's economic independence, entrenches inequality and undermines the wellbeing of families."

The report also found parents from minority backgrounds and casual workers were more vulnerable.

It has been decades since the Sex Discrimination Act has been changed when it comes to family responsibilities.

Sex discrimination commissioner Anna Cody said the legislation was "not keeping up with modern families".

"To have a very old-fashioned idea of who should be working, that's confounding to me when we've come so far in other areas of our society."

Twenty-one women told Four Corners they had been made redundant or dismissed, only to discover their role still existed.

This practice is known as a "sham restructure".

The report also calls for tougher laws to prevent redundancies connected to pregnancy leave or caring responsibilities, backed by "meaningful penalties for non-compliance".

As part of the proposal, employers should have to show stronger evidence that a redundancy was genuinely required before letting a pregnant worker or mother go.

The commission's report also calls for changes to the Fair Work Act, which include making flexible work a presumptive right.

"Rather than it just being a right to request [flexible work], the presumption should be … that flexible work is provided by an employer," Dr Cody said.

A former high-ranking counterterrorism official tells Four Corners she experienced discrimination after falling pregnant.

Of the 104 women who shared their stories with Four Corners, almost one-third said they had flexibility requests refused.

Some also reported challenges returning to their jobs after parental leave.

Australians are not eligible for unpaid parental leave unless they have worked for the same employer for a year.

If an employer allows them to take leave anyway, the employee does not have a right to return to their old job.

Researchers and the commission have urged the government to close that loophole for years on the grounds that it leaves women exposed to discrimination.

Earlier this year, the federal government expanded government-funded paid parental leave from July, offering up to 26 weeks of pay at minimum wage rates.

"The first few months with a new baby are precious," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement at the time.

"My government is making it easier for parents to spend that time together."

Anthony Albanese says his government wants to help families. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Dr Cody said she welcomed the government's focus on women's rights and said she expected it would now look at ways to implement the report's recommendations.

In 2014, the Australian Human Rights Commission made several recommendations to better protect working mothers from discrimination, many of which have not been adopted.

A 2008 Senate inquiry also made similar recommendations, which have not been enacted.

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth told Four Corners issues around parental leave were being investigated in an ongoing inquiry into workplace standards, but the government has not yet committed to any of the recommended changes.

"We will always look at how we can do better when it comes to dealing with these issues," she said.

"We don't want to see women discriminated against, but just as important as the law is also changing behaviour and culture out there.

"We've already shown and demonstrated through the law changes we've made, we take this seriously. We know there's more to do and we'll continue to work on it."

Dr Cody said change was overdue.

"[Mothers] contribute across all of the areas in which they work, whether it be public service, mining, construction, teaching, nursing," she said.

"Being able to benefit from that rich experience, those ways of being in the world, we benefit from having that breadth and all women being able to participate."

Watch Four Corners' full investigation, The Pregnancy Penalty, tonight at 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

Topic:Cricket

Kim Garth struck the winning runs after a dramatic Australian collapse. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Australia has beaten New Zealand by two wickets in the first ODI at North Sydney Oval.

The hosts survived a dramatic late collapse to get home with seven balls to spare.

The series continues at the same venue on Tuesday.

Australia has survived a dreadful collapse to claim a tense two-wicket victory over New Zealand in the opening Twenty20 International at North Sydney Oval.

The reigning T20 World Cup champions won with seven balls to spare, scoring 8-165 in reply to New Zealand's 2-162 on Sunday night.

Number 10 Kim Garth faced eight balls without scoring before hitting a boundary to give Australia a 1-0 lead in the three-match Rose Bowl series, with the remaining matches at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

Australia overcame the early LBW loss of Georgia Voll and were charging towards victory when star veteran Beth Mooney and Ellyse Perry were involved in a dreadful mix-up.

They had taken the score to 86 in just 8.2 overs when Mooney was struck on the pad and charged off for the most ambitious of runs.

Perry sent her back, Mooney was slow to turn, and was run out well short of her ground.

The loss of Mooney for 38 from just 25 balls prompted a collapse.

Perry raced to her equal fastest T20 half century in just 27 balls but on 52 dragged a short ball from Jess Kerr to deep backward square, where she was well caught by Issy Sharp running to her right.

Georgie Wareham (10 from 7 balls) sliced a leg-spinner and Kerr's younger sister Amelia straight to point.

Ash Gardner (23 from 17) gave Jess Kerr her third wicket on review and Annabel Sutherland (9 from 5 balls) became her fourth, pulling a short ball to deep square leg.

Nicole Cary (4 from 3 balls) was run out by the recalled Tahlia McGrath and when captain Sophie Molineux (11 from 5 balls) fell, Australia had lost 7-62.

But the home side hung on for their 11th T20 win in a row, while the White Ferns have now lost six of their past nine matches.

Not even a record partnership and a record-equalling total in Australia could secure New Zealand victory.

After a difficult start by the White Ferns, Georgia Plimmer and Maddy Green combined for an unbeaten 127 in 80 balls.

Plimmer made a career-high 85 off 68 balls and Green 56 from 37 balls.

It was a breakout innings for the 22-year-old Plimmer, her fourth T20 half-century in 54 matches for New Zealand.

Going into the game she had an average of 16 and a strike rate of 104.

She was the beneficiary of two difficult chances, a stumping and catch from wicketkeeper Beth Mooney standing up to seamers Sutherland and Hamilton.

A beloved dog was saved from several feet of Alaska snow more than 50 hours after being separated from her owner during an avalanche.

LouLou, a 4-year-old huskydoodle, was out on a hike with her owner, Brian, and his friend in Chugach State Park in Anchorage, when the avalanche struck near Eklutna Lake, separating the dog from her owner.

Brian and his hiking partner suffered injuries, but were rescued and taken to hospital, without LouLou.

Lauren Padawer, LouLou’s other owner and Brian’s partner, said she was out of town when the incident happened, but quickly started organizing a search team to go out and find her lost dog.

Initial search parties had no luck finding LouLou, but they remained determined.

After 50 hours, two people involved in the search, Amanda Barker and Dave Beckett, went back out in a helicopter after receiving an AirTag ping with the dog’s location.

Video shows Barker and Beckett landing the helicopter as close to the AirTag ping as they could.

Spotting the white pooch standing in the snow in the distance, alive, they began making their way to her.

They got out of the helicopter, climbing through the snow on their hands for 20 minutes to reach LouLou, who barked as they got closer to her.

The pair called her by name, trying to get her to come along with them, but she was hesitant at first.

“Come on, sweetheart,” Barker said. “Let’s go for a ride, LouLou.”

Eventually, the pair were able to leash the pup, slowly and carefully sliding down the mountainside to get back to the helicopter.

The last clip shows LouLou getting lots of love and well-deserved pets on the helicopter after her journey.

“To Dave, Amanda, Kathy, Barney, James, the ground search parties, the military pararescue personnel, and everyone who offered a hand: thank you,” Padawer said on Facebook.

“I will never forget what you did for LouLou, for Brian, his hiking partner, and for me. Sometimes it takes a mountain to remind you how extraordinary people can be.”

Retired FBI special agent Rob Chadwick joins Brian Kilmeade to discuss the school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, where three children and one teacher were killed.

Three children and a teacher were killed on Oct. 15 at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, just 20 minutes from our home in central Oregon. Four precious lives were stolen, leaving families facing a grief no parent, spouse, or loved one should ever have to endure. Children who should be coming home to their families will never walk through those doors again. A teacher who devoted a life to educating and caring for children is gone.

Among the critically injured is 7-year-old Saylor, a child who had previously been honored in Bend as a "Sparrow" through a program that supports children facing serious medical challenges. Already familiar with adversity, she is now fighting for her life after being shot in the face. Our hearts break for Saylor and for all the other victims of this devastating violence.

Our community and our nation are in mourning.

ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS

As an anti-bullying specialist and expert witness, I've witnessed more than 20,000 students around the world publicly apologize for bullying and related behavior. Some of these apologies have helped prevent students from harming themselves or others.

We don't know the motives of the 16-year-old shooter. We don't know whether he was bullied at Silver Rail or any other school. But this tragedy raises questions about a destructive pattern that requires entire communities—not just teachers and schools—to confront bullying. After all, bullying is a cultural problem, not merely a "school problem."

The Secret Service's report, "Protecting America's Schools," examined 41 targeted school attacks. Among the 35 attackers whose backgrounds were analyzed—all male—80% had experienced bullying. For 57%, that bullying was persistent.

There is no evidence at this point that bullying played any role in the Silver Rail attack. But research into past targeted school attacks shows why bullying remains one of the behaviors communities should take seriously.

Each time our nation reels from another school shooting, a dangerous misunderstanding is often treated as fact: The shooter must be severely mentally ill. Yet most people with severe mental illness are not violent. Equating psychiatric diagnoses with dangerousness stigmatizes people who need care and distracts from the specific behaviors that should concern us.

HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK

Having worked with countless targets of bullying for more than 25 years, I've witnessed how persistent abuse can leave children emotionally inflamed. Some turn their pain inward, while others express it outwardly through anger, aggression and sometimes violence. Too many are expected to endure a level of persistent abuse that no adult would tolerate.

Telling a child to ignore cruelty is not intervention. Admonishing a child to "turn the other cheek" in the face of relentless abuse is one of the most tortured applications of Scripture. Requiring an apology without checking whether the abuse has stopped is not accountability. Moving the targeted child to another classroom or school—an all-too-common practice—while leaving the aggressor unchecked only deepens the injustice and resentment.

POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING

Students need trustworthy adults and clear reporting options, including anonymous reporting. They also need protection against retaliation. When reporting makes life worse, children learn to remain silent precisely when adults most need information.

What most people don't understand is that bystanders possess the greatest potential power in the theater of bullying. Bullies often seek an audience, and that audience can either reward their cruelty through laughter, encouragement, or silence—or help stop it through courageous action. When witnesses intervene safely, they can shift the balance of power in favor of the targeted child.

With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.

It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)

The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.

The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

Democrats are running up lopsided majorities of the early votes as Americans head to the polls and mail in their ballots, carving out a clear majority of the votes cast so far.

Of early and mail-in voters, 54% were Democrats, 30% Republicans and 16% independents or “other,” according to state election data compiled by TargetSmart and NBC News.

The early vote advantage carries over to the marquee Senate races, including several held in Republican-leaning states.

In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is battling former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the Democratic edge is 55-36%, based on voters’ registrations.

In Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is in a tough race with Democrat Josh Turek, the edge from registered Democrats is 57-29%, with 14% from “other.”

In Maine, where Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is trying to fend off Democrat Troy Jackson, the Democratic edge is 55-19%, with more than a quarter “other” vote ballots in.

None of the data show how people actually voted – just who showed up or sent in their ballot.

“We know the Democrats have the enthusiasm advantage,” said University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss.

But what remains to be seen is whether the early numbers point to a predicted overall wave of voters or merely “upper status voters who always vote anyway,” he added.

One way to explore that is to compare numbers to four years ago.

In Republican-leaning Nebraska, where Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts is battling independent Dan Osborne, the Democratic edge has expanded from then. It’s 45-38 now, compared to 44-41 at this point in voting in 2022.

Eighty-nine percent of Democrats who have voted in Nebraska also voted in 2022 and 2024, while 10% are new voters, according to the secretary of state.

For Republicans, 91% voted in the past but just 7% are new voters.

Virginia is seeing a flood of early turnout, with 519,000 ballots in compared to 260,000 by this point in 2022, with the total doubling in left-leaning Fairfax County.

In Texas, the which features a high-profile race between Democratic state Rep. James Talarico (D-Texas) and AG Ken Paxton (R-Texas), Democratic edge is an overwhelming 62-32%.

Democrats historically tend to vote early or by mail, although President Trump has regularly blasted mail-voting in favor of in-person voting on Election Day, calling it “inherently corrupt.”

But this year, on campaign stops and online, he has been changing his message.

In a video last weekend, Trump told supporters from the Oval Office: “If your state has early voting, do not wait. Go out and vote. Vote early, vote by mail, or vote in person on Election Day, November 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left ‘Dumocrats’ in a midterm victory that is too big to rig.”

He also told voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Garrett Langley, founder and CEO of license plate camera maker Flock Safety, defended his company’s surveillance technology onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco this week, even as Flock contends with canceled contracts and layoffs nationwide.

TechCrunch reports that speaking during a panel interview, Langley pushed back on critics who say Flock’s cameras amount to invasive surveillance. He argued that progress shouldn’t stop just because a technology is imperfect. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” he said.

To make his case, Langley reached for an analogy: driverless cars. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. A single crash, he argued, shouldn’t be grounds for pulling the technology entirely. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future.'”

Langley also addressed Flock’s relationship with the cities and police departments that deploy its cameras, saying the company tries not to dictate policy. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he said. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies.”

Asked about concerns that the technology could be abused, Langley said oversight is possible without hampering police work. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” he said.

When pressed on expectations that Flock’s technology should be flawless, Langley invoked a comment he attributed to an unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect, I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said.

He defended Flock’s role by pointing to staffing shortages in law enforcement, which he said have worsened since the coronavirus pandemic. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said.

Langley acknowledged the toll of leading a company at the center of national controversy but said he believes the trade-off is justified. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim.”

You search Google for Claude, the popular AI assistant, and spot a sponsored result. The link points to Bing, Microsoft's search engine. Nothing immediately screams scam. However, that click could send you through several websites before landing on a convincing fake Claude download page designed to trick you into running a dangerous command on your Mac.

Security researchers at Push Security uncovered a clever attack that uses legitimate search engine links to hide a malicious installer. The technique, which researchers jokingly call "Adception," takes advantage of how Google ads and Bing redirects work. Even more concerning, the fake installer shows one command on the screen while secretly copying another. Here's how the scam works and what you should know before downloading AI software.

HACKERS HIJACK VERIFIED STREAMING ACCOUNT TO SPREAD MALWARE, RESEARCHERS FIND

Cybersecurity researchers uncovered a fake Claude AI download page that tricks Mac users into running a potentially dangerous Terminal command. (Photo by Phil Barker/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

The attack begins with a Google search for "Claude Mac." According to Push Security, researchers discovered a sponsored search result that displayed bing.com as its destination. That address might seem reassuring because Bing belongs to Microsoft. However, clicking the advertisement sends users through a series of redirects. First, Google's advertising system processes the click. Next, Bing's legitimate click-tracking service forwards the browser to a compromised WordPress website belonging to a South American retailer. Finally, that website sends the visitor to a fake Claude download page.

The final website, claude-desk-code[.]com, imitates the real Claude download experience. It presents what appears to be a legitimate macOS installation option. By the time someone reaches the page, they may have little reason to suspect the journey began with a malicious advertisement. Researchers say the attackers deliberately used a real Bing search result for a compromised website. This allowed the attackers to display Bing's legitimate domain in the Google advertisement while using Bing's click-tracking redirect to send visitors toward the malicious destination.

The scammers added another layer of deception to make their operation harder to detect. The compromised retailer's website checks whether visitors arrived through Bing and whether their browsers send certain information. Meanwhile, the fake Claude website checks whether visitors came from Google or Bing. Someone who visits the malicious website directly may see a 404 error page instead of the fake installer. That behavior can make it harder for security scanners to investigate the attack because they may never encounter the page that victims actually see.

Push Security calls this technique cloaking. Attackers use it to control who reaches their malicious content while showing something harmless to other visitors. In this case, the researchers observed two separate checks designed to protect the attack from unwanted attention. The result is a carefully constructed path that makes a dangerous destination appear more trustworthy than it really is.

Here's where the attack gets particularly sneaky. The fake Claude page displays an installation command that appears to come directly from Anthropic, the company behind Claude. The command references Claude's legitimate website and looks like something a technically confident Mac user might recognize. However, the page's Copy button places a completely different command on the clipboard.

According to Push Security, the substituted command uses Base64 encoding to conceal an attacker-controlled website. When someone runs the pasted command in Mac Terminal, it first displays a reassuring message claiming that Claude is being downloaded from its official website. Behind the scenes, the command decodes the hidden address, downloads a remote script and sends it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. That means the person running the command sees references to Claude's legitimate website even though the Mac is executing code from an unrelated server.

This attack follows a technique known as InstallFix, a variation of ClickFix. These scams convince people to execute malicious commands themselves, often by disguising the instructions as a software installation or troubleshooting step. Push Security identified several additional websites associated with the same malicious toolkit, which it tracks internally as AcSig. The researchers found matching installation commands and similar fake installer interfaces across those sites.

The research confirms that the malicious command is designed to download a remote script from an attacker-controlled server and pass it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. However, Push Security's published findings do not identify the final payload or establish what the downloaded script does after execution. That uncertainty is important. Running an untrusted Terminal command can give malicious code an opportunity to operate with the permissions of the person executing it. Depending on the script, an attacker could potentially steal information, modify files or install additional software. The researchers have not confirmed those specific outcomes in this campaign.

The bigger concern is how easily the attack can persuade someone to bypass their own caution. The user voluntarily pastes the command, believing it came from a legitimate software provider. Meanwhile, the actual destination stays hidden inside encoded text. Push Security reports that four out of five ClickFix attacks it detects reach victims through search engines. That figure comes from the company's own detection data rather than a measurement of all attacks worldwide. Still, it shows why malicious search advertisements deserve attention.

Google confirms it has taken action against the advertiser accounts associated with the reported campaign. "We've suspended the advertiser accounts running the reported campaign. Using ads to distribute malware is an egregious violation of our policies, and we consistently update our detection systems to stay ahead of bad actors' evolving tactics," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also says attackers use cloaking to show its advertising review systems different content from what people actually see. The company says it continues monitoring attempts to evade its protections and updating its detection systems.

Microsoft also responded to CyberGuy's request for comment, confirming that its security protections identify the malicious indicators described in the research. A Microsoft spokesperson told CyberGuy, "We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect customers from evolving threats. Microsoft Defender protections detect and block the malicious indicators identified in the report." We also reached out to Anthropic for comment on the findings but did not hear back before our deadline.

ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK

Scammers are using Google search ads and legitimate Bing redirects to steer Mac users toward a fraudulent Claude AI installer. (Photographer: Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

You don't need to understand every line of computer code to avoid this scam. A few precautions can help you recognize suspicious downloads before they put your Mac at risk.

Instead of searching for a download and clicking the first sponsored result, go directly to Claude's official download page. Anthropic provides a macOS download there, so you can install the desktop application without relying on an unfamiliar website. You can also access Claude through your browser at claude.ai.

Be especially careful when a website tells you to copy a command into your Mac's Terminal. Terminal commands can download software, change system settings and execute scripts. Even legitimate-looking instructions can become dangerous when they come from an untrusted source. For the regular Claude desktop app, Anthropic provides a downloadable installer. You don't need to paste a command from a search advertisement to get started.

A website's Copy button can place different text on your clipboard than what appears on the page. Before running an unfamiliar command, paste it into a plain-text editor and compare it with the instructions. Watch for unexplained web addresses, encoded strings or commands that download and immediately execute remote scripts. However, even a command that looks harmless may contain hidden risks. When in doubt, stop and verify the instructions with the software developer.

Install macOS security updates and keep your browser current. Additionally, use strong antivirus software that offers real-time protection against malicious downloads and suspicious activity. Security software may help detect harmful scripts or their effects, although no antivirus product can guarantee protection against every attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

A sponsored placement means someone paid to promote a link. It does not guarantee that the destination is safe. Before clicking, check the advertiser by selecting the three dots next to a Google search ad. You can review who paid for it and check the advertiser's verification status. Google's Ads Transparency Center at adstransparency.google.com/ offers another way to research advertisers. Always confirm you're visiting the software developer's official website before downloading anything. If an ad looks suspicious, use its three-dot menu to select "Report this ad."

If you pasted an installation command from a suspicious Claude website into Terminal and pressed Return, treat your Mac as potentially compromised. The researchers have not established what the final payload does, so don't assume everything is safe simply because nothing unusual appears on your screen.

WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM

A fake Claude download website displays a legitimate-looking installation command while secretly copying a different command designed to execute a remote script. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)

What concerns me most about this attack is how much effort the scammers put into making everything look familiar. You start with Google, pass through a legitimate Microsoft service and eventually arrive at a page that looks like it belongs to a popular AI company. Then, with one click of a Copy button, the website quietly substitutes a command that could put your Mac at risk. I've always encouraged people to pay attention to website addresses before downloading software. That's still important, but this case shows why checking the address alone may not be enough. The attackers used trusted services to disguise where their link was taking people. My advice is to go straight to the software developer's official website, especially when installing AI tools. And whenever a download page asks you to run something in Terminal, make sure you understand exactly what you're authorizing. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache.

Would you trust a software download if it appeared in a Google ad and showed a familiar Microsoft link, or has this kind of scam made you question whether search results can be trusted at all? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

A massive shelter dog that weighed the same as a baby hippo has shed the pounds—and found a new home.

The huge bulldog named Peggy Sue swelled to 70 pounds (32.5kg) before she was taken to the RSPCA’s West Hatch Animal Centre in England.

She was so large she struggled with walking, infections, and overheating, and couldn’t take a few steps without collapsing.

When she arrived in July, the shelter in Somerset had to carry her in a crate from the van to her kennel and physically move her around.

“It was awful to see her struggle with every day movement,” said RSPCA Deputy Centre Manager, Anita Clark. “She really needed some care and attention.”

Peggy Sue’s exercise regime was increased gradually over time by a dedicated foster caretaker, which led to slow improvements every day.

She now continues to enjoy exercise and a strict diet plan.

Recently, SWNS reported the happy news that she was re-homed during the charity’s ‘Adoptober’ drive.

Peggy’s new weight sits at a much healthier 23.5kg—down twenty pounds from when she first arrived at the charity.

Her new owners, Emmie and Andy from Taunton, say she is quite a water-baby and enjoys rock pools and streams.

He also gained a best buddy in the Taunton household, a Jack Russel-mix that just lost its 16-year-old brother, Mr Woo.

“Peggy-Sue is our sixth rescue and they have all turned out to be the most amazing dogs ever,” said Emmie.

“The RSPCA and her foster home had already done a great job getting her weight down by five kilograms (11 pounds), so we just had to keep the progress going.

“When she first came home she only showed small bursts of energy, but little by little she has built up her strength and now she is utterly amazing and loves her walks and trips in the car.”

“Rehoming a rescue dog is the best thing you could ever do!”

phoenix_pay_transition_cheque_missing_20:
Cindy Mitchell left the federal public service this past spring through workforce adjustment, the process used when federal positions are being cut or eliminated. She was entitled to a transition payment, including $42,151 that was supposed to be transferred into her registered retirement savings plan.

The money was issued as a paper cheque. It never reached her bank.

Her compensation adviser, the federal pay specialist handling her file, later told Mitchell in correspondence reviewed by The Hill Times that the cheque appeared to have been “intercepted behind the scenes” and that the same thing had happened on “numerous files.”

Mitchell is one of three current and former public servants who told The Hill Times they have encountered delayed, missing, or unresolved payments while moving through workforce adjustment. Their stories come as thousands of employees move through the government’s workforce-reduction process, raising questions about whether the federal pay system can keep pace with a surge of complex departure transactions Ottawa knew was coming.

Those transactions can include transition payments, severance, final pay, and unused leave payouts, while unresolved older Phoenix pay issues also have to be settled. The decade-old pay system has cost over $5-billion and has left tens of thousands of people overpaid, underpaid, or waiting years for compensation.

According to Treasury Board Secretariat data as of Sept. 14, 4,613 public servants had selected a workforce adjustment option under the government’s spending review. Of those, 4,119 chose options that include a Transition Support Measure, like Mitchell.

In a March update on the government’s effort to address these longstanding issues, Public Services and Procurement Canada’s (PSPC) point person told reporters those facing layoffs and severance would a receive “white glove” service, with trained staff in place.

“I feel pretty comfortable we’ll be able to manage the volume at this point,” said Alex Benay, PSCP’s then-associate deputy minister, who has since left the role.

Ottawa has also allocated additional funding to increase Pay Centre capacity.

But Mitchell’s troubles started before the cheque went missing.

Her Natural Resources Canada position was not being eliminated. After about 25 years in the public service, she left through alternation, allowing another employee whose position was at risk to move into her job. Treasury Board data shows 888 staff have chosen to leave via this option.

Mitchell’s Transition Support Measure totalled about $131,000. She took $20,000 in cash in 2026, directed $42,151 into her RRSP, and deferred roughly $68,800 until 2027 to spread the tax impact across two calendar years.

Before the payments could be finalized, old unresolved pay issues on Mitchell’s file had to be fixed, adding another delay.

She eventually received the first cash portion and her severance. But her adviser told her the RRSP payment had to be issued as a paper cheque, routed through Environment and Climate Change Canada, where Mitchell had been transferred on paper through the alternation, and then forwarded to her bank.

Correspondence reviewed by The Hill Times shows Mitchell was told the cheque should reach her bank within about two weeks of Aug. 26. By Sept. 17, she had told her adviser the bank still had not received it.

Mitchell said she was never told where the potentially intercepted cheque went. A replacement was scheduled to be printed Oct. 7, and to be sent through the same process.

“I am not confident,” Mitchell said when asked whether she believes the second cheque would actually arrive. “That’s why I’m going to watch it closely.”

Mitchell said she could absorb the delay, but worried about workers leaving government without the same financial cushion.

“What if I was a single mom or dad or whatever, or even a single person who had bills to pay and was struggling with this process?” she said.

For another federal worker, the strain came from waiting months for her Transition Support Measure.

The worker, who asked not to be named because she is still moving through workforce adjustment, submitted her departure option back in April.

Correspondence reviewed by The Hill Times shows Health Canada told her the Pay Centre would generally send the forms needed to arrange the payment about three to four weeks after departure.

Once the Pay Centre had the completed form and required documents, the standard processing window was about 25 business days, according to the correspondence.

She said she did not receive the form until June, several weeks later than expected. After returning it, she repeatedly sought updates and eventually asked how to escalate her case, citing financial hardship. Her payment arrived July 29.

“I burned through all of my savings waiting for this to come in,” she said.

She still had a mortgage, car payments, and a dependent attending college, she added.

The Hill Times asked Health Canada whether employees going through workforce adjustment were experiencing pay or departure-processing delays beyond the timelines communicated to staff, and whether the department had raised any concerns with Public Services and Procurement Canada about Pay Centre capacity or timeliness.

Health Canada said it is not aware of employees whose workforce-adjustment pay or departure processing has exceeded those expected timelines, and said it has not raised concerns with PSPC about Pay Centre capacity or timeliness related to the current workforce-reduction exercise.

Spokesperson Marie-Pier Burelle said a dedicated Pay Centre team recently reported that it was meeting the required service standards for workforce-adjustment cases. The department did not provide those figures.

Past Phoenix failures have had severe consequences for workers. In 2017, Nunatsiaq News reported that then-Nunavut senator Dennis Patterson had received accounts of federal employees who had depleted their savings and faced eviction, including a young Inuk worker who sold his snowmobile to pay bills and support his family. The following year, Parliament heard the case of a Service Canada worker whose daughter left a Camosun College program after unpredictable pay left the family struggling to keep up with its mortgage and utilities.

For a third worker whom The Hill Times spoke with, the wait began before anyone had even picked up her file.

The former public servant—who asked not to be named because she is pursuing the issue through her union and is considering seeking legal advice—left through alternation in the spring. She said it took almost four months for the Pay Centre to assign her file to a compensation adviser.

More than five months after leaving, she said she is still waiting for a complete accounting of her final pay, including unused vacation, earlier pay still owed, and any overpayments the government may seek to recover.

Federal guidance says money an employee owes the government, including past overpayments, can be deducted from severance or other final payments.

She has received the paperwork to direct her severance, but is holding off on signing it until she knows what the government believes she is owed and what it may deduct.

“It creates a limbo, but the administrative delay created it,” she said.

Her Transition Support Measure is not late; she chose to defer it to later years.

Union figures show pay problems related to workforce adjustment are reaching bargaining agents, although the early counts do not establish how widespread they are.

The Agriculture Union, which represents more than 7,700 federal workers, is aware of roughly half a dozen cases, national president Milton Dyck told The Hill Times.

Dyck said recurring problems include transition payments held up by unresolved earlier transactions, including older Phoenix issues. He said the union has had to intervene or escalate some cases.

The Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada (PIPSC) reported a lighter caseload.

PIPSC communications officer Johanne Fillion said its team helping members with Phoenix problems had encountered only two pay cases related to workforce adjustment, and both had been resolved.

“Maybe it is still too early to tell about Phoenix pay repercussions,” Fillion said.

Ottawa had already begun preparing the Pay Centre for an increase in work tied to the government’s workforce reductions.

In its spring economic update, the feds earmarked $36-million specifically for added Pay Centre capacity to carry out the spending review.

Warnings about the complexity of that work also came early.

At a Feb. 23 news conference, PIPSC president Sean O’Reilly warned that workforce adjustment would bring a surge of complex pay transactions, including early retirements, alternations, and layoffs, risking new errors and a larger backlog.

Less than two weeks later, at Benay’s update, he told reporters the department’s was managing the pay backlog and prepared to support those facing layoffs.

Whether that added capacity is keeping pace is harder to determine.

The Hill Times asked PSPC how long workforce adjustment files are taking to process, how many remain outstanding, whether delays or a backlog have emerged, and whether it still has enough capacity to handle the volume.

Nicole Allen, with PSPC media relations, said the department is still looking into the questions and was unlikely to provide a full response before publication, but expects to provide more information later this week.

PSPC instead pointed The Hill Times to its general Pay Centre dashboard, which does not separately identify workforce adjustment files.

By entering your email address you consent to receive email from The Hill Times containing news, analysis, updates and offers. You may unsubscribe at any time. See our privacy policy

                        
                    
                
                The dashboard nevertheless shows a Pay Centre carrying substantial outstanding work as workforce adjustment departures pick up speed.

As of Sept. 23, it shows 198,000 transactions ready to be processed. Of those, 33,000 were outside their applicable service standards but less than a year old, while another 66,000 had been waiting for more than a year.

Those figures cover the Pay Centre’s entire workload, so they do not show how quickly transition payments, severance, or other departure files are moving.

Federal workforce adjustment guidance says Pay Centre requests to process departure-related pay actions are usually subject to a 25-working-day service standard.

Declan Meredith has been named at fly half for the Wallabies' final Bledisloe Cup Test on Saturday.

ABC Sport will live blog the Wallabies' Test against the All Blacks from 4pm, AEDT.

Declan Meredith will start at fly half against the All Blacks for just the fourth time in his young Test career, as the Wallabies make changes for Saturday's final Bledisloe Cup clash at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Meredith, who made his Test debut against France in July, replaces Ben Donaldson in the number 10 jersey.

Donaldson was ruled out with a minor upper leg injury in the wake of the 50-19 thrashing dished out by the All Blacks at Auckland's Eden Park last Saturday night.

Back-up fly half Harry McLaughlin-Phillips will make his Test debut if he comes on as a reserve in Sydney.

He is joined on the bench by reserve scrum half Kalani Thomas, who is yet to play a Bledisloe Cup Test.

The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

It will be a tough initiation for Meredith, although he will be playing outside Brumbies teammate and scrum half, Ryan Lonergan.

The 27-year-old got his first taste of playing the All Blacks after coming on as a reserve at Eden Park last weekend.

Meanwhile, the Wallabies have moved Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres.

He started on the wing in the Wallabies' past two Tests, but the absence of Len Ikitau (concussion) forced Wallabies coach Les Kiss to shift the ex-NRL star back to the midfield.

He will partner Isaac Henry, who switches from outside to inside centre, while Harry Potter will start on the wing.

Ikitau is a massive loss for the Wallabies, who are also missing Hunter Paisami (suspension) from their midfield options.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted back to the centres for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Elsewhere in the Wallabies' match-day squad, former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead prop, alongside hooker Josh Nasser.

Ross replaces Angus Bell, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa (rested) made way for Nasser.

Hooker Billy Pollard, lock Josh Canham, openside flanker Carlo Tizzano and utility back Filipo Daugunu have returned to the Wallabies' squad as reserves.

The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

"We got a clear picture last weekend of where we need to be better," Kiss said in a Rugby Australia statement.

"We've said all along we'll continue to work hard and grow our game, and the squad has been impressive in the way they have prepared this week."

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who retained his place alongside Jeremy Williams in the second row, will appear in his 50th Test.

The Bledisloe Cup Test will cap off a historic "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos play Scotland earlier in the day, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams meet New Zealand and Fiji respectively.

It is the first time all four national teams have featured on the same match-day schedule.

meet-the-supervillains-ruining:
Peachy Keenan’s latest book, Supervillains: Architects of America’s Decline, is funny, concise, and surprisingly profound.

Along with annoying girlbosses, forced diversity, and predictable narratives of class oppression, one major signifier of a wokeified product is the complete inversion of good versus evil. Creators of popular entertainment deconstruct heroes and reimagine them to be privileged jerks with sinister motives, while they redeem villains by imbuing them with justifiable reasons for their villainy. In accordance with this, the creators of the past 15 years have churned out endless slop telling a familiar story from the villain’s perspective or deliberately making the hero flawed to the point of becoming unlikeable.

Naturally, writers will pretend that this treatment adds dimension and nuance to their stories, exploring common tropes and themes from different sides and subverting harmful narratives. In reality, it makes an incoherent, dissatisfying mess of the story and deprives it of any deeper moral meaning or lessons about the human condition. If woke entertainment succeeds in anything, it is to erode clear moral standards and relativize good and evil. No one is good or bad, nothing is right or wrong, and everything is a matter of perspective.

Not only has this mindset ruined modern entertainment, but it has also done the same to political and cultural discourse and in the same way. No one is simply good or evil — except Donald Trump, of course — they are simply acting according to their beliefs or “their truth.” Consequently, it becomes impossible to judge people with power and influence. Even if what they do is horribly unjust and destructive, they can never be called evil.

But what if these individuals really are evil? What if they knowingly do harm in the interest of enriching themselves, amassing power, and picking on those who are weaker than them? Would it not be more appropriate to label such people villains — even supervillains — to be clear on who means to destroy the country and make life miserable for everyone? And wouldn’t this be good to know before voting in the midterm elections this coming November?

It most certainly would, which is why writer Peachy Keenan has written Supervillains: Architects of America’s Decline. With her usual wit, Keenan catalogues today’s worst people actively destroying the country. The list is long and includes well-known figures from science, politics, business, culture, and academia. Although leftists are usually the ones deeming their opponents evil, Keenan demonstrates that conservatives have the much stronger case. Moreover, these problems will only worsen if conservatives remain ignorant about their perpetrators.

In the interest of relevance and keeping her book to a manageable length (290 pages instead of 2,900 pages), Keenan limits her review to the present day, although many of the names got their start during the dark days of Covid six years ago.

As such, she begins with the public health officials, the oxymoronically labeled “Sick Doctors” who swore up and down that the Covid virus came from a Chinese wet market and that the vaccine was safe and necessary. Before they were doing this, though, they were leveraging their unquestioned medical authority to push transgender interventions on vulnerable minors. In retrospect, it should not have been a surprise to see these unaccountable “medical professionals” with no discernible conscience capitalize on a serious health crisis for nefarious purposes.

This dynamic of using their elite status to exploit crises or fabricate them altogether is repeated endlessly with the other supervillains. There are the “Great Replacers” who flood the country with immigrants and demonize critics as bigots; the “Female Liberation Theologists” who promote toxic feminism, abortion, sexual promiscuity, and transgenderism, all for the purpose of ruining men and making women as miserable as themselves; the proud members of the “American Injustice System” who do their utmost to keep criminals on the streets, punish do-gooders, meddle in elections, and shake down organizations that aren’t sufficiently woke; and the “DEI Hards” who have drained away all competency and fairness from every institution, elevating race hustlers and career criminals while silencing and suing conservatives who call this out.

Not surprisingly, Keenan particularly shines in her criticism of today’s cultural supervillains “executing a hostile takeover of our cultural output” since this is the world she comes from. The first of these are the “Illiterati,” the ultra-woke leftists who rule the literary world with a rainbow-colored iron fist. Keenan is hilariously candid about what has become of today’s literature because of these people:

A tiresome array of stale, postmodern tropes are still going strong in the publishing industry: gender confusion, trans kids, abortion memoirs, threesome memoirs, divorce memoirs, the cozy story your abuela told you before she handed you over to human traffickers, the evils of slavery, “growing up brown in a racist world,” “growing up female in a misogynist country,” the plight of the immigrants and the refugee, the evils of white men, the struggle of angst ridden teenage asexual werewolves: it’s all there between the covers.

Naturally, she follows this up with a plethora of receipts to prove that this is intentional and just as bad as it sounds. Although the Illiterati turned away the majority of potential readers from contemporary literature, they were a major influence on the group responsible for wokeifying popular entertainment: the “Hollywood Wreckers.”

These are the genius producers and filmmakers who destroyed popular franchises in the name of female empowerment and diversity — Star Wars, Marvel, The Lord of the Rings, Disney Princess movies, and now The Chronicles of Narnia. They also ruined popular books adapted to film like Little Women, A Song of Ice and Fire, and The Three-Body Problem. It’s clear that these people are the ones most responsible for the current miserable state of Hollywood.

My favorite chapter in the book concerns the crazy-rich ex-wives and widows of the world’s richest men. As Keenan rightly notes, “The former wives of billionaires may make up the tiniest demographic of supervillains, but together they are doing more damage than all the male supervillains combined.” She goes on to discuss the odd phenomenon of divorcees Melinda Gates, MacKenzie Scott Bezos, and widow Laurene Powell Jobs shoveling billions of dollars to leftist organizations devoted to destroying the West.

My other favorite chapter, “Biohackers,” describes a group of mad scientists who could stand to have a little more attention. These are the eugenicists at Orchid, trying to “have a ‘cure’ for genetic abnormalities and disease” by killing live embryos; the “‘bodyoid’ researchers” who manufacture “cloned humans, grown in artificial wombs, genetically modified to lack brain stems, and kept alive for their owner’s organ needs”; and the “Baby Merchants” who run surrogacy clinics where babies are essentially manufactured as sellable merchandise to homosexual couples. Once again, Keenan’s incisive honesty about these individuals helps bring out the unappreciated truth that what they are doing is almost unfathomably evil.

Keenan also discusses the “Media Malefactors” who are the demagogues and shills who use their platforms to inform their sheep-like audiences about politics, the “Fat Cats” who use their immense capital to influence society and bankroll underhanded political projects, and the laughably incompetent leaders and representatives of “Motel California.”

Before moving into her conclusion, Keenan devotes two brief chapters to the “Supervillain Dynasties” and “Lesser Villains,” which respectively consist of elite families with legacies of failure and corruption and non-elites who nevertheless partake in destructive and disreputable behavior. For readers interested in talking sense to these lesser villains, many of whom they probably encounter daily, Keenan provides a helpful lexicon to dispel some of the confusion that tends to arise in these conversations.

Finally, the book ends with some suggestions on how to deal with this large cast of supervillains. This mainly consists of seeing past their propaganda, bravely speaking the truth, and following the pro-family, just-be-normal advice of her book Domestic Extremist. Rather than seeking to understand, accommodate, and even imitate these elites, people should recognize such types as the supervillains they are and thwart them as much as possible. After all, “they’re essential to the timeline. To the story. … You can’t have a great hero unless he’s got a great bad guy to fight. It is our fate, I’m afraid, to always be locked in a war with people who think they’re the good guys and just exterminate the other side and they’ll reach their version of the Promised Land. Tale as old as time!”

Overall, Keenan is funny, concise, and surprisingly profound (see the quote above) in her analysis. She wisely avoids simply dishing out red meat to a conservative audience or making glib equivocations between both sides in the vain attempt to seek out common ground. Yes, this conflict largely takes place beyond the right-left political and cultural spectrum, and it stems from certain fallenness in human nature, but at the moment, the worst offenses are overwhelmingly coming from the leftist worldview. While all human beings have the capacity to become villains, and some even have the means to become supervillains, it is undeniable that leftism is facilitating and encouraging the bulk of today’s evils.

With the midterms coming up, American voters would do well to read Supervillains and remind themselves of how far we have come as a society and how far we have to go. Sometimes, life isn’t so morally gray and indeterminate. Sometimes, the evil is so apparent that one can’t help but laugh at it like Peachy Keenan does. And sometimes, there comes a moment when one hears the call to heroism, dispenses with the usual misgivings, and proceeds to save his world from the villains destroying his country.

When it comes to their love lives, young people are leaning into the mystical.

Manifestation, psychics, astrology, tarot cards, love spells — 64% of Gen Z and 51% of millennial adults have tried at least one, according to a new survey of 1,013 Americans ages 18 to 60 by DatingNews (with an estimated margin of error of ±3.1 percentage points at the 95% confidence level). That compares with 25% of Gen X and 12% of Boomers.

Amy Chan, relationship coach and author of "Unsingle: How to Date Smarter and Create Love That Lasts," is seeing these trends now more than ever. "Especially the astrology thing," she says, adding that, "I can't escape the conversation about astrology and Mercury in retrograde."

New York City-based psychologist Sabrina Romanoff has seen an uptick in this behavior among her clients as well. "In the past I've heard people bring it up as a joke," she says. Now they're embracing it.

A tarot card reading can cost up to $162, according to Thumbtack. Love spells can go for as little as $2 on Etsy. Here's why Chan and Romanoff think young singles are getting witchy, and their advice to people trying these tactics as they look for love.

The bottom line of why people try psychics and love spells is uncertainty.

"When people don't feel like they're in control — and right now, dating is a dumpster fire," says Chan, "people become more vulnerable to magical thinking." It gives them the sense that they're taking the reins and even provides some hope.

Gen Zers in particular are just starting their adult lives and face many unknowns. "There's just so much uncertainty," says Romanoff, "not just with love, but every single expectation that a lot of Gen Z had about their future has kind of just crumbled." That might make them more susceptible to leaning into the mystical than anyone, she says.

Young people are also very online and could be more exposed to astrology and manifestation than other generations. "They're on TikTok, they're on Instagram, and they're being served" content about these activities, says Chan.

Neither Chan nor Romanoff would say it's inherently bad to try mystical love tactics. They both have clients who have. The point is to use these tools in the right way.

If you "use the universe or magic or fate as a way of avoiding your own responsibilities and accountability" and do nothing else, then you're not moving your love life forward, says Chan. That's not a productive way to lean in.

But if, instead, trying a love spell or a tarot card reading makes you feel more confident and hopeful, and you take that change of attitude and sign up for a new class or strike up a conversation with a stranger, then these activities are helpful, says Romanoff, adding that the practice becomes "a springboard to actually get what they want."

Megan Schutt (right) was superb with the ball in Australia's defeat of Bangladesh. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Australia claimed an eight-wicket win over Bangladesh in the third and final ODI at Allan Border Field.

The hosts won the series 3-0.

Megan Schutt starred with the ball for Australia, taking 4-16.

Australia has coasted to an eight-wicket ODI win over Bangladesh to secure a clean sweep of the three-match series.

Ellyse Perry (65 not out off 64 deliveries) and Annabel Sutherland (74 not out off 52) added 137 for the third wicket, guiding Australia past Bangladesh's total of 172 all out inside 23 overs.

Australia lost openers Georgia Voll (11) and Beth Mooney (21) early in the run chase at Allan Border Field.

Mooney, in her 100th ODI match, was cleaned up by Bangladesh debutant quick Disha Biswas.

Beth Mooney is still smarting over Australia's World Cup loss to India last year, and as the star prepares for her 100th ODI against Bangladesh, she still has her eyes set on a couple of long-term goals.

From that moment, it was plain sailing for the hosts as Perry and Sutherland went through the gears.

Earlier, fast bowler Megan Schutt, who was named player of the match and the series, produced another masterclass.

Schutt bowled an incredible 10 overs straight to snare 4-16 and restrict Bangladesh after it was asked to bat first in the third and final ODI.

She bowled 53 dot balls in her spell and took her series haul to 10 wickets at a miserly average of 7.1.

Schutt now has 28 wickets in 14 ODIs at Allan Border Field, the most of any bowler in history.

Australian opener Phoebe Litchfield was ruled out of the match with a low-grade hip strain.

The star batter was replaced by all-rounder Nicola Carey.

Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Mike Collins trade accusations over alleged neo-Nazi activity linked to Collins' family and campaign donations from Jeffrey Epstein associate Reid Hoffman.

Georgia's contentious U.S. Senate race erupted into a heated confrontation Tuesday night as Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., accused GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., of allowing the dissemination of "neo-Nazi propaganda" inside his own home, prompting Collins to fire back over Ossoff's financial support from a billionaire with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The exchange unfolded during the candidates' second and final debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, which was hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and broadcast by Georgia Public Broadcasting network.

During the debate, Ossoff sought to tie his GOP opponent to White nationalism and repeatedly demanded that Collins commit to stopping the dissemination of hateful rhetoric involving his campaign staff, in particular Collins' son-in-law, which Ossoff alleged has continued despite blowback. Meanwhile, Collins accused his Democrat opponent of fueling threats against his family, refusing to return campaign support connected to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and questioned Ossoff over his support for candidates linked to controversial streamer Hasan Piker.

DEM ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK BACKFIRES AS TOP CANDIDATES FUNDED BY EPSTEIN-TIED BILLIONAIRE

Republican U.S. Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins of Georgia speaks to supporters at a primary night event on May 19, 2026, in Jackson, Georgia. (Jason Allen/Getty Images)

"How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for the Senate?" Ossoff asked, referencing reporting about his opponent's son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, who was the subject of a CNN investigation about sharing Nazi propaganda imagery, promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories and polling his online followers about whether he should produce a video titled "Why Gen-Z Doesn't Hate Hitler."

"How about this, Mike? We can shake hands on it," Ossoff continued to press. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign, it's just three weeks, Mike, you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house? Can you make that commitment?"

Collins responded by accusing Ossoff of inflaming hostility toward his family, pointing to threats he said he and his son-in-law had received.

"I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "There's a crazy person in jail right now because of your rhetoric," he alleged, before saying he had received another threat just the previous day.

JON OSSOFF SILENT ON SPLC INDICTMENT AFTER TAKING MORE THAN $700K FROM AFFILIATE OF INDICTED GROUP

"You have not denounced, you've not condemned Reid Hoffman, one of your largest donors out there, one that's been supporting you with over $1 million," Collins shot back. "Why don't you denounce that? Why don't you return that money?"

Collins was referring to Reid Hoffman, the billionaire LinkedIn co-founder and major Democratic donor whose past relationship with Epstein has drawn scrutiny. Hoffman has acknowledged meeting with Epstein after the financier's 2008 conviction for sex offenses and visiting his private island. Hoffman also contributed $7,000 directly to Ossoff's campaign and $1 million to a political action committee supporting the Georgia Democrat, according to previously reported campaign finance records.

Billionaire Reid Hoffman (left), a known former associate of Jeffrey Epstein, made contributions to the campaign for Sen. Jon Ossoff (right), D-Ga., and to a PAC opposing Ossoff's challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Ben Hendren/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Earlier in the debate, Collins went further, accusing Hoffman of sending Epstein ice cream with a message referencing girls, while again pressing Ossoff to reject his financial support.

"Jon Ossoff, his number one donor, one of his largest donors, is Reid Hoffman, the same guy that's in the same files, the same guy that sent ice cream, ice cream to Jeffrey Epstein on his birthday and said, 'This is for the girls,'" Collins said during an earlier exchange in the debate.

THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE'

The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Hoffman sent Epstein ice cream in 2014 with a message indicating it was intended for him or "for the girls." Hoffman has apologized for his association with Epstein, which he said stemmed from fundraising activities involving the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and has not been accused of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein's crimes.

Ossoff rejected the Hoffman comparison, however, arguing that the allegations against Collins involved someone living in the congressman's home rather than a political donor.

"Mike, if any of these folks were based in my house, then I'd understand you to ask me to take responsibility for them," Ossoff said. "What I asked you, Mike, was, can you commit for just three weeks to stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from your home?"

Earlier in the debate, Collins was directly questioned about concerns from Black Georgians over allegations of White-nationalist ties involving members of his political operation.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., condemned Hasan Piker's latest remarks about antisemitism and American Jews' support for Israel. (Ben Hendren/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.

“That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said.

The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years.

The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock.

Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX.

Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime.

Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers.

Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have been operating continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity 24/7.

To hit its cost targets, Ambrosia has been finding ways to simplify its components, including solar mounts and battery packs. By reducing part counts, and manufacturing many components in a factory, the startup has been able to reduce costs relative to buying from outside suppliers.

“We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. ”We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems.”
