(Photo by Mary Rooke)

Welcome back to Good Life, a newsletter about navigating our modern culture and staying sane in the process. This week, we talk about the importance of standing alone, even if it costs you a lot.

Enjoying this newsletter? Share it with your friends and family! And if you’re one of those friends or family members, you can sign up to get your own copy every week right here.

Last week, my husband and I spent time hunting elk in Idaho. There is so much to witness and experience on a trip like this that you will probably see me unpacking it over the next couple of newsletters. But one point stood out to me immediately on the first hunt as we made our way up the ridge.

This was only our second hunting trip in Idaho, and we still didn’t know the mountains well enough, so we had a guide. As my husband pointed out, there’s no sense in getting lost in the woods just to prove a point. Especially not when four daughters are patiently waiting for us to return safely.

If you’ve ever hunted before, you know it’s important to get to your spot before the sun comes up and the animals start moving around. You want to try to blend in with the natural surroundings as best you can so they don’t stay hidden behind tree lines and feel comfortable exposing themselves. As my husband and I sat on top of a ridge glassing for elk, I noticed the pine trees seemed to bunch together in groups. There were so many on the opposite ridge from us that it was as if their seed hadn’t missed a single spot on the ground. It was a mini forest.

But right smack dab in the middle of this pine-tree eternity stood a break, with a single pine in the gap. I knew I was supposed to be looking for elk. By this point, the morning sun had peaked over the ridge behind us, spotlighting the side we thought the elk would be traveling on. When the sun hits their bodies, they shine like gold dots against all that green. But I wasn’t exactly doing my job. I had become distracted by the single tree by itself, and the thought wouldn’t leave my mind that sometimes I feel like that lonely tree.

Politics is a team sport in many ways. You find your side of the aisle, and camaraderie naturally forms between your like-minded friends. It can help, especially in times like these, when doing the hard work means swimming against the current. But it can also be an incredibly lonely experience that, if you aren’t strong enough, can make you second-guess how you see the world.

I think specifically about the immigration debate and how far we’ve come in talking about it. Even just two years ago, I couldn’t write about the perils of legal immigration without my side of the aisle balking. They’d tell me that our country needs immigrants and that it didn’t matter if communities were changing because their presence uplifts the national economy. This point has always particularly angered me. Keeping a shared heritage should be the ultimate goal of any policy decision.

Sometimes I feel like I’m the only one who sees what I see. The dangers or the potential of different policy decisions. And like that tree, I stand alone, unnerved by the forest staring back at me. I’ve never been someone who backs down easily from a fight I think is just. My opinion, once set, is not easily changed. This is an admirable quality I think more people should embrace, but it comes at a cost. People will misunderstand your point, seemingly on purpose. They’ll attack you and magnify your loneliness. You have to be willing to weather the storm on your own until other trees find their way to you.

Now, Vice President JD Vance openly discusses the abuse of specialty visas, and my comment section is filled with people calling for the programs to end. On this, I’m no longer the lonely tree.

Just as I was getting lost in this thought, a fleck of gold peeked out behind a tree. All three of us turned our sights on the sparkle. It wasn’t an elk, just a tree stump catching the light as the sun rose higher.

“It can be like hunting ghosts,” our guide whispered. We all let out a soft chuckle at the truth of his words and went back to our silent reflections.

Almost immediately, I looked for that lonely tree again. I hadn’t finished processing it and wanted more time to work through my thoughts. That’s the funny thing about hunting. You can sit in the same spot for hours waiting to see something. It gives you a lot of time to think about life and how you want it to go. It’s important to have time to reflect. You can plan course corrections and build protections in your mind while everything is still. We don’t have many opportunities in our instant-connection society to do this anymore. That’s part of why I love it so much.

Ironically, on top of the ridge is one of the few spots where I got cell service. It was just strong enough to get intermittent messages but not enough juice to reply. Almost as if by divine design, I received an email response from a reader who had just finished my latest newsletter on absentee grandparents. It only partially loaded, but I could see the preview started with “Great Column,” and I smiled and put away my phone. The ones that get it truly do. The ones that don’t often lash out because they are hurt by how it magnifies their faults.

I started thinking about how it was yet another example of being the lonely tree. I’m happy in that spot, reflecting on that tree. It helped remind me that it’s okay to be the only one who sees. It won’t last forever. More and more people will realize what’s happening and come over to stand next to me. I made a mental note to talk to our girls about this when I get back. I want to raise them to be willing to stand in the gap between the aisle. Not as a moderate trying to appease both sides, but as a lone tree ready to withstand the storm and do what is right, even if it means standing alone.

Nithya Raman claimed she was in a “fugue state” and could barely remember her own mayoral debate with Karen Bass — just moments after the Los Angeles challenger spent the night dodging questions about her plans for the LAPD.

The challenger made the remark in a bizarre interview with NBC4 just moments after leaving the stage in Universal City on Tuesday night.

“I’m so sorry but I was in fugue state and I don’t remember very much of it at all,” Raman told NBC4’s Robert Kovacik in a bizarre interview moments after Tuesday night’s debate in Universal City.

The remark came after a bruising showdown in which Raman refused to commit to a timeline for firing LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell, prompting Bass to accuse her rival of being unprepared to lead the nation’s second-largest city with the 2028 Olympics looming.

Asked directly whether she would replace McDonnell before the Games, Raman repeatedly refused to give a deadline, insisting the decision depended on other city bodies.

“I wanna replace the police chief. I’ve been very open about that. I’ve been very clear about that,” she said, arguing that McDonnell had lost the trust of Angelenos, particularly over his response to federal immigration raids.

But when NBC4 political correspondent Conan Nolan pressed her on whether she would make the move before the Olympics, Raman again hedged.

“It will depend on these other factors, on other decision-making bodies,” she said.

Bass shot back that firing the chief was within the mayor’s power and warned that a leadership shake-up could disrupt preparations for the Games.

“The problem is that you [Raman] have a tendency to take different positions on different days of the week,” the mayor said.

The incumbent’s top City Council ally, Monica Rodriguez, piled on after the debate, accusing Raman of misleading voters about her authority over the police department.

“That’s nonsense,” Rodriguez told reporters when asked about Raman’s claim that removing McDonnell would require cooperation from the Police Commission and City Council.

“It clearly means that she has no idea the power of the mayor’s office,” Rodriguez said, accusing the challenger of telling different audiences what they wanted to hear.

“She’s intentionally, I believe, trying to mislead the public.”

The rivals also traded blows over homelessness, housing costs and city spending. Raman accused Bass of being “MIA” during Los Angeles’ biggest crises, while Bass questioned whether her challenger could manage the city and prepare it for the Olympics.

“If you cannot manage the work of your committee, how on earth are you going to manage the second-largest city in the country?” Bass asked.

Raman took just two questions from reporters after the debate, while Bass had Rodriguez field questions on her behalf.

Then came the head-scratching explanation for how the debate had gone.

Asked to identify her strongest and weakest moments, Raman claimed she could barely recall the event.

According to the National Institutes of Health, a fugue state is a rare psychiatric condition involving unexpected travel away from a person’s usual surroundings, often associated with an altered state of consciousness and a desire to flee.

“Traumatic circumstances, leading to an altered state of consciousness dominated by a wish to flee, are thought to be the underlying cause,” the NIH website states.

Dr. Azita Sayan, a licensed family therapist with a PhD in psychology and CEO of Embrace Growth Inc., cautioned against using the clinical term as a convenient explanation for a difficult public appearance.

“My concern would be if it gets used as a political out,” Sayan told The Post.

She stressed that she could not determine from Raman’s brief remarks whether the candidate had experienced a genuine dissociative fugue, noting that people sometimes use the phrase casually to describe feeling overwhelmed or struggling to remember a stressful experience.

Clinically, however, dissociative fugue involves more profound disruption, potentially including significant memory loss surrounding a person’s identity or personal history.

“Imagine finding yourself somewhere unfamiliar and being unable to remember who you are or how you got there,” Sayan said.

People experiencing the condition may appear outwardly normal while struggling with confusion about their identity, she said. Some may even assume a different identity, although not everyone loses all memory of their past.

The American Psychological Association classifies dissociative fugue as a feature of dissociative amnesia rather than a separate diagnosis.

Sayan questioned whether that description matched what Raman had publicly described.

“In this case, the person knew who they are, they knew where they were,” she said. “They didn’t forget their identity.”

Still, Sayan emphasized that Raman’s choice of words was not enough to draw a clinical conclusion.

“What I would want to ask Nithya Raman is, what does she mean by a fugue state?” she said.

Sayan acknowledged that overwhelming stress or trauma can precede the condition, but said the phrase can also be used to explain a mistake or an answer someone struggles to defend.

“It could also be an excuse,” she said.

Her broader concern was that invoking a psychiatric term as political cover could undermine people who genuinely experience the condition.

“Then if someone genuinely has a problem, then we no longer believe them,” Sayan said.

It remains unclear whether Raman has ever been diagnosed with the condition or whether her post-debate remark was flippant.

The comment quickly drew fire online. An account called No Show Nithya mocked the challenger, posting: “Ah yes, exactly what we need, a mayoral candidate who blacks out when she gets stressed. That’ll go really well.”

Others defended Raman, arguing that she at least stayed to answer questions after the debate.

“No one blanks out when stressed better than Karen Bass does. At least Nithya took questions after the debate. Karen had to run and hide as usual,” one X user wrote.

The extraordinary exchange added another twist to a mayoral race entering its final stretch. Raman, once a political ally of Bass, upended the contest in February when she announced her bid to unseat the incumbent.

Bass has never lost an election during a political career spanning Sacramento, Washington, DC, and Los Angeles.

It has been two full years since the Trump administration outlawed “diversity, equity, and inclusion” policies (DEI) in federal government hiring and contracting rules. How much has changed?

In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court found “race-conscious” quota systems in place at Harvard University and others were unconstitutional. In his first days in office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration ended what it called discriminatory DEI programs in federal contracting and hiring practices. Simultaneously, the Trump administration began reviewing federal funds that had gone to universities where quota systems ensured a minimum enrollment of black students and other “underrepresented” people.

Two years on, how are these hotly contested changes progressing?

“I remember an interview with Harmeet Dillon, who’s with the Trump administration Department of Justice’s Office of Civil Rights,” says co-host Eric Eggers on the most recent episode of The Drill Down. He quotes her as saying “Look, one thing we’re committed to doing is playing offense on civil rights.” “And nothing is more — pardon the pun — offensive to some people than the executive order Trump issued on day one, in which he directed the Office of Management and Budget to terminate federal DEI offices.”

DEI policies have been in place for many years but accelerated in the frenzied response to the George Floyd riots in 2020. They are an upscaling of previous policies known as “affirmative action” that have been around since before the passage of the 1964 Civil Rights Act.

The phrase “affirmative action” was coined in 1961 by a Black attorney named Hobart Taylor in John F. Kennedy’s administration back in 1961, pitched as a way to help minority job and college candidates who had previously suffered racial discrimination to get a leg up. Famously, as Schweizer recalls, it became less obviously a numbers game after the High Court’s Bakke decision in 1978 that outlawed direct quotas but did allow racial consideration in college enrollment.

Over the years, these programs expanded and widened, showing up in medical school enrollments and in military promotions. Schweizer notes that Trump fired the second Black Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who had declared he wanted to set racial percentage goals for fighter pilots.

“They wanted 67 percent white officers, down from 80 percent,” Eggers notes. “Seriously, it was the stated goal of the U.S. Air Force to get the number of white people in the military down.”

“They wanted 13 percent percent African American, up from 10 percent. They wanted 10 percent Asian, up from 8 percent, 7 percent ‘multiracial,’ and 1.5 percent Native American,” Eggers cites.

Schweizer doubts America’s adversaries are so fastidious: “I don’t know, XI Jinping might say, ‘Hey, we need more Uyghurs in the senior ranks of the Chinese military,’ but I kind of doubt it.”

In federal contracting, the Government Accountability Institute (GAI) has previously exposed corruption within the Small Business Administration’s minority set-aside contracting programs, finding that oftentimes those programs are ripe for corruption.

“We’ve all heard the stories about white guys who hire somebody of Alaskan heritage, give them fifty-one percent of the company so they can get minority set-aside contracts,” Schweizer says. “We’ve learned about those abuses.”

Still, the problems in those programs are that they create an ongoing constituency for continuing the DEI practices that these firms have profited under. “Let’s say you were one of those businesses who set up shop to pursue minority-only contracts,” Schweizer explains. “You would now be incentivized to want to keep the DEI practices in place because it limits the competition.”

Washington accumulated large numbers of such companies, competing for those set-aside contracts. “So, there’s huge financial incentive for people to have the old system to remain in place,” he adds.

How should people who don’t work for the government view this issue?

Even as the government has officially removed DEI policies, there are still plenty of large companies that are clinging to them. Costco, Apple Computers, and United Airlines still proudly commit themselves to race-conscious hiring and promotion efforts.

“United Airlines has a policy favoring [United Airlines] Academy candidates based on race and gender. CEO Scott Kirby recently reaffirmed the airline’s goal for ‘fifty percent of United Airlines Academy graduates to be women and people of color,’” Schweizer says. “Again, I don’t have a problem with whoever the pilot is, but when you say we’re going to fill slots based on their ethnicity, or their gender, rather than their skill set, that’s when I start to get a little a little jiggy.”

“This mindset of treating people differently based on their racial background or their sexual preference or whatever does have real implications, I would argue, when it comes to corruption and when it comes to enforcing the law,” Schweizer says.

He notes the recent raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home under a judicial search warrant obtained by the Department of Homeland Security. Omar has been controversial for her radical politics, but has also come under fire for questions surrounding how she came to be a naturalized American citizen and over irregularities in her required financial disclosure statements.

“The first thing she did was cry ‘racism,’” Schweizer says, before noting her ties to Somali fraudsters in the “Feeding Our Future” scandal in Minneapolis. “She has been ‘hands-off’ by federal law enforcement for a long time,” he says.

The Atlanta teacher who was killed after falling from the “Goliath” Six Flags ride was a member of a roller coaster enthusiasts Facebook group.

Hassan Kariem, 42, joined the public Facebook group “Roller Coaster Enthusiasts Club” on March 15 – seven months before his death at the Six Flags Over Georgia theme park.

The group, which was created 15 years ago, has more than 104,000 members and provides a space for amusement park enthusiasts to share their experiences of rides.

Members of the group have flooded the page with tributes to cancer survivor Kariem — with strangers describing the beloved family man as “one of our own” and a “brother.”

Kariem’s most recent role was as an IT manager at the Atlanta charter school Wesley International Academy – and a spokesperson said they were “devastated” by his death.

“Throughout his time at Wesley, Mr Kariem served as our IT manager, a technology teacher and a robotics coach, leaving a lasting impact on generations of students and colleagues,” they said.

“His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did.

“Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community.”

His cause of death hasn’t been made public and an investigation into the accident is underway.

“Goliath,” which is Georgia’s tallest rollercoaster, has been temporarily closed.

“We do not have an anticipated reopening date at this time,” Richard Pretlow, the Six Flags Over Georgia park president, said.

Kariem was on the ride with his niece when he was ejected from the ride.

Disturbing souvenir pictures were shared on social media – which appeared to show Kariem flailing upside down as riders screamed.

Many fellow riders ended up covered in his blood, and four others were injured.

“He didn’t fall directly onto us. He fell onto a girl two rows in front of us. He fell and hit the cart three different times,” one woman who was on the ride told 11 Alive Monday. “He was in our pictures.”

Parkgoer Logan Conner, who was riding Goliath with his fiancé, said the man “started levitating in the air sideways” as he tumbled through the air.

Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son before the accident, said Kariem fell headfirst back into the coaster.

Kariem was then ejected from the 3 ½ minute ride on its final turn, according to Mendenhall.

“It felt like slow-motion, but it happened in an instant,” he said.

“I was just praying in those moments. I was praying, ‘God, please let him stay in that car.’”

Summer Bates, who had rode the hypercoaster earlier Monday, also watched the fall happen.

“One thing I think that will stick with us is the sound of his body coming down,” the mom said.

openaustralia-funding-crisis:
Ben Fairless

OpenAustralia Foundation is running out of money. Unless more of the people who use our library start supporting it every month, we will have no choice but to begin an orderly wind-down of Planning Alerts, Right to Know, They Vote for You and OpenAustralia.org.au. While we can’t say exactly when this will happen, we are talking months rather than years.

I’m Ben, the CEO. I have been part of the foundation for over a decade, first as a volunteer and now on staff. For most of that time I was the volunteer administrator of Right to Know, and for long stretches the only one: keeping it running, answering the emails, and when an agency wrongly refused people’s requests, taking the complaint to the Information Commissioner myself. I believe deeply in what we do, and I know what this library means to the people who use it. I want to tell you what’s going on now, rather than have to write a farewell letter in a few months.

In short: donations have fallen, some of the larger organisations that paid us for data have gone, and keeping everything running is costing us more than ever. Together, this has created a perfect storm.

For those who don’t know us, OpenAustralia Foundation is a charity that runs a free, public online library of what Australian governments do. It is made up of four unique collections you use – likely without knowing they are connected:

Everything in the library is free. Everything in it is built on open source code. And we are strictly non-partisan: we don’t tell you what to think about a development, a vote or a document. We make sure you can find it, and help you effect the change you want to see in your community.

We are relied upon by journalists, content creators, councils, advocates, businesses, government and everyday people. A regulator recently used our collection to check whether government agencies were publishing what they are required to publish. Mostly, though, it is used by people who just want to know what is going on, and who have every right to.

If we are forced to close, the alerts stop. More than 142,000 active Planning Alerts subscriptions go quiet. More than 14,400 Freedom of Information requests and their responses on Right to Know, the voting record of every federal representative on They Vote for You, and more than 936,000 entries of Hansard on OpenAustralia.org.au lose the home that keeps them free and searchable. The software that gathers all of it from government websites every day stops running.

A large one-off gift helps enormously, and we welcome every one. What keeps a library like this open year after year is steady, predictable income so that our small team can keep collecting new information from hundreds of government websites every day, answer your questions, fix what breaks, and get on with the things we have wanted to build for years. We are not short of plans. We are short of the steady income that lets a small team carry them out. That is what monthly supporters give us: the difference between building something and scrambling from one month to the next.

So, I’m asking you for one thing today: become a monthly supporter at $20 (or more) a month. $20 a month is about the cost of a coffee a week, and right now it is the single most useful thing anyone can do for this library.

If you already give monthly, thank you. You are the reason we are still here to write this. If you can increase your gift, that helps more than you might think. And if a one-off gift is what you can do, large or small, it is just as welcome.

If you can’t give, you can still help. Share this with one person who uses any of the collections. Tell your local paper, your council, your union, your community group. Most people who rely on this library have no idea it is run by a charity.

While we are a charity registered with the ACNC, at this time, donations are not tax deductible. We are actively working to change that, but we don’t know how long that will take.

We will tell you how this goes, honestly, either way. This library has been open since 2007. Whether it is still open next year is now, quite literally, up to the people who use it.

Thank you.

Ben FairlessChief Executive Officer, OpenAustralia Foundation

How ironic that the feminist labor movement that promised to liberate women may actually vitiate their happiness and undercut the successful work they hoped to find.

“The share of women in heterosexual marriages who make as much or more than their husbands has nearly tripled over the past five decades, according to the Pew Research Center,” The Washington Post notes this week. Another report from last year found that women now comprise almost half of managers in the United States, an increase of more than 50 percent from 1980, and one that is occurring across a host of professional categories. And, as was reported last month, women accounted for almost all new job hires in August.

Feminists laud this as an unqualified victory in the march toward equality in all things. But is it good for work? What we know about female leadership, and my own experiences as a manager, would suggest perhaps not so much.

“This has been beyond a doubt the best office I have ever worked in.” As a supervisor, the comment was an honor, but it was particularly remarkable coming from a woman in an office culture that was almost entirely male. My employee was a hard-charging, demonstrably successful young woman with a graduate degree from one of the most left-wing private universities in the country. She was not the only woman (or man) to express such a sentiment during my time as a supervisor in that particular position.

When I was part of an office leadership team that was almost exclusively male, the dynamics were about as antithetical to the stereotypes as you can get; indeed, a significant body of research shows there is little-to-no difference in abusive male versus female supervision. There was no “toxic masculine” chest-thumping, nor was there any sexual harassment or innuendo. There was no observable favoritism toward certain men. All the male managers were family men, though apart from me, none of them were particularly religious. All of us had served in either Afghanistan or Iraq.

Without a doubt, this male-dominated leadership fostered a result-oriented, assertive, competitive, and risk-tolerant environment whose successes made it the envy of other teams in the organization. As Doug Barry and Daniel O’Connor observe in their recent book First Line of Defense, “Men are fighters. … [They] were made for risk and adventure.”

That work environment was also, no surprise, not a particularly emotive or “chatty” work culture. Meetings were comparatively few and short, and managers voiced their annoyance with those incapable of getting to the damn point. Yet, also contrary to the stereotype, it was famously accommodating to those with family responsibilities. As long as the female employees did good work, no (male) manager ever questioned pregnant or nursing mothers who required time for medical appointments, pumping, or other maternal necessities.

So why did so many female employees — who, so the feminist narrative tells us, are suffering under patriarchal societal structures — tell my fellow male managers and me how grateful they were for what they acknowledged was a superior professional structure? Some of the reason was simply that my fellow male managers were decent men, the kind who recognize that while employees need professional challenges to keep them engaged, they also need to feel appreciated, respected, and free to have a fulfilled personal life. And, as many female employees told me, they were quite surprisingly not getting this when they were led by female supervisors.

Women, so the research tells us, are more nurturing, empathic, and communicative. One would think these would be unmitigated benefits in professional environments. In many cases, they are. But these qualities can also be a double-edged sword for the workforce, as qualities typically associated with women — including agreeableness, conflict avoidance, and risk aversion — are disadvantages for supervisors.

I certainly heard complaints from male employees about previous work cultures that were female-dominated, in which they felt excluded or bullied, feminist bosses seemingly having decided to direct all of their anger over supposedly centuries of patriarchal oppression on some hapless new male hire. But by far the most complaints I heard about female-dominated work came from women I managed. Women who had been pregnant or had little children told me their female bosses were less sympathetic to the various needs related to motherhood than male counterparts who seemed more willing to grant mothers some slack. They told me how they tired of cattish work cultures defined by inscrutably complex cliques.

The reason for this, as even recent research supports, has as much to do with a feminine overreaction to the “evil patriarchy” as it does with certain feminine qualities that prioritize personality and communication style and thus ostracize those who fail to navigate female-dominated social structures. Women who, for the sake of their careers, never had children or placed careers over their kids — research refers to them as “queen bees” — not only lack sympathy for those colleagues who do, but seem to punish them, perhaps because they feel the loss of not having kids of their own. This is likely aggravated by female leaders thinking they need to manifest male qualities such as assertiveness or hiding their emotions. One first-time nursing mother told me a previous female boss told her that if she wanted to have a successful career, she shouldn’t have any more children.

I have no desire to apply rose-colored glasses to a past, male-dominated work environment in which women were routinely subjected to derision and sexual harassment, nor to the obvious fact that men today remain just as capable of doing such terrible misdeeds when given the reins of power. Rather, my point is that men, because of various qualities more common to their sex, also possess the capacity for transformative, self-sacrificing leadership. As a sex, they are generally more able to overcome resentment and bitterness, to overlook slights, and to exemplify physical, mental, and emotional resilience. When properly formed, they can be inspired to what Teddy Roosevelt in 1899 called “the doctrine of the strenuous life, the life of toil and effort, of labor and strife,” willing to risk failure to avoid being labeled a “man of timid peace.”

As men’s influence over work wanes — especially as woke ideologues claim that “historic wrongs” demand a reverse, female-dominant workplace — I suspect we will see less of a utopia of so-called gender equality and more of a feminist dystopia, as essayist Helen Andrews last year provocatively warned us. Those workplaces will be more cliquish and more beholden to gossip and personal grudges. They will be defined by micromanagement, indecision, and an aversion to risk. And, counterintuitively, the attempt to exhibit masculine traits will make them less welcoming to women seeking a balanced family life and the freedom to be engaged, devoted mothers.

How ironic that the feminist labor movement that promised to liberate women to discover fulfillment and flourishing in a competitive career may actually vitiate their happiness and undercut the successful work they hoped to find.

HUNGARY’S RECENTLY ELECTED government has voted to get rid of legislation that discriminated against the LGBTQ+ community under the leadership of former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán.

The new centre-right government that beat Orbán’s party in April elections, ending his 16-year tenure, has unravelled a law that significantly restricted the visibility of LGBTQ+ people in media.

Hungary has faced international pressure in recent years over its treatment of LGBTQ+ people, including from the European Union’s Court of Justice and Irish activists and politicians.

In 2021, the Hungarian parliament under Orbán passed legislation to restrict the visibility of LGBTQ+ content, embedding into law that only over-18s should be allowed to engage with information and media that pertains in some way to LGBTQ+ people.

The law had numerous ramifications, like forcing bookshops to take books for children or teens that included characters who were LGBTQ+ off the shelves or wrap them up in plastic.

One of the country’s bookshop chains, Líra Könyv, was fined $34,000 (€30,000) in 2023 for failing to wrap up “Heartstopper”, a popular book-turned-Netflix hit featuring a relationship between two teenage boys.

The new parliament has today voted to amend the legislation to protect minors from material that can “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development”, removing the specific ban on LGBTQ+ information.

The Orbán government also passed legislation in 2025 restricting freedom of assembly, which it used alongside the LGBTQ+ content prohibition to ban last year’s Pride parade in Budapest.

The Journal visited Budapest in July 2025 to report on the anti-LGBTQ+ politics in Hungary – and how there was still a vibrant community in the capital holding events and working together despite the efforts to push them to the margins of society.

Budapest’s Pride parade went ahead in the face of the government’s attempted ban and threats to prosecute participants and organisers, amassing its largest-ever crowd.

When Stephanie Zebrowski retired and started collecting Social Security in 2018, she was able to get by on her monthly payment with a little left over before the next one arrived.

That’s no longer the case. Zebrowski, who worked as a financial editor at a brokerage firm, now finds that the $2,200 monthly payment she receives (after her Medicare premiums are deducted) has not kept up with inflation in recent years. That’s forced the 75-year-old to drain her savings to pay for essentials – such as groceries, gas, doctors’ visits and utilities – and make some unpleasant decisions.

Zebrowski, who once considered herself middle class, started visiting a food bank last year and keeps her home colder than she’d like in the winter, even though it aggravates her arthritis and leaves her in pain. She’s had to start creating meals “out of practically nothing,” adding that she’s “learning to like beans.”

“I’m strapped every month,” said Zebrowski, who lives in rural Jefferson, New York. “I’m spending almost every penny. It didn’t used to be that way.”

Like Zebrowski, many senior citizens are finding that their Social Security benefits are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living, especially in recent years. The payments are adjusted every year based on inflation, but many older Americans and their advocates have long said that the annual cost of living adjustment (COLA) formula doesn’t match the actual increase in expenses.

This year, the bump was 2.8%, or an additional $56 per month for the average retiree, who receives $2,071 a month. But a $17.90 increase in the standard monthly Medicare premium – the second-largest hike, in dollar terms, in the program’s history – to $202.90 ate into that raise.

Is Social Security keeping up with your cost of living? Share your story

The 2027 monthly adjustment, which is scheduled to be announced on October 14, could be around 3.5%, based on early indications. That would provide a retiree with around $72 more a month. But the benefit boost won’t go that far when the price of gas, beef, healthcare and other needs have soared, Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security policy analyst, told CNN.

“The inflation we have had in recent years has not gone away. It has not disappeared completely,” she said. “It just heated right back up again with the war in Iran.”

(Medicare’s standard premium is forecast to increase $6.60 a month for 2027, according to the program’s trustees.)

Social Security benefits have lost 13.7% of their buying power over the past decade, according to a recent analysis by The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group. Put another way, a dollar of benefits in 2016 is only worth 86 cents today. That’s taking into account increases of 5.9% in 2022 and 8.7% in 2023 when inflation skyrocketed after the pandemic.

Payments would have to jump by nearly $296 a month, or about $3,550 annually, to restore their buying power for the average beneficiary, the analysis found.

Many older Americans depend on Social Security for a large portion of their income and can’t easily adjust to higher prices, Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director, told CNN.

“Gas prices are going to be gas prices, right? You can’t substitute that. You can’t substitute your medications for something else,” Benton said. “These are things that there’s just no wiggle room for seniors.”

Lawmakers, advocates and think tanks have floated myriad ideas for changing Social Security’s annual adjustment, though they haven’t gone far on Capitol Hill. One proposal would shift the formula to an inflation index tied to price changes based on the spending patterns of senior citizens, known as CPI-E. However, other measures would curtail the COLA as part of an effort to improve Social Security’s overall finances.

Pat and her husband, who asked that their last name not be used for privacy purposes, are both around 75. She said they had been able to make ends meet on Social Security and savings because her husband did some handyman jobs for their neighbors in their Florida senior community. But health issues forced him to stop this summer, leaving them dependent on credit cards to pay for groceries, gas, medical and dental care, medicine and other expenses. They used to pay off the balance each month but can no longer do so.

Big increases in home and auto insurance premiums over the past two years have added to their financial strain.

Though Pat said a 3.5% adjustment would be better than they’ve received in some prior years, it’s still insufficient to keep up with all the other cost increases.

“These little raises just aren’t enough,” said Pat. “We’re still trying to catch up from previous years.”

The couple, who receive a total of roughly $2,850 a month after Medicare premiums are deducted, estimate they are about $1,000 short each month, even though they cook at home nearly every night and don’t take vacations. A looming concern is the expiration of the interest-free period on their credit card early next year.

The next step is to sell some of their possessions, like her husband’s tools.

“There’s nowhere else to cut,” Pat said.

For Peter Jovanovic, Social Security’s annual increases never fully kept up with inflation. But the 69-year-old said his roughly $1,700 monthly check buys considerably less these days since “everything has gone up in price.”

A former truck and taxi driver who had to stop working in his early 50s for medical reasons, Jovanovic had been able to get by because he found a cheap apartment to rent in upstate New York. However, he was then hit with a big rent increase after being forced to move because of issues with his landlord. That left him thousands of dollars in credit card debt that he’s been unable to whittle down.

Though he’s now living in subsidized senior housing, Jovanovic is still feeling the bite of higher grocery prices and utility costs. He doesn’t own a car, and his friends have started asking him to chip in for gas when they drive him to the supermarket and on other errands. Taxi and Uber rides cost more, too.

The estimated 3.5% adjustment for 2027 wouldn’t do him much for him since “everything is so expensive,” he said. He thinks he’d get about $57 more a month.

“It doesn’t come close to what I need to live halfway comfortable, just to afford little things in life,” he said. “I don’t have any luxury stuff.”

HALF MOON BAY, Calif. — A pumpkin named Rocky won a major annual pumpkin-weighing contest in Northern California, tipping the scale at 2,389 pounds, but fell far short of a possible new world record set just days earlier in Rhode Island.

Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin across the country from Minnesota to win the contest for a fifth time. He’s going home with $21,501 in prize money after beating dozens of other giant pumpkin-growers in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco.

He missed out on last year’s contest because his pumpkin broke while growing. Hoping for a comeback story, he named this year’s pumpkin “Rocky” after the iconic boxer played by Sylvester Stallone.

“Five-time champion, that’s what we came here to do,” Gienger said following the win.

Meanwhile on Saturday, a new world record for the heaviest pumpkin appears to have been set by Ron Wallace of Greene, Rhode Island, at a contest in New England. His giant squash weighed 3,156 pounds — nearly the weight of three concert grand pianos. It hasn’t yet been verified by the Guinness Book of World Records, which lists a 2,857-pound squash grown by Ian Paton, of Lymington, England. That record had been set only a few days earlier.

“My hat’s off to him, that’s a big pumpkin,” Gienger said.

Gienger grows his gourds in his backyard pumpkin patch in Anoka, a city on the banks of the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis, according to Ronan Fowler, the competition’s organizer. This year, Gienger had to deal with temperatures that dipped below freezing, and he says that in order to start competing more seriously, he’ll likely have to start growing pumpkins in a climate-controlled environment.

“The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable,” Fowler said.

Gienger and his family drove 35 hours over the weekend to get the pumpkin the size of a small car to California.

Hundreds attended the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off to enjoy food trucks, music, and pumpkin-related jokes. Earlier in the day, the crowd went wild when a very symmetrical pumpkin named Tinkerbell won the prettiest pumpkin contest.

The prize money was calculated at $9 per pound of pumpkin and Gienger’s winning gourd will be showcased during a parade through Half Moon Bay this weekend. Gienger missed out on an extra prize of $30,000 for breaking the world record.

Sadly, these giants are grown for their size, not flavor, so there were no giant pumpkin pies at the end of the festival.

Parenting requires a lot of learning on the job. Raising a 7-year-old, I’ve benefited enormously from the wisdom of teachers, psychologists and other caregivers who have taught me ways to navigate a minefield of tantrums and meltdowns.

The more I learn about how to help a little kid through big feelings, the more I realize I need these strategies as much as my son does.

Adults often get so wrapped up in the demands of everyday life that we don’t recognize when we’re struggling emotionally, Dr. Jessi Gold, chief wellness officer for the University of Tennessee System and associate professor of psychiatry at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences in Memphis, told me. “We are really focused on the task, not the person doing the task.”

Parents teach their kids that their feelings are valid and treat them with compassion, she added, “but we don’t do that to ourselves.”

So I’ve started stealing these parenting tricks for myself — and you don’t need to be a parent to make them work for you.

A time-out is usually used as punishment, but I submit it can also be a gift you give yourself. When I am feeling overwhelmed — usually because my kid is asking more of me than I can deliver in the moment — sometimes the only way to keep from yelling, “Could everyone just shut up?!” is to remove myself from the situation. I send myself to my room.

Being a parent is hard work and ‘massively inconvenient.’ Dr. Becky Kennedy offers 5 tips to help you cope

It’s a “preemptive time-out,” Gold told me. Stepping away from the thing that’s causing the extreme stress or emotion gives you a chance to cool down before saying something you might regret, she said.

When I can’t physically escape, saying something like, “I need a minute,” buys me time to collect myself.

I stole this one from a preschool handout intended to help pint-size pupils manage their outsize reactions. Young kids tend to respond to spilled milk-level challenges with DEFCON 1-level intensity. It wasn’t until recently that I realized I do the same thing.

Maybe I don’t scream and cry and throw myself on the floor, but in my head I’m freaking out. I am inclined to sweat the small stuff, make mountains out of molehills, and let the perfect be the enemy of the good. I will obsess and ruminate and beat myself up for minuscule mistakes. Or spend a disproportionate amount of time and energy weighing a low-stakes decision.

Now I try to channel the wisdom of a preschool teacher and ask myself: Is this a big or little problem? If it’s a little one, I can address it quickly or maybe not, but either way I stop letting it rent so much space in my head and push myself to move on.

It is hard for a kid to switch from one thing to the next, whether it’s ending playtime to have dinner or putting on shoes to go outside. Transitioning from one activity to another commonly triggers tantrums, according to the Child Mind Institute, a mental health nonprofit. One way to forestall that is to offer a preparatory countdown. It can be something like: “Five more minutes of playing, then we’re leaving the park.”

We give kids structured schedules to make their day more predictable and make it clear what’s expected of them. We could give ourselves the same courtesy, Gold said.

What ‘gentle parenting’ does for your kids

I’ve recently learned (with the help of a therapist who specializes in ADHD) that I need a countdown clock of my own. I easily lose track of time, especially when I am focused on something, such as writing this article.

I’ll know, for example, that I need to leave work in an hour. Then I will look up from my screen to find that 75 minutes have passed. Experts call this “time blindness.” Now I give myself a five- to 15-minute warning (in the form of a calendar alert or phone alarm) before I need to wrap up what I’m doing.

It’s so simple and so profoundly helpful. There are several ways that slow, deep breathing can help diffuse stress. It can ratchet down the infamous fight-or-flight response, slow a racing heart, stabilize blood pressure, and stimulate the vagus nerve to trigger the part of your nervous system that makes you feel relaxed.

Whenever my son gets worked up, my go-to move is to tell him to take three deep breaths and count to five. You fell down and skinned your knee? Oh no, let’s take three deep breaths. You’re on the verge of a tantrum because I turned off the TV? Three deep breaths. Nervous walking into a new classroom? I hear you, dude: three deep breaths.

I’ll slowly inhale through my nose and exhale through my mouth to show him what I want him to do. Secretly, I am also trying not to lose it.

Breathe better to live better: Why breathing is your superpower

There is a reason that parents of young children travel with snacks: We know that a hangry kid is a recipe for disaster. Yet I’ll run for hours on a cup of coffee during a busy day, then wonder why I feel unfocused, bedraggled and downright grouchy. It could be burnout or a migraine or the patriarchy — or I might just be dehydrated.

“Our physical health is integrated very much into our mental health,” Gold said. If you don’t eat, drink or sleep, “you’re going to be meaner and crankier, and you’re going to cry when you don’t expect it, just like your kids would.”

It is amazing what a glass of water and a handful of pistachios can do. If only we all had a mom with a purse full of snacks to help us through the day.

Pamela Atkinson, a tireless advocate and organizer for Utahns who needed help — children, the elderly and people dealing with poverty — has died.

Atkinson died Saturday, according to Fox 13 News. She was 93.

Over her long career speaking out for people in need, Atkinson was often called — by former Gov. Gary Herbert, among others — “Utah’s Mother Teresa,” referring to the Catholic nun who ministered to the poor in Kolkata, India. It’s a comparison Atkinson once said embarrassed her.

“I don’t feel like a Mother Teresa,” Atkinson told a Salt Lake Tribune reporter in 2001. “I feel like I’m just an ordinary person who’s gotten some things done.”

(Ryan Galbraith | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson loads groceries for preparing Thanksgiving meals to the homeless in 1999.

(Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson makes her way to a lecture at Judge High School in 2001.

(Ryan Galbraith | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson plays games with her grandchildren Nate, Will, and Chase in 2001.

(Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson talks with a member of the unsheltered community in 2005.

(Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson joins others at Pioneer Park in 2005 for a candlelight vigil in honor of those Salt Lake residents who died while homeless over the last year.

(Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson waves while providing homelessness services to people in Salt Lake City in 2005.

(Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson speaks at the annual candlelight vigil for homeless Utahns who died in 2011.

(Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune)
Pamela Atkinson delivers a hot meal, boots and a warm coat to a homeless man who lives in a camp along the Jordan River in 2012.

(Chris Detrick | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson greets the Dalai Lama at the Huntsman Center at the University of Utah, Tuesday June 21, 2016.

(Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson, right, attends a news conference in Salt Lake City regarding homeless resource centers on Friday, Feb. 24, 2017.

(Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) Sharonne Zippel talks with Pamela Atkinson prior to a Shabbat candle lighting at the Chabad Lubavitch of Utah in 2019.

(Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Eva May Densley, carried by her mother Michelle, calls out for "grandma" after catching a glimpse of Pamela Atkinson while touring the YWCA Center for Women & Families in Salt Lake on Tuesday, March 20, 2018.

(Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Gov. Gary Herbert and Pamela Atkinson at the groundbreaking ceremony for Pamela's Place Apartments in Salt Lake City on Wednesday April 17, 2019.

(Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson at a temporary shelter as it gets ready to open for the night in Sugar House, Thursday, Jan. 23, 2020.

(Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson helps hand out warm meals as The Rescue Mission of Salt Lake serves their annual Thanksgiving Banquet as part of their ongoing outreach to help the homeless on Monday, Nov. 22, 2021.

(Rachel Rydalch | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson and Gov. Spencer Cox take a tour of Pamela’s Place Apartments located in Salt Lake City on  Tuesday, Feb. 15, 2022.

Atkinson — who in her career advised governors and mayors, and consulted with clergy across faiths — had three passions, she said: children, or “little ones,” as she called them; education; and helping people experiencing homelessness and poverty.

Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson posted a remembrance on X Saturday, saying that “Pamela has been an example to me of loving your neighbor unconditionally. Our state is in a better place because of her influence for good.”

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Gov. Spencer Cox followed Sunday on X with a statement that read in part: “There are angels on this earth — and yesterday, one of them went home. It is possible to make the case that Pamela Atkinson has had a bigger impact and done more good than anyone in Utah over the past 30 years. She was more than an advisor and confidant, she was a friend. She treated me the exact same way she treated her homeless friends — with love and respect.”

Senate President J. Stuart Adams, in a post Sunday on X, wrote that “Pamela didn’t just talk about service; she lived it every single day. She brought people together, inspired action and showed us the difference one person can make.”

In a statement issued Sunday, Utah House Democrats wrote: “Pamela Atkinson’s dedication to her community was remarkable. She worked with so many of us over the years, but what we’ll remember most is the kindness and respect she showed everyone she met. Our communities and our state are better because of her. We will deeply miss Pamela and the example she set for all of us.”

In 2001, just before she retired from her position as vice president of mission services for Intermountain Healthcare, Atkinson said that when she was in her 20s, a group of her school friends were talking about their various talents, from singing to crochet. When it was her turn to speak, Atkinson said she stayed silent — and another young woman said, “Pamela doesn’t have any talents.” The comment stayed with her many decades, and many accolades, later.

(Al Hartmann | The Salt Lake Tribune)
Pamela Atkinson delivers a hot meal, boots and a warm coat to a homeless man who lives in a camp along the Jordan River in 2012.

When author Sue Bender met Atkinson at a dinner party and was told of her work for people living in poverty, Bender blurted out, “Pamela, you are an artist!” Bender recounted this moment in her 2001 book, “Stretching Lessons,” which Bender, who died in 2025, said Atkinson inspired.

“I realized that Pamela sees the dignity in her homeless friends,” Bender told The Tribune shortly after the book was published. “Her art is her caring.”

One of her motivators, Atkinson said, was anger. What made her angry? “Injustice. When people are not treated fairly. Abuse,” she said. “If I’m angry about something, I darn well better do something about it.”

(Trent Nelson | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson speaks at the annual candlelight vigil for homeless Utahns who died in 2011.

Atkinson was born Pamela Collin in the London borough of Bromley, the third of five children. She knew poverty firsthand in her youth. Her father was a gambler who owned greyhounds for racing. He once sold the dogs and lost the family’s money, then left for good.

Her mother held menial jobs, but had no career skills, she said. She and her siblings survived on bread and potatoes, using newspapers as toilet paper. The kids slept three to a bed, with mice running around the house.

“It’s very hard going to school with people knowing you’re so poor,” she said in 2001, adding that she never invited friends home because “our house was horrible.”

After finishing high school — she was the only one of her siblings to do so — she traveled the globe, and spent a year as an exchange student in New York. She landed in the Bay Area, attending night classes at the University of California at Berkeley and San Francisco in the 1960s. She worked as a nurse to support herself, using credentials she earned at a London hospital.

She married and raised three children. She divorced, but remained on good terms with her ex-husband, she said.

She arrived in Utah in 1966 — and while she sometimes went back to England, she declared emphatically that “[Utah] is my home.”

(Ryan Galbraith | The Salt Lake Tribune) Pamela Atkinson loads groceries for preparing Thanksgiving meals to the homeless in 1999.

As an administrator at Salt Lake City’s LDS Hospital in the 1980s, one of Atkinson’s initiatives was holding a “teddy bear clinic,” to help children overcome their fear of seeing the doctor. She also helped organize mock disaster drills for doctors and paramedics.

Atkinson took on several positions at LDS Hospital’s parent company, Intermountain Healthcare, including director of its senior services, rehabilitation services and medically needy services. In 1990, she was promoted to vice president of mission services — a job created specifically for her.

The job, Intermountain’s senior vice president, Steven D. Kohlert, said at the time, was designed “to coordinate more effectively all of [Intermountain’s] charitable programs for the needy, the aging and the homeless.” Atkinson was “the ideal person” for the job, Kohlert said, “because of her long and active involvement with such programs.”

Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune
Pamela Atkinson, right, stands with political leaders in 2017 — from left, House Speaker Greg Hughes, Salt Lake County Mayor Ben McAdams, Salt Lake City Mayor Jackie Biskupski and Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox — during an announcement that Salt Lake City was dropping two of four planned homeless resource centers.

During her time at Intermountain Healthcare, Atkinson also was the only person to serve simultaneously on Utah’s three educational boards: the state school board, the higher education Board of Regents and the board of the Utah College of Applied Technology.

In 2001, in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Atkinson was one of the Utah civic leaders to take part in the “Alliance for Unity,” formed by billionaire Jon Huntsman Sr. and then-Salt Lake City Mayor Rocky Anderson. The group, in its formation statement, set a goal “to help people cross boundaries of culture, religion and ethnicity to better understand and befriend one another.”

(Trent Nelson  |  The Salt Lake Tribune)  
Pamela Atkinson speaks at the groundbreaking ceremony for Pamela's Place Apartments in Salt Lake City on Wednesday April 17, 2019.

The Salt Lake Tribune named Atkinson “Utahn of the Year” in 2005.

In 2019, Salt Lake City’s Housing Authority broke ground on Pamela’s Place Apartments, a 100-bed facility on the western edge of downtown, devoted to permanent supportive housing for people experiencing homelessness. Three years later, a homeless resource center in South Salt Lake was named for Atkinson. The Fourth Street Clinic near Pioneer Park also bears her name.

Her name also appears on the Pamela Atkinson Trust Fund, a state fund that pays for emergency services, housing and other support for people in need. Utah residents are given the opportunity to contribute to the fund on their state income tax returns, or when rounding up their purchases at state liquor stores.

When such honors were given to her, Atkinson often deflected the praise. At the groundbreaking for Pamela’s Place, she said, “Today belongs to the building, and what it is going to do for a hundred of our homeless friends who are going to take those steps out of homelessness right here.”

Information on Atkinson’s survivors was not immediately available. Memorial services are pending.

Correction, Sunday, 12:02 p.m. • An earlier version of this article had Atkinson’s age wrong.

Chris Detrick  |  The Salt Lake Tribune

The procedure will take place at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, with the operation set for the first days of this week, according to Vatican News. Holy See press office director Matteo Bruni told reporters the pope should need roughly a week to recover afterward.

A few weeks ago, I attended the Science Writers 2026 conference in Corvallis, Oregon.

After a pretty grueling 13-hour journey from New York City, we had finally made it to the Oregon State University campus. The journey involved a six-hour flight, a few hours of twiddling our thumbs at the airport upon arrival waiting for a coach, and a three-hour drive.

The weekend was filled with different science talks (from the ethics of artificial intelligence to recent research on GLP-1s) as well as sessions on practical skills, like how to incorporate short-form video into your work.

My favorite event was the closing ceremony, a panel discussion about reporting on the MAHA, or Make America Healthy Again, movement. Physician-journalist Jeremy Faust, nutrition researcher Kevin Klatt, and science journalist Tara Haelle led a conversation about the many difficulties of covering the intricacies of this topic.

They discussed the inherent trickiness of covering a movement that people define and understand differently, as not everyone is aware of RFK’s multi-decade promotion of vaccine hesitancy. Many readers still assume that MAHA is a well-intentioned move to promote healthier eating and living. Because of this, the speakers urged journalists to tie their reporting more directly to MAHA: Haelle highlighted that while many reporters are covering RFK’s policies, not everyone is tying their consequences back to the MAHA mindset directly, meaning readers do not always tie the two together.

Overall, the weekend was full of inspiring conversations and fun networking activities (including a wine and cheese tour of the OSU campus!). If you haven’t already been to the conference, it’s worth checking out!

Public Health

New research adds to a growing body of work illustrating the effect of gun violence on overall physical health.

Share

Research has consistently shown that cigarette smoking, chronic stress, and a sedentary lifestyle can speed up a person’s biological clock. A new study suggests that aging may also be accelerated by exposure to gun violence, a finding that exposes the hidden toll of trauma.

In a report published in the September volume of SSM-Population Health, researchers showed how exposure to deadly neighborhood shootings affected nearly 1,800 15-year-olds. They found that over half of the teenagers in the sample lived near at least one deadly shooting in the prior year, and those exposed to gun violence showed an estimated two-and-a-half-month difference in biological age acceleration and a 5.3 percent faster pace of aging. To measure for aging, the study’s authors used three highly regarded epigenetic clocks — biochemical tests that estimate a body’s biological age.

“It’s very easy for folks to say, ‘Well, this doesn’t directly affect me and doesn’t directly affect a lot of people,’ when in fact, we know from studies like this — and many that preceded this — that those early life exposures, where living in close proximity to where an incident of gun violence happens, can have real long-term implications for young people as they age,” said Julia Fleckman, an author of the study and an associate public health professor at Washington University in St. Louis.

To assess the adolescents’ exposure to gun violence, the researchers used survey data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study, a long-running longitudinal study of nearly 5,000 children born between 1998 and 2000. They defined neighborhood-level gun violence as the number of fatal shootings within one mile of respondents’ homes in the prior year.

Nandita Somayaji, a doctoral student studying public health at Johns Hopkins University, led similar research published in 2025 that looked at the association between neighborhood gun violence and children’s general health status.

“Their study complements ours,” said Somayaji. “What I really took away from that was they used different data, different methods, and different ways to measure the outcome, but we’re seeing that same pattern that proximity to gun violence affects children’s health trajectories, even without the direct victimization.”

Somayaji and her colleagues found that children living in census tracts with more gun violence were 20 percent less likely to report excellent or good health compared to their peers living in communities with fewer shootings.

“Kids who live in these neighborhoods who hear gunshots, see the police tape, know a friend who unfortunately died or got hurt by gun violence — they’re really absorbing that stress, even though they’re not physically harmed,” Somayaji said.

The new study revealed that Black and Hispanic teens were more likely to be exposed to gun violence and experience a higher intensity of violence, which Fleckman emphasized is more indicative of structural forces rather than biological markers. Gun violence exposure at a younger age in marginalized groups has also been linked to higher rates of emotional distress and adverse mental health, which is associated with accelerated aging.

“By isolating and weighting against essentially different characteristics, and taking out race, all kids that had exposure to gun violence were at increased risk of accelerated aging,” said Fleckman, who is also a director of Washington University’s Center on Violence and Health. “So that helps tell you that it’s not something genetic, but It’s about the exposure to the stressor.”

As gun violence remains the leading cause of death for children and teens, researchers are examining how these deaths will negatively affect the younger generation’s health in the future. Adolescence is a particularly vulnerable period for exposure to trauma that can affect the longer-term trajectory of a person’s life.

“We often talk about the acute, direct effects of gun violence like firearm fatalities and we talk a little bit less about the thousands of non-fatal gun injuries in the U.S. and how those can have life-changing implications,” said Esther Lee, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Michigan’s Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention.

In 2025, Lee published a study that looked at the connection between cardiovascular death and gun violence among adults in Michigan. Her study found that each additional 10 firearm incidents per year within a census tract was linked to a 1.6 percent increase in the odds of stress-related cardiovascular death among residents.

“We talk even less about the downstream implications of gun violence when people are exposed to it in their communities,” Lee said. “So what’s interesting is that these sorts of studies are evidence that violence is physiologically embedded … which helps to understand some of these broader impacts of firearm injury, and to lay some of the fertile grounds for that.”

Economy

October 11, 2026

Finance ministers and central bankers are gathering in Bangkok for IMF and World Bank annual meetings amid renewed global inflationary pressures.
The Iran war has driven Brent crude roughly 30 per cent above prewar levels, with the Strait of Hormuz's partial closure disrupting energy supply chains.
The US Federal Reserve entered a new tightening cycle in September, with traders anticipating three further rate hikes by July 2027.
Low-income countries face a compounding crisis of higher borrowing costs, slower growth and shrinking aid flows, with multilateral institutions mobilising billions in emergency financing.
"We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries," said a senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative.

The world’s finance ministers and central bankers are set to gather for this year’s IMF and World Bank annual meetings as a new set of inflationary drivers descends on the global economy.

This year, representatives from the IMF and World Bank member countries will meet in Bangkok, Thailand, from Monday. The meetings are typically held in Washington for two consecutive years and in another member country every third year. The 2029 annual meetings will be held in Abu Dhabi.

During the meetings, the Bretton Woods institutions’ board of governors hold discussions on how international monetary issues should be addressed, while other talks are held on emerging economic trends and regional programmes.

World Bank says Middle East economy to contract 2.1% in 2026 due to Iran war

This year's meetings come amid a renewed threat of inflation. Supply disruptions from the Iran war are pushing up energy prices, with the Strait of Hormuz’s prolonged partial closure driving the price for Brent crude roughly 30 per cent higher than prewar levels.

The expansion of artificial intelligence is placing additional pressure on electricity demand, and the massive debt issuance it requires partially accounts for the recent rise in bond yields, also driven by the US national debt reaching $40 trillion.

The global economy is still grappling with the inflationary after-effects of the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Inflation has remained above 2 per cent in the US for more than five years.

“While this rise in inflation pales in comparison with what we saw in the immediate wake of the pandemic, it is large enough to be of real concern to central banks, many of whom hadn't wrestled inflation back to its target before this episode had begun,” Karen Dynan, non-resident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute, said during a round-table discussion on Tuesday in Washington.

Speaking in Singapore on Tuesday, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said the environment was right for most countries to adopt a “prudently hawkish” posture.

The US Federal Reserve, the world’s most influential central bank, entered a new tightening cycle in September after it raised interest rates by a quarter point. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan have also recently raised rates due to rising inflation. The Bank of England is expected to hike rates next month.

Meanwhile, US government borrowing costs have reached multi-decade highs. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, recorded a 24-year high this week. Bond yields in Germany, the UK and Japan are also on the rise.

Against this backdrop, Ms Georgieva suggested austerity was back on the menu for advanced economies.

“After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, populations have grown accustomed to state support. Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” she said.

The question persists whether the IMF and World Bank have done enough to support low-income and conflict-afflicted countries facing higher funding costs, slower growth and shrinking aid flows.

“We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries,” said Marina Zucker-Marques, a senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative.

Since the Iran war broke out at the end of February, the World Bank has pledged up to $60 billion in financing to help countries absorb the impact of the conflict's energy shock.

The African Development Bank Group has launched a $5.1 billion framework to offset the impact of the war's energy and fertiliser crisis on the continent. The Asian Development Bank said it is mobilising $4 billion in financing to help countries withstand the war's impact.

The IMF last week said it would provide non-financial support to war-torn Yemen, and reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that would unlock $1.21 billion for the country that is dependent on Gulf energy imports. Bangladesh has also requested a programme due to the war's impact.

“The international financial institutions are weathering these crises remarkably well compared to other multilaterals,” Rachel Glennerster, president of the Centre for Global Development, said during a webinar.

However, Ms Zucker-Marques questioned how eager low-income countries might be for more funding from the IMF, citing the fund's conditionality for programmes.

Ms Georgieva said in April that the fund expected at least a dozen countries, including several in sub-Saharan Africa, to seek new loan programmes to respond to the war's impact on energy prices and supply chain disruptions.

The US central bank's new tightening cycle is also expected to lead to higher borrowing costs for low-income countries seeking loans.

The Federal Reserve's rate-setting activity directly influences borrowing costs from the IMF, World Bank and other multi-development banks.

Traders anticipate the Fed will raise interest rates three more times by July 2027, according to CME Group data.

“A lot of people are talking about the bond yields, which is quite important for countries that have access to markets, but also we need to pay attention that the interest rate hike in the US is actually increasing the tide to all types of lending,” Ms Zucker-Marques said.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is the latest tech executive to offer lengthy thoughts on how AI safety might be improved.

In a Saturday morning post on X, Nadella wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” Nadella wrote, using the Trump administration’s preferred term for AI.

As outlined by Nadella, this approach “means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” as well as “externalizing controls and safeguards.” He also called for “every meaningful model action” to be documented with “tamper-proof human readable evidence,” and for systems where “an authorized person” always has the ability “to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he said. “Think of it like an emergency brake.”

Nadella’s comments come as leading AI companies acknowledge more and more incidents where they seemed to lose control of their models, and after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a plan for more cautious AI development.

Naperville leaders denied a data center proposed for the northwest corner of Naperville and Warrenville roads, but a subdivision of 262 townhouses at the same site could be on its way toward approval.

The city’s Planning and Zoning Commission on Wednesday night endorsed the proposal, called Townes of Naper Commons, which would occupy a 42-acre vacant site that formerly held a large-scale Nokia office building.

Commissioners voted 6-3 in favor of the plan from builder Pulte Homes — on a condition that the developer continue to work with city staff on a few kinks, including those related to parkway trees, buffering between the new townhouses and their neighbors and a concern about invasive species listed on a landscaping plan.

No one from the public spoke in favor of or against the townhouse plan — in stark contrast to the previous data center proposal, which drew long lines of speakers during a series of multi-hour meetings before the Commission and the City Council, ending early this year.

After the data center denial, project attorney Caitlin Csuk said the property owner specifically sought out potential buyers whose ideas aligned with the city’s comprehensive land-use plan.

Since 2022, the plan has recommended medium-density residential for the site, which lies slightly north of I-88, near entrance and exit ramps at Naperville Road and Freedom Drive.

Pulte’s plan for the Townes of Naper Commons calls for three types of townhouses — a flat-roofed style with the option for a rooftop deck, which Csuk called “uniquely designed for
Naperville,” a rear-loaded variety, and a traditional version with garage entrances in the front.

Units are expected to sell for between $515,000 and $680,000, Csuk said.

The subdivision is envisioned as an extension of another new residential development immediately to the north, called Naper Commons, which features about 60 townhouses and 160 single-family homes, also built by Pulte on former Nokia land.

“We believe this will be a compatible and cohesive use for this very important part of the (I-88) corridor,” Csuk said about the new proposal.

Several commissioners agreed and voiced support for the plan, which would require rezoning from an ORI designation for office, research and institutional uses to R2 for residential, as well as variances related to front yard setbacks, parkway trees and how building heights are measured. The City Council is set to consider these requests at a future meeting, also taking into account the Planning and Zoning Commission’s positive recommendation.

“I think this may be a huge complement to the I-88 corridor as the residential to support the businesses,” commissioner Mark Wright said about the plan. “To me, this actually becomes an
enhancement to the I-88 corridor.”

Commissioners who voted against the plan, however, said they worry that changing the zoning to residential may not be the best move economically.

“I’m concerned, are we giving away valuable land that could have a much better use down the road?” commissioner Tom Castagnoli said.

Commissioner Derek McDaniel, who also voted in opposition, along with Commissioner Judith Heather Mcgowan, said it’s best to maintain the ORI designation in order to balance commercial and residential development.

“It’s easy to vote ‘yes’ for residential development, but the easiest ‘yes’ vote isn’t always the best when it comes to long-term economic development for Naperville,” McDaniel said.

IKEA WILL NOT physically inspect furniture sold through its new second-hand marketplace in Ireland, instead relying on sellers to accurately describe the condition of their items.

The Swedish furniture giant launched the service on Wednesday, allowing customers to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea furniture directly with one another.

The move puts Ikea into a second-hand market already served by sites including DoneDeal, Facebook Marketplace and Adverts.ie, where its furniture has long been bought, sold and given away.

There are currently more than 8,300 furniture listings on Adverts.ie featuring the word Ikea, including more than 400 free items.

Among the items being offered for collection are old potties, egg chairs, lamps and cots.

Under Ikea’s new system, sellers are responsible for describing the condition of their furniture and uploading photographs of the actual item.

Products must be classified as ‘As new’, ‘Used’ or ‘Very used’, and all items must be fully functional.

Recalled or modified products, mattresses, appliances and food cannot be listed.

Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea UK & Ireland, told The Journal that the company reviews listings before they go live but does not inspect individual items in person.

He explained that only customers who have signed up to Ikea’s free Family loyalty scheme can sell furniture through the marketplace.

Payments are processed through the platform, with Ikea holding buyers’ money for 48 hours after they accept an item.

During that period, buyers can report products that are significantly different from their listings and seek a refund.

After the 48-hour window, disputes are generally left to buyers and sellers to resolve themselves.

From Billy bookcases to Kallax shelving units, Ikea furniture has long found new homes through Facebook Marketplace and Adverts.ie.

Unlike some resale platforms, Ikea will not take a commission from sellers at launch.

Instead, the company hopes to encourage customers to keep spending with Ikea by offering a 15% bonus to those who accept payment in the form of a digital refund card rather than cash.
