Lucas said the credit could also be used to purchase second-hand furniture through the company’s existing Buy Back & Resell service, as well as other products and food.

While buyer protection is currently free, Ikea’s Irish policy provides for a mandatory fee of 5% of the purchase price.

The company says this fee is waived until 1 January 2027.

As purchases are made from private sellers rather than Ikea itself, the usual statutory right to cancel an online purchase from a business does not apply.

Ikea says the marketplace is intended to extend the life of furniture and prevent usable items from being discarded.

However, the large number of Ikea products already being given away for free on second-hand sites highlights how some owners regard the furniture as something to dispose of rather than resell.

The company has also faced criticism over the environmental impact of its supply chain.

In 2024, Greenpeace linked seven manufacturers supplying Ikea to the destruction of old-growth and other high-conservation-value forests in Romania.

Ikea disputed aspects of the investigation and defended its timber sourcing standards.

Lucas said the company wanted to make it easier for customers to repair, reuse and resell furniture rather than throw it away.

“By helping customers buy and sell pre-loved Ikea furniture, we’re supporting a more circular approach to home furnishings and challenging the idea that furniture should be disposable,” Lucas said.

Ikea claims products sold through its marketplace are priced, on average, 60% below comparable new items.

The marketplace is available online to members of the free Ikea Family loyalty programme.

Barbara Kingsolver’s new book is a canny feat of art imitating art. Partita is about a pianist, Livia, looking back at her life and trying to understand what art means to her.

It’s structured the same way the composition from which it takes its name is. A partita consists of a series of dance movements, typically written for a solo instrument, that vary in pace and mood. All these parts must come together to form the whole. In much the same way, Livia and the reader must bring these movements together to achieve a sense of completeness and understanding.

Each chapter is named for the various elements common in musical compositions and they follow their moods and pace. For instance, the novel’s sarabande chapter is calm, reflective, or emotionally intense like it would be in a piece of music. In this way, the book doesn’t have a linear structure as various chapters serve as refrains (a rondo) or go back to the beginning (Da Capo).

The story alternates between formative events from Livia’s adolescence and early adulthood as well as the present when Livia is in her mid-40s. As the pieces come together, we see Livia as a whole. She was a prodigious young piano talent working hard to keep up her prestigious scholarship. She then gets pulled into the exciting world of an older trade unionist and starts questioning everything. In the present, she has become a middle-aged woman who is an inspirational local music teacher in Tennessee.

Our reviewer found Partita to be a virtuosic work that in its inventiveness creates a fascinating character study of a middle-aged woman’s life and relationships. This book is a testament to the importance of access to art and celebrates those who help provide it. In this vein, I really enjoyed the listening list of classical songs that Kingsolver provides to accompany your reading. This in itself is a quiet but lovely gesture, as our reviewer notes, “including [the reader] in a world that may feel out of reach”.

Partita by Barbara Kingsolver is out now

Another American who wanted us to questions our relationship to and how we consume art was Robert Ryman.

Ryman thought that “you cannot understand a painting by explaining something. You can only understand painting by experience”. And so, in his show, Robert Ryman: The Real Thing, at London’s Barbican you won’t find much information to go on. In fact, as our reviewer can attest to, there arnen’t even labels to identify the paintings.

Bringing together 68 works from the mid-1950s to the early 2010s, this is a show that demands your attention. There are a lot of white canvases, which if you glance over seem indistinguishable but you need to look closer. Every choice the curators have made – from the lack of information to the way the lighting is directed – forces the viewer to engage. This is a difficult show in a modern age where our brains refuse to sit still and I think it is a challenge many of us should take on.

Robert Ryman: The Real Thing is on at Barbican Art Gallery, London until February 28 2027

Read more:
      Robert Ryman: The Real Thing at the Barbican – these mesmerising paintings must be seen in person

If you’re looking for something a bit more traditional then you can catch Renoir and Love at The National Portrait Gallery. Now the title would make you think you might be confronted with rooms full of his kistch nudes, however, this show is more a celebration of life’s many loves – from a good catch up with friends and a dance to that wonderful feeling you get after a very good meal.

It is an ambitious show bringing together his breakthrough impressionist paintings  from the 1860s to 1880s. Our reviewer was in awe of Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) in particular. Getting to see this impressive, large painting, he described the experience of seeing it in the flesh as startling.

Renoir and Love is on at The National Gallery, London until January 31 2027

On the big screen this week comes the follow-up to The Social Network. The Social Reckoning shows a company and a CEO which have become very different beasts. There’s been a mutation of Mark Zuckerberg from awkward nerd (played by Jessie Eisenberg) to sinister billionaire CEO of tech conglomerate Meta (played now by Sucession’s Jeremy Strong). Meta is also now a company that in Zuckberg’s words sees itself as “post-government” and is doing untold damage to the world through social media.

The Social Reckoning is part of the growing genre of films about crusading journalists trying to break a big corruption story. Think Spotlight (2015) about Boston Globe journalists who uncover systemic cover-ups of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church. Here, we follow The Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and engineer Frances Haugen whose conscience drives her to whistleblow on some of the company’s most guarded secrets. Our reviewer thought it was remarkable, especially in how it reflects a world increasingly managed by Silicon Valley logic.

the-giant-power-of-tiny-parks:
Wesley Allsbrook

Anna Rogers3 hours ago

A velvety butterfly called the coastal green hairstreak once peppered the fog-capped hills of San Francisco. But then the city began to build out, and new structures fractured the jewel-toned insect’s native range. The butterflies were scattered into isolated populations, some only a few blocks apart—an astronomical distance for a creature that, over its lifetime, can venture only a few hundred feet or so from the native shrubs it depends on.

In 2007, when the species was nearly gone from San Francisco, a local nonprofit got to work on a simple solution: Create a butterfly highway between some of the scattered populations by adding more of the insect’s host plants. “We planted microhabitats wherever we could get—a swath of a triangle or a long stairway edge,” says Amber Mahlberg, executive director of Nature in the City, the organization leading the project.

It worked. Butterflies from previously isolated populations followed the breadcrumb trail and interbred, boosting their genetic diversity and odds of long-term survival.

Microhabitats like these are good for wildlife like butterflies, and they benefit humans, too: Mounting research shows that small green spaces could improve the health of people who live nearby. “Americans tend to think about [the] nature benefit from the great outdoors, our national parks,” says Kathleen Wolf, a University of Washington social scientist focused on urban greening. However, for both humans and other animals, ease of access tends to trump grandiosity. Over the past decade, scientists have found that when tiny green spaces are scattered across cities, their cumulative effects are greater than the sum of their parts.

Mini-parks can give migrating birds passing through urban areas a place to rest and feed, says Frank La Sorte, a Yale scientist who studies avian ecology and behavior. In a 2023 study, La Sorte found that cities studded with small parks have a greater number of bird species than those with just a few large parks.

As for human benefits, a 2026 study determined that Americans with easier access to parks had lower rates of obesity, high blood pressure, and diabetes. Advocates for mini–green spaces pointed to such correlations in their push for changes in the federal rules for parks funding, though many of the new grants approved in the name of environmental justice were promptly eliminated by the Trump administration, which dismissed them as “DEI.”

Federal and state governments have long prioritized bigger parks, says Will Klein, research director at the nonprofit Trust for Public Land. That can make it tricky to get the necessary funding to build small green spaces in park deserts. So the group developed a new metric to assess a park’s value: the “10-minute walk.”

The idea is that everyone in US cities should be able to stroll from their home to a public green space in 10 minutes or less—which the group estimates is currently not the case for one-third of Americans. More than 300 mayors have embraced the idea, and now almost every major US city has incorporated the “10-minute walk” into its planning criteria, Klein says.

As part of the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), Congress approved more than $1 billion for urban greening. “All sorts of organizations lined up, scrambled, put in grant proposals, were awarded funds, and were beginning to do the projects,” Wolf recalls.

“The thing with urban parks is that they’re not as isolated as they might appear.”

Just across the bay from San Francisco, home of the successful butterfly highway, the community of North Richmond secured some of those much-needed dollars from another IRA program. During my recent visit, I could see why the community so desperately needed the funds. Amid a dense mix of residential and industrial properties, there were just a few public outdoor spaces. I saw two of them; one was a sports field and the other was called Landfill Loop, a former dump that, as far as I could tell from the prints in the dirt, isn’t frequented by anyone but raccoons.

In December 2024, through the IRA’s Community Change Grants program, North Richmond was promised $19 million to establish new green spaces, among other things, but the vast majority of that money never arrived. North Richmond, along with more than 100 other communities across the country, was left in the lurch.

In July, a judge ordered the Trump administration to pay out the grants, but the funding remains on hold while the administration appeals the ruling. Now, the work of micropark building often falls to nonprofits and volunteers.

That’s not so bad in high-income zip codes—like the ones the green hairstreaks needed to cross—where private resources for neighborhood improvement are often ample. It’s much harder in places like North Richmond, which is ironic, because these poorer communities tend to have plenty of neglected patches that would make for perfect tiny parks. Green spaces can slot into almost any oddly shaped, leftover parcel that no one knows what to do with. As ecologist La Sorte put it, “The thing with urban parks is that they’re not as isolated as they might appear.”

It could be the strip of dirt by some train tracks or a gravel-filled schoolyard or sometimes even guerrilla gardening on abandoned lots—a kind of living patchwork with the potential to transform an entire neighborhood.

Brilliant while stretched for four scoreless innings in Game 1, Taylor hasn’t fooled Guardians hitters since and allowed four hits and two walks without recording an out on Thursday night.

Michael Reaves/Getty

Share

This week was supposed to bring the White Sox clinching a postseason series win at home for the first time in 120 years.

“It sucks, you want to do that for the fans,” said second baseman Chase Meidroth after his club’s 9-5 loss to the Guardians in Game 4 of the American League Division Series. “We all wanted it so bad for the fans.”

But behind 18 runs and 17 walks allowed in two games to a Guardians offense that finished 11th in the AL in runs scored, but upgraded at the trade deadline in a way the Sox pitching staff was not, it won’t be happening. Not in this series, and without an about-face in two days, not this year at all.

“Certainly, that’s something that we wanted to give our fans,” said manager Will Venable. “I think we just want to win this series however possible, and wherever that is, we’ll take it.”

It’s fitting that an inter-division battle between Chicago and Cleveland, separated by a game in head-to-head matchups, separated by a game in the AL Central standings, is heading to a final showdown at Progressive Field. At least that’s how a quiet Sox clubhouse is rationalizing two deflating and lopsided losses in front of sold-out crowds.

“I got asked that yesterday and said we turned the page today,” said outfielder Sam Antonacci, asked about turning the page. “We turned the page, but we lost. So, we’ll turn three pages and hopefully win.”

Staff ace Sean Burke walked to the bullpen after the fifth, when the Sox held a brief 4-3 lead and it seemed like he might get the final outs, if Grant Taylor could hold the Guardians at bay. Instead he’ll be available for Game 5; a reason for confidence against a Cleveland team that needed a sixth inning to even register a hit against him in Game 2.

But Taylor did not hold the Guardians at bay, instead allowing all six hitters he faced to reach in a six-run sixth that assured a return to Progressive Field on Saturday. Anthony Kay had begun the inning and retired one of the three hitters he faced. Before him, stalwart rookie Hagen Smith walked the bases loaded and could not complete the first.

“Body felt good, stuff felt good, just didn’t execute,” said Taylor, downplaying workload concerns. “It truly was just execution. I walked two guys and they put the ball in play.”

With Burke at the ready, it’s hard to argue that the White Sox are fully out of pitching, or out of hope for knocking off an 85-win Cleveland team that has taxed their own staff, and asked presumptive Game 5 starter Gavin Williams to get the last three outs of Game 4. But it’s hard to figure what would look different if a Sox postseason pitching plan built on bullpen games was running out of gas.

Erick Fedde had the performances of a lifetime on Thursday, rescuing Smith from his first-inning jam, and keeping the Guardians scoreless until the fifth. A sold-out crowd dressed in black chanted his name in a way the 33-year-old former first-round pick had never previously enjoyed.

“Probably the most surreal moment of my career,” Fedde said. “Hard to put into words.”

Yet when Fedde departed with one out in the fifth, there was still more than half the game to go and not enough Sox arms to navigate it. There were also no answers left for third baseman Jose Ramirez, who looks rejuvenated after homering and driving in three to send the series back to Cleveland.

“Every guy will have their jersey on in the bullpen ready to throw [in Game 5], whether they feel good, whether they feel bad.” Fedde said. “I believe in these guys.”

Inspiring, but also a realistic view of what Sox pitching will be working from at the end of a series that’s stretched them to their limits.

Two Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in southern France last month have been found, and six people arrested, local authorities said on Friday.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the town that hosts the Renoir Museum, Bryan Masson, issued a statement praising investigators who tracked down the paintings and suspects.

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," Mr Masson said.

Mayor Bryan Masson addressed the press outside Musée Renoir after the heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The statement did not elaborate on how the paintings were tracked down.

The two missing paintings were Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well.

Police officers patrolled the front entrance of the Musée Renoir after the early-morning heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The thieves sliced through a fence, climbed through a window and initially stole four valuable Renoir paintings in the heist last month, but abandoned two of the artworks as they fled, authorities said.

Thieves sliced through a fence, grabbed 9 million euros worth of art, dumped half of them in a garden and escaped in under three minutes.

The whole operation took less than 3 minutes and targeted the most valuable works in the Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the regional prosecutor’s office said.

Investigators launched a national search for the perpetrators.

The theft conjured up painful memories of the spectacular heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France’s landscape.

Just weeks after the United States commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorists attacks, a new poll reveals more than one in five undergraduate students believe America deserved the attacks, while nearly half of all undergraduate students think physical violence is justified to stop so-called hate speech.

The Buckley Institute’s 2026 National Undergraduate Student Survey polled 803 American undergraduate students between September 5 and 14.

A shocking 22 percent agreed that America deserved 9/11, including 28 percent of liberal students. Notably, leftist streamer Hasan Piker — who campaigned with Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and cozies up to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani — has said America deserved 9/11. Meanwhile, Aber Kawas, a Democratic Socialist of America member and nominee for the New York state Senate, has said that America brought on 9/11 because of capitalism, alleged white supremacy and racism, and alleged Islamophobia.

The poll also found that 45 percent of American college students believe physical violence can be justified to stop hate speech — among which 54 percent of liberals agree compared to 30 percent of conservatives.

“Interestingly, 72% of those who agree that physical violence can be justified to stop hate speech also agree that hate speech is protected by the First Amendment,” The Buckley Institute found.

Shortly after Charlie Kirk was murdered on a Utah college campus for his free speech, a YouGov survey conducted from September 10-12 asked respondent whether they think “it is ever justified for citizens to resort to violence in order to achieve political goals?” Twenty-five percent of respondents who identified as “very liberal” said it can be justified, while 17% of self-identified liberals said the same. Just nine percent of people who identify as either conservative or very conservative said it was justified.

Meanwhile, a recent poll conducted by the Center for Strategic Politics found “Democrats want Trump out by (almost) any means necessary” — including assassination.

The Buckley Institute similarly found that support for criminalizing free — but offensive — speech has reached its highest levels in the three years that the survey has polled this question. Forty percent of college students agreed that “offensive speech should be subject to criminal prosecution.” Forty-seven percent of liberal students supported criminalizing offensive speech and was “the only ideological group among which a plurality agree with doing so,” according to the poll.

“This year’s survey demonstrates that censorious attitudes remain stubbornly high on America’s college campuses,” Buckley Institute Founder and Executive Director Lauren Noble said in a statement.

The study also found that college students have swung in favor of socialism. Forty-two percent of respondents would rather live under socialism compared to 28 percent who would prefer to live under capitalism. The Buckley Institute states that the 14 percentage point gap is the highest one in the five years the question has been asked. Notably, the same students who favor socialism over capitalism were more likely to support shouting down speakers they disagree with and violence to stop so-called hate speech, according to the study.

The same students who favored socialism were also more likely than students who favored capitalism to believe America deserved 9/11 and think offensive speech should be criminalized.

And, in America’s 250th birth year, only 65 percent of college students said they were proud to be American.

“Liberal students are the least proud ideological group at 62%, then moderates at 67%, and conservatives at 86%. Notably, men were 20 points more likely to agree that they are proud to be American than women,” the study found.

BOSTON — In 2010, Sandra Birchmore was a 12-year-old law enforcement fanatic enrolled in a police youth program in Stoughton, Massachusetts. A decade later, she was pregnant and dead — and the feds say it was one of the cops she idolized who groomed, abused and murdered her.

That disgraced officer, Matthew Farwell, is now finally slated to face trial over five years after her Feb. 1, 2021, killing — which was originally ruled a suicide.

But federal prosecutors say Farwell killed her and staged her death to look like she took her own life.

Jury selection has been underway this week in a Boston federal courthouse, with opening statements slated to begin Friday.

In the 10 years leading up to her alleged killing, federal prosecutors say Birchmore suffered prolonged sexual abuse beginning when she was just 15 from Farwell, a married man who allegedly used his authority to groom and sexually exploit the underage girl.

But by the time she was a 23-year-old woman, Farwell feared he was “losing control” over Birchmore, and when she claimed to be pregnant with his child, he allegedly strangled her in her Canton apartment, then staged the scene to make it appear that she’d killed herself, according to prosecutors.

And he allegedly did it all just hours before his own wife gave birth.

While both Birchmore and Farwell believed he was the dad, DNA testing after the deaths concluded he was not, according to the Boston Globe.

Farwell, now 40, was not the only cop accused of abusing Birchmore. His brother, fellow officer William Farwell, along with the director of the Stoughton police’s youth program, Robert Devine, were both accused by her family of sexually abusing her over the years.

All three officers have denied the allegations — though each resigned in 2022 as investigations were opened into their conduct.

Farwell, who faces one count of killing a witness or victim and one count of killing an unborn baby, is the only of the three who was criminally charged. However, the trio are all defendants in a wrongful death lawsuit by Birchmore’s aunt, which is currently on hold until the criminal trial wraps.

William, Farwell’s twin brother, is one of 68 people named on the prosecution’s witness list for the trial, which is expected to last between five and six weeks.

Farwell, who has been behind bars since his arrest, wasn’t officially charged with Birchmore’s murder until Aug. 28, 2024, as local authorities initially ruled her death a suicide.

Below is the full and fraught timeline leading to that moment:

2010 — Birchmore joins the Stoughton Police youth program

In March 2010, a 12-year-old Sandra Birchmore, infatuated with law enforcement, applied to join the Stoughton Police’s youth program, known as “Explorers,” according to an arrest affidavit.

Raised by her mother and grandmother, Birchmore grew up in a difficult household in Stoughton and dreamed of joining the police when she grew up.

That spring she enrolled in the Explorers program.

2012 — Farwell joins on as Explorers volunteer

Officer Farwell joined the Stoughton Police Department in March 2012, after serving with the Wellesley Police since 2008.

He signed on as an instructor for Stoughton’s Explorers program — which he had participated in himself as a teenager, the Boston Globe reported.

2013 — Farwell allegedly first assaults Birchmore

On April 10, 2013, the 27-year-old Farwell allegedly had sex with Birchmore when she was just 15, according to prosecutors. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is 16.

Investigators were able to pinpoint that date from skin-crawling text messages Farwell and Birchmore exchanged years later in 2020, in which she talked about how nervous she was the first time they had sex.

“Me too it was such a big day,” Farwell wrote, joking about how “If I pushed I absolutely could’ve f****d you without condoms from day one,” according to the affidavit.

The month after first having sex with Birchmore, Farwell married his wife.

“Farwell began to groom Birchmore when she was a child. This grooming culminated in Farwell raping Birchmore in April 2013, when she was only 15 years old,” prosecutors alleged.

2016 — Major changes for Birchmore and the Stoughton Police

Birchmore remained in the Explorers throughout high school. After graduating in 2015, she served two months in the US Army Reserve, before starting at Massasoit Community College in nearby Brockton, according to the Boston Globe.

The next year in May, her mother died at just 52, and the following month her grandmother died at 89.

Meanwhile, the Stoughton Police Department closed down its Explorers program after an internal probe found that its director, Officer Robert Devine, lied during an internal probe over allegations of harassment from a woman he was allegedly having an affair with. The program officially closed later that year over flagging interest.

The next year, William, also a former teenage Explorer’s member, joined the Stoughton Police.

2019 — Relationship continues as Birchmore sets her eyes on joining police

In 2019, Birchmore took and passed a Massachusetts civil service exam and became eligible to begin the process of becoming a police officer. That year, vile text messages appear to show that she and Farwell were still having sex — and that the police officer fantasized about her being underage when they did.

“Farwell and Birchmore exchanged text messages in which they discussed role-playing during their next sexual encounter. Farwell asked Birchmore how old she was going to pretend to be during that encounter. When Birchmore responded ’14,’ Farwell replied with a smiley face emoji,” prosecutors said.

“In another conversation between Farwell and Birchmore on February 21, 2020, Farwell described pinning Birchmore down during sex and asked her: ‘Will you say Matt stop I’m 13 I’m not ready for this omfg please stop,'” the affidavit continued.

Farwell also allegedly asked her to pretend he was an older brother coming into her bedroom to have sex at night. Other records indicated that he enjoyed choking Birchmore during sex, according to prosecutors.

2020 — Farwell begins “losing control” as Birchmore becomes pregnant

In October, 2020, Birchmore drafted a text message to Farwell’s wife disclosing that he’d been cheating “before you guys were even married,” but apparently did not send it.

That month, Birchmore learned Farwell’s wife was pregnant with their third child, and she began to threaten to reveal the affair unless Farwell impregnated her. Farwell agreed, but text messages from October and November showed Farwell was becoming resistant to the deal as Birchmore began saying she wanted him to be part of the child’s life.

On December 28, Birchmore told Farwell by text message that she was pregnant. The two immediately began to fight, and text messages from the next day seemed to suggest Birchmore was afraid Farwell was going to hurt her when they met to discuss the child, according to prosecutors.

But she reportedly told friends she was “over the moon” about the pregnancy, even as she confided that Farwell had been violent with her on numerous occasions.

February 2021 — Birchmore is found dead after Farwell visits her apartment

On February 1 at 5:33 p.m., Birchmore was seen on surveillance footage entering her apartment building elevator.

At 9:14 p.m., Farwell was caught on the same camera entering the elevator dressed in a hoodie and medical facemask. At 9:43 p.m., he was seen leaving the building, and his wife gave birth hours later.

Birchmore’s body was discovered after co-workers called in a wellness check on February 4. She appeared to have hung herself from a doorknob, and was wearing the same clothes she was seen in before Farwell arrived.

Her phone was also found next to her, and prosecutors said its last recorded movement was on February 1 at 9:40 p.m. — just minutes before Farwell left the apartment.

“Based on my review of the frequency of Birchmore’s phone use over weeks, months, and years leading up to her death, her failure to access her phone is inconsistent with her usual habits when alive and awake,” the affidavit read.

Farwell was interviewed by police two days after Birchmore’s body was found. He acknowledged going over to the apartment, but said it was to deny being the father of her child and to end the relationship, according to the Globe.

He was placed on administrative leave by the end of the month, and medical examiners ruled Birchmore’s death a suicide that May.

2022 — Farwells and Devine accused of heinous misconduct by Stoughton Police

Farwell resigned from the Stoughton Police on April 1, 2022. His brother, William, was put on leave days later and resigned by August while denying any allegations connected to Birchmore. Officer Devine that month also announced plans to retire, while also denying any inappropriate connection to Birchmore.

The next month, the Stoughton police released the results of a 19-month internal investigation which found the Farwells and Devine had “inappropriate” relationships with Birchmore, violated “human decency,” and “should never have the privilege of serving any community as a police officer” again.

By December, members of Birchmore’s family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the Farwells, Devine, the town of Stoughton, and the police department. That suit was put on hold last year to let the criminal case play out.

2024 — Birchmore’s death ruled homicide and Farwell is indicted

In March, Dr. Michael Baden — formerly the chief medical examiner for New York City — released the results of an autopsy he performed on Birchmore, which found that she most likely died by strangulation, and not by hanging.

He found that she’d fractured a U-shaped bone in her neck, that breaks “rarely, if at all, in suicidal hanging” but does in nearly “half of homicidal strangulation of women.”

On August 28, Farwell was indicted by the feds for Birchmore’s killing.

He’s been held at the Wyatt Detention Facility in Central Falls, Rhode Island, according to a report by The Herald News.

2025 — Feds hit Farwell with additional charge, opt out of seeking the death penalty

In October 2025, federal prosecutors hit Farwell with a second charge tied to the death of Birchmore’s unborn baby.

Then in December, then-US Attorney General Pam Bondi announced the Department of Justice wouldn’t be pursuing the death penalty against Farwell.

chatgpt-teens-safety-failures:
By

Rhitu Chatterjee

OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August, but a watchdog group that studied it recommends that people under 18 not use the artificial intelligence platform.
                
                    
                    Matt Cardy/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.

"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.

"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.

"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."

But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.

The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.

"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.

Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.

Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.

"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."

For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.

However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.

For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."

"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.

"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."

Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.

"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.

OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."

In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."

Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

EXCLUSIVE: American autism care providers who backed the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud are now sounding the alarm, warning that efforts to root out abuse could have unintended consequences after reimbursement cuts put therapy for Georgia foster children at risk.

The Autism Families Alliance, which describes itself as a national advocacy organization dedicated to supporting Applied Behavior Analysis providers and the families who rely on their services, said that efforts by the Trump administration and state leaders to fight fraud have gone too far, potentially leaving many of Georgia's children with autism in foster care without the care they need.

This warning is in response to a move by Amerigroup, the insurer that covers Georgia’s foster children through Medicaid, to cut what it pays autism therapy providers by 30%. Providers caution that they may no longer be able to afford to treat vulnerable children and that many foster families will be unable to switch them to another insurer.

"It's scary to see that so many different things are being slashed in terms of Medicaid, and that we're seeing this drastic outcome," Taylor Sanders, a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital. "It's so important that we keep in mind that children with autism are in a very vulnerable place where they're still needing to learn safety skills. There are some children who have extremely aggressive behaviors, challenging behaviors. So, when we're seeing some of these cuts, we're seeing it affect the providers who are able to provide access to these services."

AUTISM PROVIDERS CHEER TRUMP CRACKDOWN AFTER MILLIONS ALLEGEDLY STOLEN THROUGH MEDICAID FRAUD

American autism care providers backed the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)

"If we're not able to provide a good amount of pay to our providers, we're not able to make sure they're set up for success to be able to give some of these services, and we're going to see less and less children being able to access services at all," she added.

Sanders said 75% of clinics will have to close their doors or stop serving foster kids due to the massive cuts.

The 30% cut will not only affect providers' ability to provide access to these families, but it will also limit foster children's opportunities to learn essential skills, according to Sanders. Foster children with autism depend on regular therapy to develop everyday skills, but a sudden loss of that support could set them back.

"If they don't learn these school skills at an early intervention or an early age, it'll be a lot more costly later on," she said.

In August, the Autism Families Alliance put its support behind the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud, arguing that the alleged theft of millions of federal funds has hurt both taxpayers and children with autism who rely on those services. Some states, including Georgia, have also taken steps to enhance oversight of autism services.

The group backed eliminating fraud and prosecuting suspected criminals, but also feared that broad federal and state efforts to root out fraud could unintentionally make it more difficult for legitimate providers to care for children with autism. The coalition called on policymakers to ensure fraudsters are removed from the system without creating what they described as unnecessary barriers for families of vulnerable children seeking care.

RFK JR ANNOUNCES 'LARGEST AUTISM FRAUD BUST IN AMERICAN HISTORY' WITH $46.6M MEDICAID SCHEME INDICTMENT

The Autism Families Alliance said that efforts by the Trump administration and state leaders to fight fraud have gone too far. (REUTERS/Kylie Cooper)

Now, the group says Georgia’s foster families face the risk that they had previously raised concerns about.

"I think fraud should be prosecuted by all means," Sanders said. "Anybody who is engaging in fraudulent behavior should be prosecuted to the highest extent of the law. Are we able to not only tackle the fraud, but still give access to services for our children? Why can't we do both at the same time?"

"What's really happening here is we're going in with a sledgehammer when really we should be going in with a scalpel," she continued, adding that officials need to be "approaching this in a way where it's not going to totally obliterate the care to our families."

One Georgia foster mother has already been told her nearly 3-year-old son’s provider may be forced to stop treating him after he started making progress, according to the Georgia Recorder.

"Reforms that improve care, increase efficiency and prevent abuse are something we all support, but when those efforts make it harder for children with autism to get the care they need, something has gone terribly wrong," Kelsey Bennett, a family advocate with the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has returned Poland's highest state honour amid an escalating historical dispute between the two allies, after Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the award.

Zelenskiy said on X he had sent back the Order of the White Eagle, which he received in 2023 as a symbol of friendship between Poland and Ukraine.

While calling the decoration a symbol of Poland's "highest trust," he suggested it no longer held the same meaning after Nawrocki's decision.

He said, however, that Ukraine was still open to co-operation with Poland despite the public row that started when Zelenskiy renamed a military unit in honour of World War II-era Ukrainian insurgents accused of massacring Poles.

"Ukraine will remain open to all meaningful formats of interaction with Poland, in order to strive to avoid misinterpretations of the complex and painful pages of the past of our peoples and to ensure due respect for all innocent victims of the 20th century," he wrote.

Nawrocki said on Friday that the revocation was not directed against the Ukrainian people and did not alter Poland's strategic support for Ukraine.

The dispute stems from a historical row over the legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), whose members are honoured in Ukraine for resisting Soviet rule after World War II.

During the war, however, the group massacred tens of thousands of Poles and Jews in what is now western Ukraine.

Zelenskiy triggered the controversy at the end of May when he bestowed the nickname "Heroes of the UPA" on a Ukrainian army unit fighting Russian forces.

The head of the Ukrainian presidential office Kyrylo Budanov has also announced that he will return a Polish state award.

Budanov wrote on Telegram on Saturday that he was renouncing the Golden Officer's Cross of the Order of Merit of the Republic of Poland, which he received last year.

Budanov described Nawrocki's decision as an "unfriendly gesture toward the Ukrainian people and a gift to the aggressor Russia".

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier also announced the return of a Polish award.

Later on Saturday, former Ukrainian president Leonid Kuchma also announced he would give up his Order of the White Eagle, according to media reports.

Former president Viktor Yushchenko also announced he was renouncing his award in protest.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called on both presidents to show restraint.

"The conflict between Poland and Ukraine is a source of delight for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin and shock to our allies," Tusk wrote on X on Friday.

The dispute comes less than a week before a reconstruction conference for Ukraine in the Polish port city of Gdansk.

The Ukrainian president urged allies to provide support in the wake of massive Russian attacks

Ukraine's president has used a speech at the Nato summit in Turkey to urge allies to deliver the air defence systems Kyiv urgently needs to protect it from escalating Russian attacks.

"We are capable of doing everything else ourselves, but when it comes to air defence, we need our partners' determination," Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning.

Zelensky's call for help rings with extra intensity after Russian missiles rained down on the Ukrainian capital twice in less than a week, crashing into blocks of flats and killing more than 50 civilians.

The summit in Ankara will also be a chance for Zelensky to hold a crucial meeting with Donald Trump and press home his case that Russia's "brutal" attacks are a show of weakness, not strength, and that Vladimir Putin should be pressured into talks towards a "dignified" peace.

The latest strikes on Ukraine come as it has been stepping up its own long-range drone attacks against Russia, hitting oil refineries and military targets there and causing significant fuel shortages and power cuts.

This video can not be played

Watch: Russian attack leaves hole in Kyiv residential building

Underscoring that threat, Moscow's mayor Sergei Sobyanin said anti-air defences intercepted "most" of the 430 unmanned aerial drones fired by Ukraine towards the capital overnight. The severity of the damage was not immediately clear.

Russian social media accounts are full of videos of people queuing for hours to buy petrol and fighting over what little they're allowed.

Speaking before the summit, Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte has urged member states to "pull their weight" and ensure Ukraine gets what it needs "to defend its sovereignty".

He underlined that Kyiv was "changing the dynamic on the battlefield", referring to efforts to stall Russian ground troops in the east.

That's also about the recent drone strikes, apparently giving Ukraine an edge. â

The phrase of the month here is "window of opportunity".

But as the war in the skies has intensified, Russia's ballistic missiles are causing Kyiv real problems.

Ukraine's air force issues a daily tally of the weapons Moscow launches alongside the number intercepted.

On Monday, almost all drones were blocked successfully but the failure rate for missiles was glaringly obvious.

Ukraine did not stop a single ballistic missile in that attack.

It isn't easy: they fly at several thousand kilometres an hour and there just aren't enough US-made Patriot air defence missiles in Ukraine to counter them.

"It is simply absurd that, in today's world, production has still not been scaled up to the level actually required to protect people from ballistic terror," Zelensky said, venting his frustration in a video address on Monday.

He has been calling on European allies to hand over their own stockpiles of Patriot missiles, arguing that they're no good to anyone in storage when civilians are being killed now in Ukraine.

"Russia is placing its bets on ballistic weapons, and those who want peace must place their bets on protection against ballistic attacks," Zelensky argued on Monday, setting out his case for meetings in Ankara.

But Patriot systems are in short supply worldwide and it's not clear how many would ever be enough if Russia were to escalate its ballistic attacks further.

That's why Zelensky also talks about Ukraine producing its own equivalent, with Nato help.

The Russian attacks, though, do suggest that Ukraine's deep strikes are getting under the Kremlin's skin.

After years of Russia targeting civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, including power stations in mid-winter, Moscow now accuses Kyiv of "terrorism" for hitting its oil refineries with drones.

Zelensky calls it an "influence campaign" and he will be keen to share details with Nato allies.

The aim is to pressure Putin into peace talks on terms that Kyiv could stomach â that doesn't include surrendering the entire eastern Donbas region, as Moscow still demands.

This video can not be played

Explosions in Kyiv during deadly Russian strikes

The campaign targets have been high profile.

An oil terminal in St Petersburg was hit with drones ahead of Putin's showpiece economic forum in the city in June. Then there were strikes on a refinery in Moscow itself, creating explosion videos that went viral.

Now there's a confirmed hit on an oil refinery in Omsk, Siberia, 2,500 km from Ukraine's border. The drone must have flown undetected for many hours, which shows how stretched Russia's own air defences actually are.

Ukraine's "influence" efforts also include Crimea, the peninsula which Putin seized in 2014 and which is deeply important to him personally.

Ukrainian drones are now hitting military logistics, oil refineries and power plants there almost every day, causing power cuts, fuel and food shortages and an official state of emergency.

A local resident told the BBC the situation was "catastrophic", reminiscent of the turbulent 1990s after the USSR collapsed.

One of Putin's great claims is that he "saved" the country from that chaos, raising Russia "from its knees".

Now his all-out war is bringing danger even to Moscow in the form of drone strikes, and widespread fuel rationing.

So Zelensky will tell Nato, and try to persuade Trump, that Ukraine has turned the tide in this war, and that its campaign of pressure can, with help, compel Russia to engage in proper negotiations for peace.

Trump has seemed impressed by Ukraine lately, although he spoke to Putin for 90 minutes by phone this week, giving the Russian leader a chance to get his war story in first.

Above all, Kyiv wants to end this war fast, through "strength or diplomacy", before another gruelling winter kicks in.

But to have any chance of that, Zelensky will argue, Ukraine needs more interceptor missiles to protect its cities and civilians.

zelenskyy_russia_interview:
In a wide-ranging interview, an upbeat Ukrainian president also discusses Donald Trump, King Charles, and how Kyiv is prepared to share its experience of drone warfare with the west

Sitting down with the Guardian in London, Volodymyr Zelenskyy seems cheerful. More than four years after Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, he believes Europe’s biggest war since 1945 appears to be slowly turning in Ukraine’s favour. The military situation is the most promising it has been for Kyiv for two and a half years, Zelenskyy says. “We can’t say Russia is losing this war. But we can say they are losing the initiative each day, day by day,” he insists.

Over the past week the Kremlin has suffered a series of setbacks. Long-range Ukrainian drones have hit Putin’s home city of St Petersburg, setting fire to oil terminals and sending smoke billowing above the skyline. Similar attacks have crippled occupied Crimea. A key supply road is littered with burning lorries and tankers and the peninsula seized by Russia in 2014 is experiencing severe fuel shortages.

Meanwhile, on the eastern battlefield, Russia’s grinding advance has come to a near halt. According to Zelenskyy, who since 2022 has consistently said he believes that with sufficient support Ukraine can defend against its invader, the Kremlin is losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month, with 23,000-24,000 killed and the rest “heavily” wounded. The true figure, he suggests, could be even higher. “Totally, this is a very big number. It means that they are not winning the war,” he points out. Ukraine has lost service personnel too on a lesser scale.

Moscow’s war may look stuck, but its destruction continues and it has in recent months intensified its aerial attacks on Ukrainian towns and cities with the apparent goal to terrorise those not involved in fighting. One attack last Tuesday featured 73 missiles and 656 drones. Eighteen people were killed in Kyiv and Dnipro, including a three-year-old boy. He was entombed under the rubble of an apartment block. According to the city’s mayor, the Russians are deliberately using cluster munitions in built-up areas.

Last week, Zelenskyy wrote an open letter to Russia’s president, suggesting a face-to-face meeting to wind down this terrible conflict. Speaking on Friday at the St Petersburg economic forum, Putin rejected the offer. He characterised the letter as “rude” and said Russia’s territorial demands – the Donbas region and two southern Ukrainian provinces – were unchanged. He also insisted Russian forces were going forward across all parts of the frontline, telling them: “Keep working, brothers.”

Putin’s implacable stance has led some observers to wonder if he is delusional, or being fed wrong information by his commanders. Zelenskyy says these theories are plausible, but he stresses that “the reason he’s lying doesn’t matter”. Putin, he adds, has lied about the war from the beginning, claiming it was necessary to seize Ukrainian land to “rescue” Russian speakers. His lies are a glue, used to “join” different elements in Russian society together, he thinks.

On the international stage, Russia has experienced several recent political defeats. In April, Putin’s closest ally in Europe, Viktor Orbán, was trounced in Hungary’s general election. Recent Russian efforts to support pro-Kremlin candidates in Moldova and – over the weekend – in Armenia also failed. “They are losing influence in different countries, including in Azerbaijan,” Zelenskyy says. He adds: “They are isolated inside Europe and from the United States also. So they are alone.”

Donald Trump began his second term in 2025 saying he would end the war and Zelenskyy has carefully praised US diplomatic efforts, despite his bruising encounter in the Oval Office, last summer’s pally summit between Trump and Putin in Alaska, and cuts to US aid for Kyiv. “I always said to President Trump that Putin is lying. He plays games with you, with the White House,” Zelenskyy says, adding that he is grateful to Americans for their “strong support” for his country.

Ukraine’s president admits that Washington’s attention has moved to the Middle East. “Of course, from the very beginning of the war with Iran their focus shifted,” Zelenskyy says of the Trump administration. He understands why the US has used up “so many missiles and weapons” in its war of choice with Tehran. He observes wistfully that Kyiv – unlike the US’s Gulf allies and Israel – never received “that volume of support”. “It’s a pity,” he says.

Since 2022 Ukraine has transformed itself into a drone superpower. Once a supplicant for western military aid, Kyiv has grown into a hub for military industrial production and technical innovation. Several Arab countries have sought its help in shooting down Iranian Shaheds. The most important weapon Ukraine now lacks, Zelenskyy says, are US-made Patriots. They are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles, which rain down nightly on sleeping Ukrainian civilians.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy held talks in Downing Street with Keir Starmer, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz and the French president Emmanuel Macron. Zelenskyy says he renewed a call to his European allies to “close” Ukraine’s skies – in other words, to help Ukraine fend off large-scale Russian drone and missile attacks. As well as antiballistic interceptors, he wants financial support to transform Ukraine’s mobilised armed forces into a European-style contract army.

He recognises that Patriot missiles are expensive, costing $4m each. The UK does not have its own antiballistic missile programme. London, Paris and Berlin and other EU states should work together to build an alternative to the US version, he believes. In return, Ukraine is ready to share its hard-won experience of drone warfare with its European friends. “The UK is among them. And Nato is very interested in it. This is priceless information. There is a huge volume of it,” he says.

Zelenskyy is reluctant to be drawn on future military operations. But long- and mid-range drone attacks have made the return of Crimea – annexed by Russia in 2014 – a tantalising if distant possibility. Ukraine’s forces are busy destroying the peninsula’s logistics, and hitting other military and energy targets all across occupied southern Ukraine, he says. “It’s all about critical infrastructure. This helps them to militarise our Crimea. We are working on it,” he adds.

For a long time many Russians have tried to ignore the war raging across the Ukrainian border. Zelenskyy says the purpose of long-range strikes – which have seen drones buzzing above apartment blocks in greater Moscow and St Petersburg – is to make residents “feel” what war means. He adds: “Victory in this war is when Russian society recognises that the war is awful, that the war is a tragedy not for someone, somewhere, but for themselves. And I think this is the momentum.”

In May, the Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich secretly travelled to Kyiv for talks with Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy says he told Abramovich he would never give up the Donbas region, as Moscow wishes. Explaining the meeting, he says: “I think there are different people around Putin. Half of them want to continue this war. Half want to stop. And I think that people who are from business, they understand that the economy is in terrible situation in Russia. It’s very close to collapse.”

Zelenskyy spoke to the Guardian shortly before going to see King Charles. The two men appear to have developed a warm and trusting relationship. Zelenskyy has previously revealed that the monarch urged Donald Trump during his state visit to the UK last year to support Ukraine, something the US president has been distinctly reluctant to do. If the war continues to go well, could the monarch one day visit Zelenskyy’s own palace in Kyiv?

Ukraine’s president grinned at the question. He nodded his head enthusiastically. “You know today in the morning when I spoke by phone with my wife [Olena], with all respect to Keir [Starmer], my wife said best regards to the king. And then to the prime minister,” he confesses. “Ukraine loves his majesty. I would like to invite him to Kyiv very much. Maybe this year. I don’t know from the point of security but of course we want to see him.”

VC Jeremy Levine has a wry solution to something that routinely annoys him, according to a new Wall Street Journal article on the rise of AI transcription apps. On Zoom, he is no longer “Jeremy Levine” but instead “Jeremy Levine I do not consent to transcribing or recording.”

It may sound petty or brilliant, depending on your point of view, but what’s clear is that always-on recording is becoming ubiquitous, thanks to a growing crop of AI note-taking apps and devices, many of which we’ve covered here at TechCrunch (we’ve even ranked some).

VC Eric Bahn tells the outlet he now automatically assumes his meetings with founders will be recorded, even before he sees a phone slide across a conference table. One founder tells the WSJ she records most of her first dates with the Granola app, then feeds the transcript to Claude afterward to see if she could be more “engaging or empathetic,” while also assessing who did most of the talking. (Dating in San Francisco is rough.)

Levine calls the whole trend “socially unacceptable behavior” that can completely kill spontaneous conversations. Others in the piece note it’s a legal minefield.

But there’s another wrinkle: if every meeting, watercooler conversation, and romantic outing gets transcribed and summarized, who’s actually reading any of it? At what point does this audio landfill of every conversation stop being useful and just become another recording no one has time to play back?

Early research has found that the majority of young people are still able to log into at least one platform. (Unsplash: Sanket Mishra / a person laying in bed holding a cell phone / licence)

Age-checking technology companies want Australia to use stronger investigative powers to verify if social media giants are implementing the under-16s ban effectively.

But legal and tech industry groups have warned the proposed information-gathering powers must be narrowed to avoid inadvertently capturing children or parents.

A Senate inquiry will consider submissions and, in August, report on Labor's bill to expand eSafety's powers and raise penalties for systemic failures to enforce the social media age ban.

Companies who sell age-checking software want Australia to grant the eSafety commissioner investigative powers to "test" if social media companies are using their technology properly.

The Age Verification Providers Association (AVPA) has backed Labor's bill to strengthen Australia's social media age laws and called on the federal government to go further with a mandatory audit of every platform captured by the under-16s ban.

The group warned social media giants could opt to wear fines, no matter how large, if it helped to sink the age laws.

Age-assurance companies, which often sign confidentiality agreements with social media platforms, also asked for legal protections for providing information "in good faith" to an eSafety investigation.

Australia will strengthen its social media ban for young people as a priority amid concerns the powers behind the world-first laws are not strong enough.

Support was mixed in submissions to a Senate inquiry into Labor's proposal to double the maximum penalty to $99 million for tech companies that failed to take "reasonable steps" to enforce the age limit.

The bill would also allow eSafety to compel documents from social media platforms and third parties when investigating suspected systemic failures to uphold the ban.

Legal experts recommended Labor narrow the scope of these investigative powers to explicitly protect children and parents, while the tech sector opposed the larger fines.

In a damning submission, the AVPA, which represents third-party age technology companies, warned big fines could still be seen as a "small price to pay" if copping them allowed Australia's ban to be "wrongly" be portrayed as a failure.

Early research into the efficacy of the ban in preventing Australians aged under 16 from accessing the likes of TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram has found the majority of young people are still able to log in to at least one platform.

AVPA said expanding the eSafety commissioner's power so it could compel documents from tech companies was "necessary to test whether social media platforms have effectively configured the age assurance systems they claim to have implemented".

The group recommended Australia go further by having a "mandatory independent audit and certification requirement" for every social media platform captured by the ban.

"The expanded power will also reach our members … which are typically bound contractually by confidentiality obligations," the submission said.

"Most such agreements already permit disclosure that is required by law, so compliance with a valid notice should not expose suppliers to significant contractual risk."

The Law Council of Australia has made a submission flagging concerns the scope of the proposed section on information-gathering extended "beyond its intended operation".

"As drafted, the provision appears capable of applying to any person, including end-users who are children and their parents or guardians, where they possess relevant information or documents," the submission said.

The council recommended the bill be amended to ensure it "better reflects" the government's policy intentions and provides "certainty" that children were not "inadvertently" captured by the expanded information-gathering power.

"If the power is not intended to apply to children and their parents or guardians, its scope should be revised to ensure that it is appropriately targeted," it said.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said eSafety would not compel documents from children and parents because "everyday Australians" did not have evidence of "systemic non-compliance with the law by billion-dollar tech companies".

Anika Wells reassures parents that the strengthened powers are intended to target third-party companies, such as age assurance technology providers. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

"Instead, these strengthened powers are intended to target third-party companies, such as age assurance technology providers and app-stores, where the eSafety commissioner suspects they may hold evidence of systemic non-compliance," she said.

"We know social media companies are doing the bare minimum to comply with our social media minimum age law; that's why we are strengthening eSafety's powers and doubling fines for non-compliance."

Digital Industry Group Inc (DIGI), an industry group that advocates on behalf of the sector in Australia, has criticised the proposed bill, arguing the government had not tested if gaps in enforcement could be addressed in other ways.

It also opposed the doubling of the maximum penalty because, with no fines yet issued, it was not clear if there was a "link" between the dollar figure and the effectiveness of the age ban.

DIGI said the eSafety commissioner already had an "extensive suite of investigative and enforcement powers" related to the social media age restrictions and argued the government should be clear about any "deficiency" the new bill was trying to remedy.

The group raised concerns about the new information and document-gathering powers being "very broad", noting they were not limited to app stores and age-assurance providers.

DIGI said any increased powers should be accompanied by greater transparency about how they were used.

"Powers of this breadth should be matched by clear public reporting on the types of services and individuals to whom notices are issued, and the basis on which the commissioner decides to open an inquiry into a service or person," the submission said.

The eSafety commissioner has backed the expanded powers as currently any investigation into tech giants suspected of failing to take "reasonable steps" to block under-16s from their social media platforms relies on "representations" from those same companies.

"Without access to primary documents relevant to compliance with the [social media minimum age] obligation, the commissioner would likely be unable to discharge the onus of proof required in any civil penalty proceeding brought to the courts against a provider of a [platform]," eSafety said.

The commission said information and documents from third parties, such as age assurance providers, would be "instrumental" in determining whether the tech giants had taken sufficient steps to comply with Australia's laws.

In its submission, eSafety also argued the "full suite" of investigative powers available to it elsewhere in the Online Safety Act, such as the ability to "compel witnesses to give evidence on oath or affirmation", should apply uniformly.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Thursday that the Trump administration's overhaul of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has cost Americans up to $26.5 billion so far, the latest Democratic critique of sweeping changes made to the agency.

In a report shared first with CNBC, Warren said most of that figure comes from moves the CFPB has taken under acting Director Russell Vought to roll back rules capping credit card and overdraft fees.

The report comes as Vought faces a Senate oversight hearing Thursday on those and other actions, including dismissing enforcement actions and consent orders and an allegation that the agency recently removed 15 years of consumer data from the CFPB website.

Since taking office last year, the Trump administration has slashed staffing, dropped or narrowed dozens of enforcement cases, and rolled back Biden-era rules to refocus the agency on what officials call its core mission.

Republicans have defended the moves as necessary to rein in what they view as an overreaching regulator. Democrats led by Warren — who conceived and helped set up the agency after the 2008 financial crisis — have contended that the Trump administration has crippled a key consumer financial watchdog and exposed Americans to unfair or deceptive industry practices.

The clash comes as the Senate weighs the nomination of Brian Johnson, a former CFPB deputy director turned Capital One executive, whom President Donald Trump tapped to lead the agency permanently.

Warren's report attributes up to $15 billion in consumer costs to the CFPB's decision to abandon a rule capping most credit card late fees at $8, a regulation the agency previously estimated would save consumers roughly $10 billion annually.

It attributes another $7.5 billion to the repeal of the bureau's overdraft fee rule, which would have limited many banks to charging $5 for overdrafts.

The remainder of the estimate comes from the CFPB's decision to drop more than three dozen enforcement actions and settlements, some of which were set to send payments directly to consumers. That totaled roughly $4 billion, according to the report.

The White House and CFPB did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Ahead of Thursday's hearing, Warren also sent Vought a letter cataloging what she described as unanswered congressional oversight requests during his tenure running the bureau.

Parents at a North Carolina elementary school are fighting for the ability to keep their children in public school while opting them out of a music class taught by a transgender teacher, and one father says critics have responded by telling families to homeschool instead.

The dispute at Middle Creek Elementary School in Wake County has centered on parents who say they were not given advance notice about the teacher and want an alternative for children whose families object on religious or personal grounds.

Parents speaking before the school board this week said children have come home "upset, confused and uncomfortable," while others said requests for alternatives have been ignored or dismissed and called on the district to provide an opt-out.

PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT

The controversy spilled into a heated Wake County Board of Education meeting Tuesday, where speakers were sharply divided over whether accommodating those families amounts to protecting parental rights or discriminating against a teacher because of gender identity.

One speaker argued that religious and conscientious exemptions effectively amount to parents demanding that their children not encounter people they dislike, while others said families should not have to leave the public school system to avoid a class they object to.

A demonstrator holds a transgender pride flag during a President's Day protest near the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 17, 2025.  (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Aaron Driver, a father of three children at Middle Creek Elementary and a member of Middle Creek Parental Rights, told the board parents "shouldn’t have to pass an ideological test to participate in public education."

"Here’s what our detractors are telling us," Driver said. "You don’t support school hiring a trans teacher. Maybe public school isn’t for you or your family. Maybe homeschool. Maybe private school.

BRAZIL PARENTS FACE PRISON SENTENCE FOR HOMESCHOOLING AFTER COURT ACCUSES THEM OF 'INTELLECTUAL NEGLECT'

"That's right," he continued. "Maybe pay taxes into the school system and then pay again to escape from it."

Aaron Driver, a father of three students at Middle Creek Elementary School, speaks during a Wake County Board of Education meeting Aug. 18, 2026, about a dispute over the school’s transgender music teacher. (Wake County Public School System/WakeCountySchools.)

Later in the meeting, another public commenter, Katrina Day, offered a striking response from the other side of the fight, proposing a free homeschooling curriculum because it would "keep the bigots away from my grandchildren." She also suggested the district "relocate the children of bigots if needed" or "expel the children of bigots if needed."

Katrina Day speaks during public comment at the Wake County Board of Education meeting Aug. 18, 2026, amid an ongoing dispute over a transgender music teacher at Middle Creek Elementary School. (Wake County Public School System/WakeCountySchools)

The fight at Middle Creek had been building prior to Tuesday's contentious board meeting.

State Rep. Erin Paré, R-Wake, publicly raised concerns in late July after hearing from parents about the possibility of a transgender teacher at their southern Wake County elementary school, floating the possibility of a state law requiring sex-based professional attire for public-school employees, according to WRAL.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Parents opposed to the arrangement have framed their objections as a request for advance notice and alternatives rather than a personal attack on the teacher.

During Tuesday’s meeting, one speaker said parents should receive "advanced notice and the option to opt out" when a teacher’s presentation conflicts with their religious or personal beliefs, while another said families had requested alternatives and called on the board to "provide reasonable alternatives to families who object."

Topic:Courts

Sun 14 Jun 2026 at 3:06pm

Sun 14 Jun 2026 at 5:13pm

An independent Judicial Commission would investigate complaints about judges and magistrates.  (Pexels: Katrin Bolovstova)

The WA government will introduce legislation to establish an independent Judicial Commission, which will handle complaints about judges and magistrates.

Any person or organisation can make a complaint about the conduct or capacity of judges but the commission will not be able to investigate the merits of a decision or sentence.

If the legislation is passed, the commission would be established by the start of 2027 and operational by the end of that year.

Complaints about the behaviour and capacity of judges and magistrates will be investigated by an independent watchdog, under new legislation to be introduced to WA parliament this week.

The legislation would see the establishment of a nine-person Judicial Commission, which would handle complaints about the state's judicial officers.

Complaints could include bullying or harassment by judges and magistrates, inappropriate comments they've made to a witness or legal practitioner and their mental capacity.

WA's Attorney-General Tony Buti said the commission would provide "transparency and confidence" in the state's judicial system.

Any person or organisation can make a complaint, but the commission will not be able to investigate the merits of a decision or sentence.

That will continue to go through the appeals process.

Attorney-General Tony Buti said the commission would operate independently from government.  (ABC News: Mya Kordic )

The commission will be made up of nine members, with six heads of jurisdiction, three community members — one of which will be a legal practitioner — and a director.

Complaints could be dismissed, referred to a head of jurisdiction or, in serious cases, be given to an independent investigating panel.

The panel would be "appointed as needed" and include two current or retired judicial members and one "high-standing" member of the community.

The commission would investigate judges from all jurisdictions, including the Supreme and District courts. (ABC News: Mya Kordic )

If misbehaviour is proven by an investigating panel, it would be reported to the attorney-general, who would table a report in parliament.

The state government said if both houses agree, the parliament could recommend to the governor the judicial officer be removed from office.

Dr Buti said the commission would be separate from government.

"It is independent, we do not become involved until they decide to hand a report to government," he said.

The establishment of a Judicial Commission would bring WA in line with most other states and territories.

The attorney-general said there had been extensive consultation with the heads of jurisdiction after the idea was first floated in 2022.

"It's needed because the judiciary have asked for it themselves, the Law Reform Commission recommended it in their report on the judiciary some years ago," Dr Buti said.

Dr Buti said the legislation was also intended to educate judges about how to deal with certain cases.

"We also want to educate judges in regard to how they should appropriately deal with matters such as domestic violence or other instances that come before them."

If the legislation is passed, the commission would be established by the start of 2027 and operational by the end of that year.

Shadow Attorney-General Nick Goiran said he welcomed the legislation "after years of advocacy".

"The opposition looks forward to now scrutinising the legislation once it is finally introduced to ensure it will meet community expectations," he said in a statement.

Nick Goiran said the legislation had been a long time coming.  (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

He also questioned when more than 20 regional courthouses would reopen after being temporarily closed due to a lack of security.

"We call on the attorney-general to outline a precise timetable as to when regional courts in our state will return from their unprecedented winter hibernation," Mr Goiran said.

"After all, no complaints against the judiciary can possibly be lodged if the courts are not even open to begin with."

WA Chief Justice Peter Quinlan said heads of jurisdiction have long been asking for a formal way to deal with complaints.

"I'm happy to say that we have a judiciary in this country that is fairly free of corruption, but you can never be complacent … and to have a mechanism to deal with complaints of a serious nature if they arise is obviously very helpful for the integrity of the system as a whole," he said.

"It is a commission which is designed to maintain the independence of the judiciary with community input."
