For all its flatness, there's something fun lurking in 'Chum.'

2:57 PM EDT on June 6, 2026

Credit: IFC

Chum opens with a meandering, overly formal, almost sleepwalk-inducing voiceover describing something horrible that happened offscreen. When the voiceover ends, that horrible something plays out in front of us with no detail spared, which begs the question: Why did we need the voiceover in the first place?

There's a lot of that happening in Chum, the latest film in a long, illustrious, often schlocky line of Jaws successors. The concept is alluring, the scenery is lovely, and no one needs an excuse to make another killer shark movie, but at every turn this film packs baffling, often derailing choices in among the flashes of horror fun. I truly don't know whether to tell you this movie is bad in a fun way or just plain bad, because I found the experience of watching it more puzzling than anything else. So, let's talk through it.

On the island of Malta, lawyer Tina (Alice Eve) is finally settling down with her dream man, investment banker and activist Tom (Eric Michael Cole) via a gorgeous destination wedding. To celebrate, Tom's best man Rick (Johnny Gaffney) rents out a catamaran to sail the bride, groom, and bridesmaids around the Mediterranean for the day. Again, the scenery's great, the bikinis are on, everyone's having a good time, until a fire forces the group to abandon ship. Fortunately, they're swiftly picked up by fisherman Roy (Jim Klock), who promises to get them back to shore and even offers them food. This detour turns into a nightmare, though, because it turns out Roy is the guy from that weird voiceover from before! He's got a tragic backstory tied to a Great White Shark who's inexplicable roaming the Mediterranean, and there's only way to lure that shark in for revenge: Live, human bait!

Why is Roy the only person who seemingly knows about this Great White roaming where it's not supposed to roam? Shouldn't marine biologists be tracking this phenomenon, which is repeatedly mentioned on the news? Why is the shark seemingly well-fed even though it apparently only wants to eat humans now? These are not questions we should be asking! The more important question is why Chum takes more than half of its 86-minute runtime to get to the meat of its premise.  Grief-Crazed Weirdo Named Roy Uses Humans as Live Shark Bait is a great premise, even if Dangerous Animals did a better version of a very similar premise just last year, and it's right there in the trailer for this film! But Chum seems determined to explain to you why you're meant to care about these people for a massive chunk of a short movie, devoting swaths of screentime to repetitive conversations meant to showcase drama in the wedding party which instead only serve to drag the movie away from its beating exploitation cinema heart.

But even these diversions would be a bit more forgivable if the film could muster a little more proficiency when it comes to the basic tools of cinema. Director and co-writer Jonathan Zuck clearly has a taste for the film's chosen subgenre, and when he's able to cut loose and just play with killer sharks there is fun to be had, but the film seems to sleepwalk its way through everything else. We're talking about a movie shot on location, with loads of open ocean and beautiful coastline, not to mention views looking out across seaside cliffs. There is so much production value waiting to be snatched up, and yet the film seems to go out of its way to choose the most uninspired staging for all of the pre-Roy sequences.

Making matters worse is the dialogue, most of which is delivered via some of the worst dubbing I can remember hearing in the last few years. I can only assume that filming on the open ocean, with boat noise and wind and surf to contend with, meant that the dialogue recorded live was unusable, so the production had to resort to ADR. It's an understandable technical challenge, but the dialogue dubbed in sounds flat, both in inflection and in the sound mix, like everyone's talking from the inside of a closet. There aren't that many memorable lines anyway, but the ones that do land lost quite a bit of their punch through this process. Throw in some clunky CGI shark action and the film almost entirely slips away.

And yet…somehow it doesn't. For all its flatness, its rickety technical issues, and its insistence on dragging out the narrative before getting to the Good Stuff, there's something fun lurking in Chum, and a lot of it comes through Klock's performance as Roy. He understands exactly the movie he's in, even if no one else does, and he commits completely to playing this madman with a broken heart, even when his dialogue strains credulity and the film around him isn't really keeping up. Eve, who also served as a producer on the film, handles herself well enough, and everyone else is just sorta there, but Klock makes Chum instantly more watchable in a sort of basic cable movie of the week sort of way.

So yes, there are reasons to watch Chum, especially if you're a killer shark movie completist, but the overall impression I have of this film is one of bafflement. It's too self-serious to be a straight-up exploitation cinema gorefest, and too gruesome to play to whatever strengths it might have had as a psychological drama. It's a ship too big to steer into the shallows, and yet it seems frightened to go all the way out into open water. That leaves it strangely adrift in a sea of strange choices and clunky filmmaking, but there's, somehow, still just enough blood in the water to draw you in, if only for a while.Chum is out now in theaters and on digital.

claire-stapleton-google-walkouts:
In 2018, Claire Stapleton helped spearhead a walkout of around 20,000 Google employees. The protest was a response to a New York Times story detailing how the company had paid multimillion-dollar exit packages to executives accused of sexual misconduct.

Now she's back with a memoir, "Don't Be Evil," that pulls back the curtain on her time in the trenches at Google. It comes as the company faces renewed employee activism over its work with the Pentagon and ICE, and departing talent as it reshuffles its AI leadership.

Stapleton joined Google in 2007 and worked on internal communications, where her quippy, humorous companywide emails earned her the internal nickname "the Bard of Google." At the time of the mass employee walkouts, Stapleton was a marketing manager at Google-owned YouTube. She left Google in 2019, writing at the time that she believed the company had retaliated against her over her activism.

In many ways, Stapleton helped shape Google's image internally. She talked to Business Insider about those early days at the tech giant, which, while successful in its aims to organize the world's information, later found its utopian ideals undermined by corporate realities. Google vowed not to become a conventional company, but sticking to that promise proved harder than its founders may have anticipated.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity. Google did not respond to a Business Insider request for comment.

The book has this central tension between Google's utopian self-image versus a pattern of bad management and lack of tolerance for dissent. Do you think Google was ever really the company it believed itself to be?

Claire Stapleton: I think that there's a lot of curiosity about whether the founding principles and philosophy were sincere, or if it was always kind of a ploy to squeeze more out of the workers.

Google had this promise that innovation and tech can solve all these problems in the world, and also an interest in creating a company culture that supported that — not just through having top talent, keeping them happy, and having them creating and firing all cylinders. It was just like, "green light, go" in all these different lanes for the company as it moved through the world.

So I think that there are always tensions and contradictions in that. I read this amazing book called "From Counterculture to Cyberculture" by Fred Turner, a Stanford professor. He talks about how one of the great ironies and contradictions of the tech industry is that they started in this quite countercultural way. There was this distrust of centralized power, democratic institutions — everything was about decentralizing.

Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Even Mark Zuckerberg's op-ed about AI uses the same language about how the future is for everyone. Meanwhile, these companies have consolidated tons of power, and it's all centralized. It's like they've become institutions, in and of themselves, with tremendous impact on society. So how does that square? How can these people who set out to be the leaders of this guerrilla movement for societal transformation now sit atop trillion-dollar companies?

You're in good company — there's been a run of books about Silicon Valley's darker side.

CS: People keep saying, "Wow, this is amazing timing for this book because there's so much going on with Google." The company remains a sort of bellwether of the economy, but also how attitudes toward work have changed, how the public ingests a company as big and successful as Google is.

How much did you feel that sentiment against Big Tech shift by the time you left Google?

CS: The last year that I was there, something was fomenting. I think Trump's first term started to make Google look less sure of its values and its virtues, and I think that there were some changes in the culture that were happening as the company was reckoning with becoming so big and more corporate.

Where does transparency sit? How does the culture evolve? I think that was spurring this very strange thing where employees were feeling a loss of identity.

If I could say it's one thing, it's that Google maintained a startup feeling even though it was a big company. But somehow these tech companies have become the infrastructure of the world, and the people that run them are like heads of state.

Looking back, what do you see as the biggest lasting impacts from the 2018 walkouts?

CS: I was so fascinated when Marc Andreessen gave this interview to The New York Times a year or two ago, expressing this anxiety that management felt the workers were going to revolt. That to me expressed what was so kind of deep and emotionally triggering for the executives about the walkout because, from our perspective, of course, we were demanding accountability.

And for an industry that doesn't have so much accountability because these companies have so much power, it seemed like the world could agree that having some pushback from employees was an important gate or some sort of limit for the company.

One of the biggest impacts was that it so freaked out the management that they were willing to kind of swing the pendulum back the other way from the corporate transparency and "we can tolerate dissent," and then it was just sort of like, "no more political speech on the mailing list," and they fired people.

And this chilling effect, which had ramifications on the culture, was worth it for them, I think, to recalibrate the power between employees and workers. It also just accelerated the disillusionment I think for a lot of people in the tech industry.

There is now an Alphabet union. Do you think employees at Google have more or less power today?

CS: It can always surprise us. The company has made a concerted effort — and you see it across the industry — in the way they're talking about workers, with the exception of the top AI people maybe. It's essentially: you could go at any given time.

"Will AI replace workers?" is a less interesting question to me than how the management sees the threat of that as quite advantageous. It's very good for the management if people feel like, "I need to work harder to prove myself even as a human being." It's such a 180 from "people are the lifeblood of this company" and all these other things that Google used to say.

Before it was all, "let's nourish the workers." Now it's sort of like, "you have to sing for your supper."

You saw from the inside how Google obsessively tried to buoy its image. The company has a lot more battles today — regulation, privacy, the AI war. What do you think those conversations inside Google look like right now?

CS: I think that the company that I saw was really eager to preserve its image. And I think that Google sort of lost control of its image in a lot of different ways. Again, it doesn't seem to harm the complete chokehold that has. It's really successful in the AI race, despite recent setbacks. It is absolutely a critical piece of infrastructure in the world at this point. So it's not like this sort of image necessarily has any huge effect on its bottom line.

They seem to have lost in the all-fronts war, the war for the hearts and minds of the employees, which I think was something that was so huge to the company back in the day. It seems like they decided along the way that's not the most important thing. They don't do the same kind of all-hands and family feeling, and sharing all the company information.

After leaving Google you started an advice column called Tech Support — "Existential advice for the modern tech worker!" What has struck you most about the letters you've received from tech insiders?

CS: It surprised me that people I thought were happy and content were struggling with some of the things I did. I saw myself as particularly angsty those last few years, but I now know that angst is widespread. I think in general people are asking themselves, "if you can't really make a good living being a creative person or following some passion project, how can those things coexist? How can someone continue to work at a job that makes their bread while also tending to their soul?"

I think because we no longer expect our corporate job to fill our soul, and it seems almost comical that at one time we thought it might, what space does that open up? The notes I've gotten have always been about the crisis of meaning, and I think AI only accelerates that.

There was someone I knew from YouTube who went and joined the circus. I think Covid pushed people who wanted to do a completely different thing to the type of tech marketing job we had, and I find that inspiring.

I have to ask — and you mention it briefly in the book — Google's first generative AI chatbot was called Bard. Given that was your unofficial title inside Google, how did that feel?

CS: It's funny that it didn't work out. But it felt to me like this nostalgic idea of Google's culture. That to me is what it was playing off of. The Bard of Google, Google Poet Laureate — it all spoke to the spirit of the company, which was whimsical and friendly and also trying to be somewhat esoteric. I used to work for the internal news, which was a lot of waxing poetic about all the geniuses and tinkerers, the gurus and sages.

It was a company that loved characters, and it loved the lore. I didn't think someone made the direct connection to me, it's just that it was a chord and a thread in the culture for sure. It was funny that it didn't end up panning out, and they switched to something else. It fit.

clear_street_databricks:
Clear Street, the prime brokerage startup that recently shelved plans for its own IPO, is now aiming to give investors access to some of Silicon Valley's hottest private companies before they go public.

The firm is close to announcing a new platform designed to let accredited investors buy interests in late-stage private companies, starting with AI software titan Databricks, valued this month at $188 billion, CNBC is first to report.

"The goal is to remove friction and give more people the ability to invest in more products," Uri Cohen, CEO and co-founder of Clear Street, said in an interview. "A lot of the wealth creation has been in private markets, and more and more retail investors and smaller investors want to be part of that."

More startups are staying private for longer, meaning much of their value creation is taking place before an initial public offering. That has fueled growing demand from rich investors seeking exposure to companies like Databricks, Anthropic and OpenAI before they debut on public markets.

Last week, CNBC reported that Goldman Sachs has created a new platform to expand its offerings for wealthy clients and family offices who increasingly want direct stakes in fast-growing private companies.

While Clear Street's pitch centers on democratizing high-growth tech, the mechanics of the deals highlight a tricky reality in today's private markets: Databricks isn't directly involved.

Instead of buying stock issued by Databricks, Clear Street investors acquire an interest in a special purpose vehicle (SPV) that holds a stake in a third-party fund that owns the shares.

To Databricks, the shareholder of record remains that external fund, where they remain legally parked, according to Clear Street.

Earlier this year, AI startups like Anthropic cracked down on unauthorized secondary transfers, voiding unapproved SPVs and indirect share sales that bypassed corporate transfer rules.

Cohen, the CEO of Clear Street, said that his firm, as counterparty, would stand behind the deals: "If there is a risk, we are taking it."

For its part, a Databricks spokesperson said in an email that the startup "does not have any engagement or relationship with Clear Street."

The rapid adoption of heat pumps in the United States is becoming little short of a revolution, such that these clever HVAC devices in a few years will effectively replace previous systems.

Indeed of all new homes built last year, 46% were completed with heat pumps, just 1% below other more recognizable systems like water boilers, gas furnaces, and air conditioners.

Heat pumps use the process of changing a liquid to a gas and back again to cool and heat air that’s pumped into the house or building they service. They generate substantially fewer greenhouse gas emissions than a gas furnace or burning heating oil, and because they rely on electricity, can take advantage of renewable energy.

Previous generations relied on the kinds of refrigerants that were 2,000-times more capable of creating a greenhouse effect than CO2, but modern EPA regulations are seeing that previous fluid exchanged for ones with lower global warming potential, or even propane.

In the first quarter of this year, there were 32% more heat pump sales in the US than older home heating systems, according to a new report from the nonprofit Building Decarbonization Coalition.

That report also showed that sales of heat pumps have doubled in the last 15 years, and the heat pumps, which can both heat and cool homes, narrowly failed to overtake sales of A/C units.

“All the trends are pointing towards increased heat pump adoption, not only versus gas, but also versus just traditional one-way air conditioning,” said Kevin Carbonnier, associate director of analytics at the coalition, told Grist.

HOMEBUILDING IN AMERICA:

“It’s not just that heat pumps are better, more comfortable, more efficient than furnaces. But also, you get the two-in-one appliance.”

A combination of climate goals, higher energy prices, and high home prices mean that both consumers and builders look to cut costs whenever possible. One method now almost universally used is electric stove tops, which when paired with an electric heat pump, means that the home builder doesn’t even need to worry about gas lines.

That can help keep energy costs (as electric burners are more efficient than gas ones) and final home prices down.

In this article

Fox Corp. has reached an agreement to acquire Roku for roughly $22 billion, marking another chapter in media consolidation as the industry grapples with changing dynamics and mounting challenges.

On Monday Fox announced it would acquire Roku for $160 per share in a cash-and-stock transaction. Fox plans to fund the cash portion of the deal with a combination of cash on hand and new debt. The company said it obtained a $12 billion loan for the transaction.

Fox's stock was down 17% in morning trading Monday. Roku fell 2%, though that stock gained 20% on Friday around initial reports of a potential sale.

The combination will bring together Fox's news and sports channels as well as its free ad-supported streamer Tubi with Roku, the maker of streaming devices and also the home of The Roku Channel, a service similar to Tubi.

On Monday, Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch called it a "defining moment" for the company.

The proposed acquisition comes about seven years after Fox's last major deal, when it shed its entertainment assets in a $71 billion deal with Disney. Since then, Fox's portfolio has primarily been made up of its TV channels, namely broadcast network Fox, which has been airing the FIFA World Cup since last week, and the Fox News Channel on cable.

In 2020 Fox acquired Tubi for $440 million. That service had long been its answer to the streaming wars, before the announcement of Fox One, its direct-to-consumer option that launched last year.

On a Monday call with investors, Murdoch noted that Fox was both "an early investor in Roku and a longtime commercial partner."

He added that since 2019 Fox has "reoriented" the company, centering it around live news and sports, and emphasized the focus on driving advertising revenue.

Advertising has taken a renewed importance for media companies as they look to build up streaming platforms and lean on live sports and events, which are capturing the biggest audiences.

Murdoch said on Monday's call with investors that the companies intend to keep Tubi and The Roku Channel separate after the deal closes. He called them "incredibly complementary services" that see about a third of overlap between their audiences.

Tubi sees a majority of its viewership for on-demand content, in contrast to the free channels that mimic the traditional pay TV bundle.

"Roku has a very large platform business that consists of advertising and subscriptions," said Roku CEO Anthony Wood on Monday's call.

Wood called Roku's platform a market leader in the U.S. and said it reaches more than 100 million streaming households globally, counting 145 billion hours of engagement annually.

Both Wood and Murdoch said their companies were entering the deal "from a position of strength."

Murdoch added that the addition of Roku allows Fox to go to "new markets to expand, obviously digitally in streaming and subscriptions, and drive the business aggressively into the 21st century."

Fox said Monday it expects to see approximately $400 million in run-rate cost synergies from the deal with additional revenue upside. After the acquisition closes, existing Fox shareholders would own roughly 73% of the combined company and Roku shareholders would own about 27%.

The deal, which has already been approved by the boards of directors of both companies, is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

“The helicopter just crashed!” a voice in the crowd yelled, drawing eyes away from the splayed-out wreckage of a bus collision that claimed two lives.

Los Angeles Fire Capt. Branden Silverman looked behind him to find a large plume of black smoke rising from a parking lot one block east. The department, which had just gruelingly removed passengers stuck between scraps of metal and glass, turned its attention to another deadly disaster Tuesday night.

Earlier in the evening, two bus passengers, Gage Weida, 31, and Daniel Castillo, 46, were killed when an SUV plowed into a bus in the suburban Los Angeles neighborhood of Chatsworth, officials said.

What authorities called a “preventable” tragedy – a woman allegedly driving under the influence ramming into a metro bus filled with passengers returning home from work – led to a domino effect, permanently altering the course of three more families’ lives.

Just two hours after the bus collision, a news helicopter for KNBC-TV NBC4 and KVEA-TV providing aerial coverage of the accident crashed and ignited a blaze, killing aerial photojournalist-reporter Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and Edy Gutierrez Mejia, a young tourist on the ground.

A loud explosion added fresh horror to the scene of the bus collision before first responders with the fire and police departments and news crews, including NBC4, quickly redirected their efforts to the inferno.

“To have two incidents of that significance in that short amount of time within a few blocks of each other is definitely a unique situation for any department,” Silverman told CNN.

Now, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are trying to determine what caused the news helicopter to go down, pointing to a video taken as the aircraft descended as a critical piece of evidence.

Meanwhile, the driver involved in the bus collision, Bailee Lynn Rios, faces a possible maximum sentence of life in prison after being charged with second-degree murder, driving under the influence and reckless driving, according to Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman.

“People on that bus at about 5 p.m. were either going to work or maybe coming from work. They might be going to get a bite to eat, to see family or friends,” Hochman said at a Thursday news conference. “What they did not expect is what was about to happen.”

In a statement, Rios’ attorney, Deputy Public Defender Ralf Jacobsen, said, “Our condolences go out to all those affected by this tragedy.”

“We ask the public to reserve judgment regarding Ms. Rios and allow the legal process to take its course,” Jacobsen told CNN Monday.

Five lives were ended by the tragic sequence of events, leaving the community shaken and loved ones grieving: a father of four, an LA resident with an upcoming birthday, a Guatemalan tourist who recently landed in LA, an engaged reporter and a soon-to-retire veteran pilot.

The heavy emotional toll on their families, first responders and the broadcast news community has prompted outpourings of grief from city and state leaders.

“My heart is with the families whose lives changed forever Tuesday night. Simply going to work, coming from work to come back to your family, you expect to see them,” Mayor Karen Bass said at a vigil Thursday. “And they never arrive.”

The dual tragedies on Tuesday evening unfolded in rapid succession.

Around 5 p.m., the Los Angeles Fire Department arrived at a chilling scene: an SUV lodged almost fully inside an LA Metro bus. Some people were trapped inside vehicles, while another was tossed out into an intersection.

Rios, driving a Ford Expedition, ran a red light and nearly struck another car before crashing into the bus as it traveled east, according to the Los Angeles Police Department. Rios was allegedly impaired by drugs and had narcotics inside the SUV as she drove “well beyond the speed limit,” Hochman said.

“She entered into opposing traffic because she was approaching a red light where cars were stopped, and she didn’t stop,” Hochman said. “At full force, she plunged into that metro bus.”

The bus driver, who had been injured in the wreck, quickly called the bus operating division for help, said Stephanie Wiggins, CEO of the LA County Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

Paramedics pronounced Weida and Castillo dead at the site of the collision. The fire department’s search and rescue team cut part of a car door away to rescue Rios while her SUV was still lodged in the bus, Silverman recounted.

After a trapped bus passenger and the SUV driver were rescued from the vehicles using hydraulic tools like the Jaws of Life and reciprocating saws, they were rushed to the hospital, according to Silverman. Four others had non-life-threatening injuries.

NBC4’s Moreno reported on television from a helicopter flying above the scene: “This is a horrific crash here in Chatsworth.”

A little over an hour after first responders flocked to the bus crash site, Silverman arrived. He stood in front of a group of reporters to provide an update on the bus collision, then waited to do a live interview with NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik at 7 p.m. at the scene.

By that point, the group of 56 personnel from the fire department had mostly cleared the scene. Silverman was the only crew member still there, along with a rescue ambulance crew completing paperwork for the victims. Several LAPD officers were nearby for traffic and crowd control.

The dust had seemed to settle: Some in the large crowd gathered at the scene pulled out their phones to livestream while others stood there to process the shock or search for loved ones, according to Silverman.

But at 6:57 p.m., Silverman was alerted about the helicopter by someone in the crowd.

“That’s when I and the rescue ambulance that were on scene … they reported it to our dispatch center immediately over the radio and we both responded over to that incident,” he said.

Silverman jumped into his white Durango trying to find the crash, as the exact location was still unknown.

When 7 p.m. came, NBC4 anchors Colleen Williams and Jonathan Gonzalez reported a thick black plume of smoke near the bus accident site, saying, “We’re not sure what this is,” adding, “All we can tell you is something has happened out there.”

Williams and Gonzalez asked Kovacik about the smoke as he reported at the bus collision scene, and he responded, “I don’t think it’s anything related.”

Kovacik, who suddenly saw people running to see what happened, later drove swiftly to the source of the smoke.

Moments before the aircraft fell to the ground less than a mile away, sounds of the engine changing speed and alerts to the pilot could be heard on video, NTSB investigator-in-charge Fabian Salazar said at a Wednesday news conference.

In the live feed from the helicopter, a person is heard exclaiming something in the background before another voice is heard asking, “You can’t pull up?”

A loud buzzing noise is then heard before the feed shakes intensely and the chopper appears to descend rapidly. It hit a shipping container on its descent, according to Silverman.

Within minutes, Silverman and the ambulance arrived at a storage facility parking lot behind a large one-story commercial building to find LAPD officers grabbing fire extinguishers and dragging a man away from the burning wreckage.

The ambulance crew started administering first aid to the victim, later identified as Mejia, but could not save him.

Meanwhile, Silverman searched for more victims inside the helicopter, which had burst into flames, and in the surrounding parked cars, igniting because the helicopter’s jet fuel leaked.

The blaze seemed unmanageable: Fire extinguishers from both the police and the fire departments “couldn’t even put a dent in the flames that were coming from the helicopter,” Silverman said.

When fire department crews got there minutes later, they immediately started attacking the fire and protecting the cars and the building near the blaze. They searched inside the building to ensure the fire had not spread there, according to Silverman. Four cars and two storage containers were damaged by the inferno, the fire department said.

A group of 67 firefighters knocked down most of the fire quickly and stopped the jet fuel from leaking further, Silverman said. Then, they searched through the helicopter wreckage to find victims on board.

As the news of the helicopter crash spread, media crews from the bus accident scene began rushing to the helicopter site and were told by law enforcement to evacuate because the situation was too dangerous, NBC4 footage showed.

Kovacik, the NBC4 anchor, heard it may have been a news chopper and saw a reporter from another station in tears, he said on air. Kovacik is heard checking in with colleagues, saying, “Are you OK? It’s not you guys, is it?”

The close-knit Southern California news community held its breath as it waited to hear which of its outlets would now be the subject of their reporting.

NBC4’s anchors told viewers the station lost contact with its helicopter crew. All the other stations told Kovacik it was not their chopper, he said. But as he realized it may have been his colleagues in the helicopter, Kovacik could be heard holding back tears.

Kovacik shakily asked Silverman who the helicopter belonged to. Silverman tells him he did not have that information.

“It soon became apparent through the news organizations … word started to travel whose helicopter it was, and it turned out to be NBC’s,” Silverman said.

Pilots and tower controllers also began deducing the downed helicopter belonged to NBC4.

“TV 4 is not up here with us. We believe it’s TV 4 that went down,” one pilot is heard saying, according to air traffic control audio obtained by CNN.

Around 9 p.m., Williams delivered the news to NBC4 viewers, her voice audibly distressed.

“We can now confirm that the chopper that went down in Chastworth tonight, about two hours ago, was in fact News Chopper 4,” Williams said.

The team had lost two fixtures of the station: Moreno, who was providing updates earlier on the bus accident, and pilot Marciniw.

“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process and to regroup,” Williams told viewers. The station temporarily switched to other programming.

On the ground, it quickly became “an emotional scene,” Silverman recounted.

“It reminded me of an incident where a firefighter is severely injured or killed in the line of duty … and normally the members of the media are giving us their condolences,” Silverman said. “In this case, it was the other way around.”

Later that night, Mayor Bass visited the crash site.

“This is a very, very, very tragic day in Los Angeles,” Bass said. “We lost five Angelenos today.”

The next morning, NBC4 anchors tried to make sense of the tragedy: “So many of us are still waking up in disbelief. It’s hard to process this,” anchor Annabelle Sedano said.

On Thursday night, Bass and Los Angeles City Councilmember John Lee honored the five Los Angeles residents at a vigil.

“May we remember Daniel, Gage, Eliana, George and Edy for how they lived, for the people they loved and for the lives they touched,” Lee said.

Weida, a passenger on the bus, was planning to celebrate his 32nd birthday with his family this Saturday.

“Instead, they’re not going to be coming out for his birthday, they’ll be coming out for his funeral,” Hochman said Thursday.

Another bus passenger, Castillo, was a devoted father of four “who had a way of bringing laughter and light into every room he walked into,” his daughter Johaunna Castillo said on a GoFundMe page for the family.

On the helicopter, bilingual journalist Moreno, 38, was passionate about telling the stories of Southern California from the sky. Her colleague, Marciniw, had decades of experience as a pilot and is remembered for “his kindness and warm smile,” Lee said.

Mejia, 29, a pedestrian, had been visiting LA from Cuilapa, Guatemala.

The back-to-back disasters in Chatsworth have left the Los Angeles community completely shaken. It is incredibly rare for a neighborhood to experience two fatal, high-profile accidents in a span of just two hours, Silverman said.

“Individually they were tragic events, and combined, I think it’s even more of a shock to community members,” Silverman said.

As the LA community mourns the losses, the LAPD is investigating the bus collision and the NTSB and the FAA were at the scene piecing together evidence and conducting witness interviews about the helicopter crash.

“In gathering that factual data, we’ll be able to paint a better picture of the actual accident sequence,” Salazar of the NTSB said.

A preliminary report on the chopper crash is expected in 30 days, followed by a final report detailing probable cause, which can take up to 18 months, according to the NTSB.

Rios, the SUV driver who had been receiving treatment for her injuries, was wheeled into court on a stretcher Friday, video shows. The judge said she was not medically fit for arraignment, according to KTLA-TV. Her bail was set at $4.1 million and she is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, according to court records.

“It’ll be a long road ahead for people to recover from this,” Silverman said.

Haitian migrants are self-deporting to Canada after President Donald Trump’s administration ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti, with approval from the Supreme Court, CNN reports.

In June, the Supreme Court gave the Trump administration the green light to end TPS for Haitian migrants living in the United States, a status that was awarded to them following an earthquake that hit the Caribbean country more than 15 years ago.

Now, reports indicate that Haitians are self-deporting from the U.S. so that they do not end up deported to their native country. Canada, CNN reports, is among the top destinations for Haitians looking to relocate outside the U.S.

CNN details:

It was a journey many Haitians like Cadet have made. During the first Trump administration, a road from upstate New York to Montreal became a well-known crossing point. But since then, the rules have changed significantly, and it’s much harder to make asylum claims at Canada’s border. Still, some are trying — including Haitians whose deportation protections in the U.S. have been revoked.

“Some people… knowing fully well all the risks and all the troubles, they’re like, ‘I will give it a shot, and I will try, because I have nothing else, and I cannot go back to Haiti,’” says Fedora Mathieu, an immigration and refugee lawyer in Ottawa, Canada’s capital, whose office has fielded a growing number of calls from Haitians in the U.S.

…

Haitians top the list of nationalities requesting asylum at ports of entry along the Canada-U.S. border, according to the Canada Border Services Agency. [Emphasis added throughout.]

Last week, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents announced that they had begun repatriating Haitian migrants to Haiti. The first deportation flight repatriated more than 160 Haitians.

On Monday, ICE agents noted that the Haitian deportees included those convicted of child sex crimes, human smuggling, and assault, as well as gang members.

It is a global phenomenon that voters are looking for change. I have to ask, change to what? In this increasingly challenging world, on recent experience, it’s best to be careful what you wish for.

Presumably the desire is for better government. Hence, the approach should be to vote for the team that is capable of good and effective governance, with the experience and the policies to make a real difference. It should not be simply a popularity contest or a protest – the objective should be beyond simply expressing disappointment or grievance.

The new Liberal Party president, Tony Abbott, and leader Angus Taylor have recently focused heavily on this “need for change”, to get rid of what they call this “rotten Labor government”. Ironically, they share a record of election losses. Their time in government failed to address the big issues effectively, with their party preferring to kick the can down the road.

The presidency of Donald Trump in the United States and the prospect of a Nigel Farage prime ministership in the United Kingdom should serve as warning against a drift to the fringes. This is becoming a particularly relevant concern in Australia with the surging popularity of Pauline Hanson and One Nation and their tendency to get ahead of themselves in assuming a capacity to win government. There is little to suggest they will have the competence or the policies to form an effective one.

Trump must serve as the most concerning example of incompetent government. When he was emerging as a potential candidate, I expressed concern that his claim to the position was as a property developer and a reality TV star with The Apprentice. I argued a property developer mostly uses other people’s money, such that if the project is a success, the investors will profit, but if it fails, they lose. The nonsense propagated in his book The Art of the Deal was the basis of his election pitch to bring a “business approach and experience” to deliver better government – in his words, “to drain the swamp”, to “shake things up”, and so on. All this under the emotive pledge to “Make America Great Again”.

It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode…

Trump has certainly not lived up to the heady promises he made. He now sits on top of an oligarchy that has mostly governed to the benefit of himself and a cabal of obscenely wealthy family and friends.

He has undermined the public service, preferring to appoint sycophants rather than qualified or experienced advisers. His domestic policy responses have been erratic, based on his prejudices rather than evidence-based analysis. He has undermined the congress and the justice system, and developed his own militia, in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have caused the deaths of innocent Americans. He has compounded the cost-of-living crisis with his ill-conceived tariffs, deportations and budgetary initiatives. This also resulted in job losses and constrained growth.

It has been estimated that in his first administration alone he added $8.4 trillion to the national debt – a 39 per cent increase. He has added another 7.6 per cent increase in this term so far. There’s nothing really “great” in any of that. His performance has the hallmarks of irresponsible government, to the detriment of average Americans and to the US’s standing in the world.

On top of this domestic disaster, Trump’s ignorance and unpredictability has undermined what had been the global rules-based order. He ignored trade deals, alliances and national sovereignty, seriously destabilising the world economy, geopolitics and the essential global energy transition – making this an even more challenging time for all governments around the globe.

Farage in the UK has been operating as a “mini Trump”, running a particularly divisive strategy “to take our country back” with strong racist overtones and claims that “Britain is Broken, Britain needs Reform”. His popularity and thrust comes from his campaign, similarly race-based, to ensure the UK exited the European Union – Reform UK is a rebadging of the Brexit Party from 2019. This is not much of a base to demonstrate a capacity for competent government. Indeed, his Brexit campaign ignored the voluminous policy warnings concerning the possible trade and financial consequences – like Trump, he would pursue populism and prejudice rather than evidence.

Nevertheless, the polls suggest he leads the fastest-growing political movement in the UK. Farage has been most active signing up a host of former and sitting MPs, mostly from the Conservative Party, including cabinet ministers and backbenchers. It is a basket of scoundrels, most excited not at the prospect of real reform but of being on a winning team.

Like Trump, Farage is also very open to accepting large donations from wealthy individuals, conspicuously a £5 million “personal gift” from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand based cryptocurrency billionaire who claimed no strings were attached. The money, which Farage said was to cover the cost of his personal protection, was given before he became an MP after seven failed attempts. It was not declared in Farage’s register of members’ financial interests. Farage has not handled the controversy well, claiming a leak of personal information (that his phone was hacked by Russian spies), then exploitation by the “deep state”.

Harborne also made a £9 million donation to Farage’s Reform UK, making him the largest single living donor in the history of British politics. The Art of the Deal indeed.

The UK branch of Transparency International has reported the huge donations from Harborne are part of a trend that’s evolved over the past decade. In 2015, just 1 per cent of donations to political parties from individuals or companies were for £1 million or more; by the last general election in 2024, the proportion had climbed to 35 per cent.

The past year has seen the advent of an even more right-wing party, Restore Britain, led by Rupert Lowe, whom Farage kicked out. Lowe has attracted considerable financial and editorial support from tech mogul Elon Musk, via his platform X, at the expense of Farage.

The surge in support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation is a reflection of the Trump-Farage phenomena. Indeed, it seems Hanson has adopted their model. Although she claims hers is the party for working Australians, she too has her controversial billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart. Hanson has also sought to attract sitting and former MPs, and her emerging electoral strategy seems to be to win seats from both the Coalition and Labor.

According to recent polls, One Nation has overtaken the government in terms of primary votes, which has encouraged some to claim the far-right party could win the next election. However, the challenge for One Nation is to convert poll standings to seats in what promises to be some pretty tough contests. Preferences are as important as ever, and it is noteworthy that Coalition preferences helped One Nation to win several seats in the recent South Australian election, and handed One Nation victory in the Farrer byelection.

The recent Australian Financial Review, RedBridge Group and Accent Research poll has posited outcomes in terms of seats in the next federal election. It sees Labor with 76 seats, One Nation on 53 and the Coalition on 12. An allocation of preferences based on the South Australian election outcome would see an exchange of about 10 more seats to Labor from One Nation, with the Coalition unchanged at 12.

While Hanson and her colleagues have declared themselves “humble”, they have got ahead of themselves if they envisage Hanson after the next election actually leading the opposition, or even becoming prime minister. The party would be ill prepared for this elevation, to say the least, in terms of both policies and the skills and experience of their prospective team. The Coalition has lost the past two elections to Labor, as voters concluded they were not ready for government and had just been in government under Scott Morrison.

Despite their recent polling and electoral success, the organisation of the One Nation party is still subpar. This has been particularly clear in relation to candidate selection and vetting, where successful candidates in South Australia and Farrer have broken ranks on their key policy of immigration, and on some social issues. Most recently we saw a disagreement between Hanson and her new MP Barnaby Joyce over housing policy, showing a lack of understanding of policy positions.

I have no doubt much of the growing support for Hanson over the past 30 years has been because she provided a platform for protest and grievance over the broad performance of the two major parties. From the start, there was an undercurrent of racism in the support, particularly against Asian migration. This carried through into the resistance to the Voice referendum and anti-Muslim sentiment. People seemed to have assured themselves Hanson would never be in government and so agreeing with her grievances felt harmless – a vote for her was without serious consequence.

This surety of minimum consequences is fading as her popularity surges and trust in the major parties continues to wane. I suggest that as we get closer to the 2028 federal election, and she and her team are subjected to greater scrutiny, they will be found wanting on their proposed solutions to the many big issues that confront our nation. Poll popularity will not transfer easily to hard votes and seats.

In the meantime, the Coalition is panicking and Abbott and Taylor have committed to preference deals with One Nation, hoping to stem the tide. It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode, opening opportunities that Hanson will try to exploit. Increasingly, though, I feel Australia will recognise she is not ready for government nor capable of the kind of global representation that Australians will want.

At least, this is my hope. May Ms Hanson never achieve her dreams.

June 19 (UPI) -- Colombia will hold one of its most polarized presidential elections in recent years on Sunday as conservative businessman Abelardo de la Espriella and leftist Sen. Iván Cepeda face off in a runoff that will test the next government's ability to address fiscal pressures, political fragmentation and security challenges.

More than 40 million Colombians are eligible to vote to choose the successor to President Gustavo Petro in a contest between two sharply different political projects.

De la Espriella, a lawyer and businessman running alongside former Finance Minister José Manuel Restrepo, has campaigned on a right-leaning platform focused on security, fighting crime and strengthening ties with the United States.

Cepeda, whose running mate is Indigenous leader Aída Quilcué, has pledged to continue much of Petro's agenda, advocating a stronger state role in the economy and an emphasis on social reforms.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_68609" });

Analysts interviewed by UPI said the next president will face immediate challenges regardless of who wins, including deteriorating public finances, the need to build coalitions in a fragmented Congress and a deeply polarized political climate.

"The first challenge is the fiscal deficit, meaning the lack of resources in state accounts, which will force the government to scale back plans and campaign promises," said Yann Basset, a political scientist at the University of Rosario in Colombia.

"The second is political because the president will not have a clear majority in Congress and will need to negotiate with other parties to pass legislation and adjust several proposals."

Basset said the next administration will also confront an opposition determined to block or challenge parts of its agenda.

Javier Mejía, an economist and professor at Stanford University, said a De la Espriella victory could trigger immediate social tensions.

"There are many reasons to think a defeat for Cepeda would lead to mobilizations. Many of them could be violent. Members of his party have publicly expressed that possibility," Mejía said.

Even if such protests lose momentum over time, Mejía said the next president would still face governance difficulties because he would lack a congressional majority, forcing him either to moderate his positions or build support through political agreements on a case-by-case basis.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_39945" });

That room for maneuver would also be constrained by weak public finances and limited capacity to increase public spending, he added.

On foreign policy, Mejía said a conservative government in Colombia would align more closely with the rightward political shift seen in several Latin American countries and could improve relations with President Donald Trump's administration.

In fact, after the first round of voting, President Donald Trump publicly endorsed De la Espriella. In a message posted on Truth Social, Trump gave him his "complete and total endorsement" and urged Colombians to support him in the runoff, a move that drew criticism from President Petro's government and sparked accusations of foreign interference in the electoral process.

A smoother relationship with Washington, he said, could ease diplomatic tensions that emerged during Petro's presidency while supporting bilateral trade and economic cooperation.

Basset agreed, describing De la Espriella as a return to Colombia's traditional diplomatic closeness with the United States.

"That has historically been Colombia's foreign policy position. There is also an obvious ideological affinity with the Trump administration. However, that strategy could face difficulties if Democrats return to power in Washington," he said.

Carlos Charry, director of the Doctoral Program in Social Studies at the University of Rosario, warned that a De la Espriella presidency could face strong resistance from other state institutions.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_98837" });

"His confrontational discourse toward traditional politics, established parties and corruption could generate significant resistance in Congress, both in the House of Representatives and the Senate," Charry said.

He also noted that some figures in De la Espriella's campaign have discussed advancing changes through presidential decrees during the first days of a new administration.

"Based on past experience, many of those decrees end up being struck down by the Constitutional Court or the Council of State," he said.

Still, Charry believes De la Espriella could enjoy better legislative conditions than Petro if he succeeds in uniting right- and center-right forces.

At the same time, he warned of the risk of heightened social unrest.

"One of the most troubling scenarios would be for Colombia to enter a period of demonstrations and protests similar to what Bolivia is currently experiencing under an Abelardo government," he said.

According to Charry, some figures close to Cepeda's campaign have suggested the possibility of a new wave of social unrest if the left loses the election.

A Cepeda victory, by contrast, would likely deepen many of the policies pursued under Petro, according to Mejía, who expects greater state intervention in the economy and higher public spending.

However, he said fiscal realities would impose clear limits.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_61876" });

"He will face even greater fiscal challenges. One would expect the adjustment to come not through spending cuts but through attempts to increase state revenues with higher taxes. That would carry significant efficiency costs given the country's current tax burden," Mejía said.

Charry agreed that many reforms promoted by Petro would continue under a Cepeda administration.

"A large share of those reforms are currently being reviewed by the Constitutional Court, particularly the health care, labor and pension reforms," he said.

At the same time, Charry said Cepeda would have to contend with corruption investigations involving Petro's administration.

"Although he has clearly stated that he will fight all forms of corruption, he will have to deal with numerous investigations inherited from the Petro government and make a major effort to distance himself from them," he said.

The academic also pointed to uncertainty surrounding the future of Petro's negotiations with illegal armed groups, known as the "Total Peace" strategy and rebranded by Cepeda's campaign as "Comprehensive Peace."

In the worst-case scenario, Charry fears security conditions could deteriorate further in some regions.

"It is not inconceivable that some areas of Colombia could experience situations similar to those seen in parts of Mexico, where drug trafficking-linked armed groups have effectively replaced state functions. In fact, that is already happening in regions such as Catatumbo," he said.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_94460" });

Beyond the election itself, Charry argued that the rise of conservative leaders across Latin America reflects growing dissatisfaction with leftist governments that came to power promising sweeping social transformation.

"Left-wing governments leave an important debt in terms of social welfare and the construction of a state that better guarantees rights," he said.

In Colombia, he argued, the promise of "Total Peace" failed to materialize and broader goals related to equality, economic well-being and social progress were not fully achieved.

Similar dynamics, he said, can be seen in countries such as Bolivia, Venezuela and Ecuador.

"There were high expectations about building more equal societies. However, deep social divisions and economic inequalities remain," Charry said.

That environment has created space for conservative movements promising rapid solutions to insecurity and organized crime.

"The fight against organized crime remains a central issue for many voters. That is why leaders who project authority and a capacity for decisive action connect with an important segment of the population," he said.
congress-ai-regulation:
Eric McDaniel

Open AI CEO Sam Altman testified before Congress earlier this year.
                
                    
                    BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP
                    
                
                hide caption

This week, some in Congress seemed to discover a new urgency to act on the complicated task of AI regulation after a slew of grim warnings from industry leaders. The only issue: Most of them leave town this week until after the November election.

And they are not just short on time — they're short on consensus on whether regulation is even a task for Congress to tackle. Take, for example, the leaders of the parties in the House of Representatives.

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., said Tuesday that "AI is serious. We do need to make sure that it's done safely but let's again let's apply common sense." He then called on the leaders of frontier AI labs to self-regulate.

"They don't need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should," Johnson said. "But we cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI. Okay? Because then we will lose our edge to China and that has serious national security implications."

Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has taken a different tack.

"It requires decisive congressional action immediately in a manner consistent with what some of the leading AI voices in the country are now saying needs to happen as it relates to slowing things down to protect the health, the safety, and the well-being of the American people," Jeffries said Monday.

The issue also cuts across party lines. Steve Bannon, a key adviser to President Trump, and Vermont progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders spoke separately at an event Tuesday in Washington, calling for the technology to be restricted.

OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the leading American AI companies, are often at odds on what regulation is necessary. But leaders from both companies recently expressed support for independent watchdogs being able to assess the development process.

Though the issue boiled over this week, AI regulation efforts have been simmering on the Hill for years. A bipartisan House task force released a report in 2024. Earlier this year, Representatives Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., released a comprehensive bipartisan proposal.

Those efforts, along with a number of others, were greeted with a shrug by leaders from both parties.

Republicans lack consensus within their on party on the right approach, Democrats appear ready to wait for now, as they anticipate their party will control of one or both chambers of Congress come January.

If and when regulation efforts do, eventually, begin in earnest, one of the key details lawmakers will have to decide is whether states will be allowed to impose their own regulations or whether their statutes will be preempted by federal rules, as desired by the Trump administration.

"The preemption issue is going to be one of the most difficult things that we navigate," Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., said at an Axios event in March. "Companies are not going to be able to have a framework for 50 different states and really survive."

While the GOP has typically supported having states lead  on most regulation, House Republican leaders, including Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, have expressed support for broad bans on states' ability to regulate AI. Many Democrats and states' rights-minded GOP lawmakers oppose them.

"What we've seen over and over again is that while Congress has essentially fiddled under the influence of big tech lobbyists, states like Texas and Florida and Utah, red states in particular," said Daniel Cochrane, "have been leading the charge to hold these companies accountable."

Cochrane, who spoke to NPR in June, is a senior fellow for the Family First Tech initiative at the Institute for Family Studies, a research and advocacy group that works to strengthen marriage, family life and the welfare of children. He worries that a broad federal ban on state AI regulation would result in inaction.

"Almost everyone in Washington agrees AI is transformative and requires some kind of policy response," Nicole Alvarez, a senior tech policy analyst at the Center for American Progress, told NPR this summer.

"The real fight," she said, "is what governance looks like."

She worries that, even if a federal framework does move forward, states will be limited if they want to place further restrictions in areas like consumer safety and protections.

While Congress sorts out its approach, Adam Kovacevich, the founder and CEO of center-left tech industry policy group Chamber of Progress worries the patchwork landscape of state regulations is imposing a muddled, de facto national standard.

"Unfortunately we're seeing a creep of blue state laws" on frontier models, fairness and algorithmic discrimination, Kovacevich told NPR in June, "but that's not the best way to regulate AI."

He thinks AI should be regulated largely at the federal level but "there seems to be little energy being spent on actually writing those standards before this year's midterm elections."

It is tough to see beyond the fight about how to regulate to the specifics what rules Congress might agree on. Protections for children appear to be one possible area of common ground.

"Some uses of AI are so structurally dangerous or misaligned with basic social values that they shouldn't just be regulated, they should be prohibited outright," Alvarez said. "For example, banning AI systems from generating child sexual abuse material."

Cochrane points to a proposal from Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., the GUARD Act, which he says "would impose restrictions on AI companions for children and impose criminal liability on anyone who makes a sexually explicit chatbot."

Kovacevich wants to see investments in competitiveness.

"We are in an AI race against China and the Chinese government is viewing AI as an existential race to win," he said. "They're making all sorts of government investments and policies to win that race. We're just not treating the race with the same level of seriousness."

caesar_rodney_historic_ride:
On this day, 250 years ago, a dying patriot rode all night through a storm so America could be born. Caesar Rodney, a delegate to the Continental Congress from Delaware, was tending to protests by British loyalists on the night of July 1st when a storm brewed to the north. Suffering from asthma and a facial cancer tumor that would lead to his death 8 years later, a letter arrived stating that Delaware’s vote was tied, 1 vote in favor of independence, 1 against it. Determined not to let this chance slip, Rodney immortalized himself by mounting a horse and riding to Philadelphia as lightning swirled around him. READ more inspiring details about this Founding Father… (1776)

Caesar Rodney was in Dover tending to Loyalist activity in Sussex County when he received word from fellow Delaware delegate and successionist Thomas McKean that he and delegate George Read were deadlocked on the vote for independence. He and McKean had already lead the effort on the floor of the Delaware Assembly to vote, 16 days earlier on June 15th, to sever all ties with the British Empire.

To break the deadlock, Rodney mounted his horse and rode 70 miles (110 km) through a thunderstorm on the night of July 1st, 1776, arriving in Philadelphia “in his boots and spurs still caked with mud” on July 2nd, just as the voting had begun. He had completed the journey that normally took 24 hours in just 18, stopping only, it is sometimes said, to merely change horses.

He broke Delaware’s deadlock with his vote for succession, making the 13 colonies unanimous in the same—and he would sign the Declaration of Independence on August 2nd.

MORE Good News on this Day:

55 years ago today, Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and Freddie Mercury performed their first show together as Queen at Surrey College, England. It was Mercury who suggested the band’s name, and the art school student illustrated their logo which combined the members’ zodiac signs and appeared on all the Queen LPs.

Queen’s third LP in 1974 produced their first US hit, Killer Queen, but it was the next album, Night at the Opera that solidified them as one of the top pop-rock bands with songs like Bohemian Rhapsody and You’re My Best Friend. Other hits include Somebody to Love, Another One Bites the Dust, Crazy Little Thing Called Love, and the stadium anthems We Will Rock You and We Are the Champions.

Mercury (whose real last name was Bulsara and was of Indian Parsi descent) died of AIDS a few years after his final concert in 1989, and his operatic rock legacy was portrayed in the 2018 film Bohemian Rhapsody. (1971)

103 years ago today, Wisława Szymborska was born in Poland. This poet, essayist, translator, and recipient of the 1996 Nobel Prize in Literature penned over a dozen poetry books that won numerous prizes from cultural organizations and civic ones. Her wit and irony belied her Communist education and upbringing, and though her body of work remained small by the time she had died in 2012, it was not for want of trying—rather only for the presence of “a trash can” in her house.

In the New York Times Book Review, Stanislaw Baranczak, who translated many of her poems into English wrote, “The typical lyrical situation on which a Szymborska poem is founded is the confrontation between the directly stated or implied opinion on an issue and the question that raises doubt about its validity. The opinion not only reflects some widely shared belief or is representative of some widespread mind-set, but also, as a rule, has a certain doctrinaire ring to it: the philosophy behind it is usually speculative, anti-empirical, prone to hasty generalizations, collectivist, dogmatic and intolerant.”

The below are select stanzas from a translated work dated to 2001 from her poem The End and the Beginning. (1923)

After every war
someone has to clean up.

Someone has to drag in a girder
to prop up a wall.
Someone has to glaze a window,
rehang a door.

Photogenic it’s not,
and takes years.
All the cameras have left
for another war.

We’ll need the bridges back,
and new railway stations.
Sleeves will go ragged
from rolling them up.

From out of the bushes
sometimes someone still unearths
rusted-out arguments
and carries them to the garbage pile.

Happy 37th birthday to the soccer forward and previously-highest-paid women’s athlete, Alex Morgan. As of publication, she has won 224 caps for the US Women’s National Team, and has scored 123 goals. While her career has never seen her stay at the same club for more than 3 seasons, her time with the USWNT has been a prosperous one indeed, earning her two World Cup wins, international publicity as one of the leading faces of the women’s game, and a spot on the cover of FIFA 2016 alongside Lionel Messi.

Playing with New York, Seattle, Portland, Orlando, and San Diego in the US, Morgan also made several moves to play overseas including to the feminine champions Olympic Lyonnais, and London’s Tottenham Hotspur. Neither move lasted more than a single season, but Morgan was instrumental in Lyon’s victory in the French Cup that year by scoring 7 goals in between the quarter and semi-finals.

As a leader of the USWNT at the 2019 FIFA Women’s World Cup, Morgan scored five goals in the opening group game against Thailand to equal the World Cup single-game goals record set by Michelle Akers in 1991. Morgan also registered three assists in the game. The team’s 13–0 scoreline set a new record for margin of victory in a World Cup match.

In that edition of the tournament final, she won a penalty that was converted by teammate Megan Rapinoe to win the fourth FIFA Women’s World Cup for the USA.

Off the field, Morgan teamed with Simon & Schuster to write a middle-grade book series about four soccer players: The Kicks. The first book in the series, Saving the Team, debuted at number seven on The New York Times Best Seller list in May 2013. (1989)

Happy 79th Birthday to Larry David, head writer and co-creator of Seinfeld. Starting with a history degree from the University of Maryland, the Brooklyn-raised comedian went on to Seinfeld fame and later wrote and starred in HBO’s Curb Your Enthusiasm. That show’s seventh season featured the cast of Seinfeld returning in a story arc involving Larry’s attempt to organize a Seinfeld reunion TV special.

David’s work on Seinfeld won him two Primetime Emmy Awards in 1993, for Outstanding Comedy Series and Outstanding Individual Achievement in Writing in a Comedy Series. Formerly a comedian himself, he went into television, including for SNL. He has been nominated for 27 Primetime Emmy Awards and three Golden Globe Awards. He was voted by fellow comedians and comedy insiders as the 23rd greatest comedy star ever in a 2004 British poll to select “The Comedian’s Comedian.”

As legendary as Seinfeld was, Curb was, in another way, on another level. Up until the fifth season, every episode was based on a very undetailed outline of activities, in which the actors would improvise the dialogue and choices in the scenes where details were lacking based on the story outline, direction, and their creativity.

David has said that his character in the show, a fictionalized version of himself, is what he would be like in real life if he lacked social awareness and sensitivity. The character’s numerous and frequent social faux pas, misunderstandings, and ironic coincidences are the basis of much of the show’s comedy and have led to the entry into the American pop culture lexicon of the expression “Larry David moment”, meaning an inadvertently created socially awkward situation. WATCH the Top 10 Cringe-Worthy Moments from Curb… (1947)

On this day in 1964, the landmark Civil Rights Act of 1964 was signed into law by U.S. President Johnson outlawing all segregation on the basis of race. The legislation, first proposed by President Kennedy, would protect constitutional rights and outlaw discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. It prohibits unequal application of voter registration requirements, and racial segregation in schools, employment, and public accommodations.

And on this day 21 years ago, Live 8 Concerts rocked 10 cities, including London, Philadelphia, Paris, Berlin, Johannesburg, Rome, and Moscow, designed to put pressure on G8 countries to address poverty and debt in Africa.

Hundreds of millions of people saw the Bob Geldof-produced events in person, on TV, or online. As a result, five days later, the G8 leaders pledged to double levels of aid to poor nations from $25 to $50 billion by the year 2010. Included in the all-star line-ups were Pink Floyd, (reunited with former bassist/vocalist/lyricist Roger Waters for the first time in over 24 years), U2, Paul McCartney, Madonna, Chris Martin, Dave Matthews, Stevie Wonder, Will Smith, and Robin Williams–covering Queen’s We Will Rock You. DVD sets are available online. (2005)

46 years ago today, the comedy film Airplane! premiered.

Written and directed by David and Jerry Zucker, along with Jim Abrahams, it won Golden Globe nominations and starred Leslie Nielsen, Robert Stack, Lloyd Bridges, and Peter Graves. A perfect parody of the disaster film genre—particularly the drama Airport 1975—Airplane! is a fast-paced slapstick comedy, with visual and verbal puns, gags, and obscure humor.

The film’s reputation has grown substantially since its release, and was marked for preservation by the United States National Film Registry at the Library of Congress as being “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

A Cairns man accused of exposing the identity of a Queensland public figure at the centre of a mysterious extortion case has been charged by police with allegedly disobeying a suppression order.

The 35-year-old spent most of his weekend locked up in the watch house after he was arrested on Friday night and ordered to shut down his social media accounts which allegedly included posts about the high-profile man, his job and his alleged affair.

The case involves a defendant facing one charge of extortion with domestic violence who is accused of threatening his ex-partner over her alleged romantic relationship with the prominent married man.

But very few details about the case can be made public due to a blanket non-publication order made by Acting Magistrate Gelma Meoli which media organisations are currently challenging in the Supreme Court.

For legal reasons, the ABC has chosen not to name the local man who's been charged for allegedly sharing suppressed details online, including the public figure's identity.

There is a highly secretive and unusual court case playing out behind closed doors in Far North Queensland.

The local man has an extensive criminal history but is not personally involved in the extortion case and it was quite by chance that he happened to be in court more than two weeks ago when the matter was first raised publicly.

On Friday night, about eight officers turned up at his home with a search warrant signed by Acting Magistrate Meoli.

Police seized his computer, mobile phone and other devices.

He was charged later that night and appeared in court early the following morning.

He said despite being granted bail, he was not released from the watch house for almost another 12 hours.

Part of his bail conditions included suspending all his social media accounts and removing all posts that might be capable of breaching the suppression order.

In a statement, Queensland Police confirmed they had charged a 35-year-old man with one count of disobedience to a lawful order issued by a statutory authority.

He is due to reappear before Cairns Magistrates Court on Tuesday morning.

When contacted by the ABC today, he said he would contest the charge and oppose any application by prosecutors to close the court to media or the public.

"It should be heard in open court," he said.
