The writer Annie Jacobsen on the terrifying realities of biological war.

Of all the extinction-level threats vying for our attention, AI, climate change, and nuclear war tend to get most of the airplay. But Annie Jacobsen thinks biological war should be near the top of our mental list of doomsday scenarios, too.

A daily, curiosity-driven guide to the big, weird, and fascinating ideas shaping the news cycle.

She should know — Jacobsen has carved out a unique niche as America’s foremost reporter on the ways we could end the world. Her bestselling 2024 book Nuclear War: A Scenario terrified readers and experts alike, and has been optioned by Hollywood.

It was while conducting dozens of interviews with high-level government sources for Nuclear War that Jacobsen was told repeatedly that biowarfare should be her next focus.

She took their advice. Her gripping new book Biological War: A Scenario follows a similar ticking-clock format that shows, step by step, just how a humanity-threatening man-made biological catastrophe could play out. (Spoiler alert: not great.)

The result feels like dystopian science fiction, albeit the kind that comes heavily footnoted with government studies that come to similarly grim conclusions. The fact that tech CEOs are also sounding the alarm that advanced AI could make creating killer germs even easier only adds to the growing sense of anxiety. And this book has also been optioned by Hollywood for a TV adaptation.

Jacobsen sat down with Today, Explained host Noel King to talk through the plot of her nightmare scenario, why we’re still developing biological weapons despite the clear risks, and what needs to happen to avoid disaster. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

How does your book start?

The inciting incident in the book is an accident at a Biosafety Level 4 lab, shorthand BSL-4, in Siberia called Vector. And it’s an actual BSL-4 lab, the highest classification. ... And there was an actual accident, an explosion there in 2019.

In that real-life incident, a deadly pathogen was not released that we know of. But of course, in Biological War: A Scenario, a deadly pathogen is released. And it’s a form of pneumonic plague, which is a nightmare pathogen and sits at the top of the Tier 1 select agent list of the CDC. And so in the first act of the book, I show the scrambling of the intelligence community and the Defense Department, trying desperately to determine if something got out and what it is. ... The release of the pathogen widens, and so once you have escape. You do not have mitigation, which has to happen in the first 24, 48 hours. Now you have a situation which is unstoppable.

You say this is now an unstoppable scenario. What is it?

A plague itself, of course, conjures up images and ideas of the bubonic plague of the 14th century, the Black Death. That killed between one half and one third of Europe. The bacteria is called Yersinia pestis. And pneumonic plague is the airborne version of plague. The problem with an airborne pathogen is that because the delivery system is the human lungs, it can move very quickly from a scientist in that lab who now has Yersinia pestis in his lungs out to the general public. And that is precisely what happens in the scenario.

How does it spread from there? The city where this BSL-4 lab sits isn’t Moscow. What happens once the pathogen is in the lungs of the people who work in that lab, or the janitor who was cleaning it that night?

That’s right. Well, suddenly it’s in everyone’s lungs, and those people go out into their community. And even though Koltsovo, the science town where Vector is located, is a small town, it is just 12 miles from Novosibirsk, which is the third-largest city in Russia. And, also, there happens to be in this scenario a group of international hunters on a hunting trip in that area who come across a dying scientist in the snow. One of them gives him CPR, being the Good Samaritan that he is. And lo and behold, those travelers suddenly are now getting on an airplane in Novosibirsk, flying home to where they reside in five or six of the continents.

What makes this form of plague so novel, so dangerous?

I pull this information from actual facts of the Soviet Cold War-era biological weapons program that we know about from Soviet defectors. And I want you to keep in mind: This is 40 years ago when gene editing was in its infancy. But there are two things specifically that the Soviet bioweapons engineers did to plague.

Their idea was to create a super plague weapon. And one of them has never been revealed before. They were working to insert the gene for euphoria into the plague pathogen. ... When you get a disease, a pneumonic-type disease, pneumonia, tubercular, you want to go home and get under the covers because you feel terrible. And when you do that, you’re infecting a lot less people than you would if a gene for euphoria had been inserted into the pathogen, which would make you feel terrific, which would make you want to go out and socialize with people, perhaps even go to a crowded disco.

And the other thing that the Soviet scientists were working on was a way to defeat medical countermeasures, but with an added component of psychological distress. They inserted a gene into the pathogen that would be triggered by the taking of antibiotics. And that second pathogen would give you encephalitis, which is a swelling of the brain. The psychological part of it, according to the Soviet scientists, was that they wanted the last thought of the person dying of what they thought was pneumonic plague, but would in fact be encephalitist to be, “My government and Western medicine has failed me.”

Those of us who try to remain optimistic think there’s a way to stop it. In the movies, there’s an outbreak, then the government gets it under control, and okay, maybe a lot of people die, but we’re all right. That is not where your book is headed. How does your scenario end?

So in the book, I take readers from outbreak to anarchy in six days. Anarchy is what will happen according to Pentagon war gaming and pandemic planning. And this is because fear of infection becomes a secondary weapon, if you will. People begin to behave like they are about to die, which is most certainly underpinning everyone’s mind. And so after those first six days, the Principals Committee, the President’s Biodefense Committee, must make a decision. The president has to declare the Insurrection Act, which allows the military to step in as a law enforcement agency.

“Imagine the president — with a few Secret Service outside the door, the military aide with the nuclear football — sitting alone in a room wearing a gas mask.”

What happens to the president really blew my mind as a reporter. He goes somewhere in the United States very far away from everyone. Because the idea, the goal, is to make sure that the president doesn’t get the airborne pathogen in his lungs. So maybe I’ll leave you with an image. Imagine the president — with a few Secret Service outside the door, the military aide with the nuclear football — sitting alone in a room wearing a gas mask.

In the book, the people who survive are the ones who have gas masks. Everyone else is gone.

And look, we hope we never get to that, by all means. But yes, the Pentagon has issued 1.7 million gas masks to its military personnel. And that is a spooky thought in and of itself, coupled with the idea that the military is predominantly male. There’s something like 17 percent women in the military. And so, unlike the Nuclear War scenario in which I had science-based nuclear winter theory to work from, in Biological War, nothing has been written on the science record about what it might be after. And so the one imaginative part of the book is the very end where I write about biological twilight. ... And it is a very, very ugly world.

Let’s back up. We did outlaw biological weapons at some point, right?

That’s right. Very mysteriously in 1969, President Nixon just unilaterally declared that the arsenal was going to be destroyed. At the same time that all of the nations of the world were working to sign this treaty called the Biological Weapons Convention Treaty, which would outlaw bioweapons. Soviet Russia at the time signed it but immediately began work on an illegal biological weapons program that was colossal. And this went without notice, without any idea really by the CIA and the Pentagon all the way until 1989, when one of the Soviet scientists named Vladimir Pasechnik had a crisis of conscience and he defected and he told British intelligence all about the program.

Where have we seen biological weapons used?

Maybe the most important example of a biological attack in the past, certainly here in the United States, are the anthrax attacks, which occurred right after 9/11. Weaponized anthrax was sent through the mail to US senators and a number of media outlets. So five people ended up dying; 22 got sick in four states. But that really kicked off what can be considered the biological military-industrial complex, if you will, which led to this buildup in BSL-4 labs around the world today. There are 110 BSL-4 labs around the world. There are more than 3,500 BSL-3 labs.

Your book has a map of where those labs are, which I found weirdly comforting, mainly because I don’t live too near any of them. If one of these things is going to be released, either accidentally or deliberately, where is the threat coming from? A rogue nation? Terrorists?

Certainly, bad actors getting a hold of a biological weapon was the great concern of the post-anthrax situation. And that is why so much emphasis was put on bioterrorism. Now I avoided that specifically in the book. ... And I didn’t even have an attack. Rather, I had an incident. I had a lab leak because I have learned in the decades since that really is the greatest concern. So many of these BSL-3 and 4 labs are in places without a lot of security, including in countries where there are wars going on.

Could somebody be making a biological weapon in a basement somewhere, off books?

Absolutely. And another disturbing document I came across, unclassified in the Pentagon, was a threat spectrum that showed weapons of mass destruction in terms of destructiveness. And of course, nuclear weapons sit at the far end of the spectrum. They are the most destructive. But very close behind were biological weapons. And even more startling was the notion that biological weapons present the greatest overall threat.

Nuclear weapons have an extremely high barrier for entry. You have to have fissile material. ... You have to have a weapons delivery system like an ICBM or a submarine. ... That creates a situation where most nuclear weapons, all nuclear weapons, if you will, are in the hands of a command-and-control system within a nation.

Biological weapons have no such barriers. In fact, the barriers for entry are getting lower literally by the day. You now can have a situation where someone with very limited knowledge of biology can create a biological weapon in their basement with the use of computational systems like an AI system, for example.

Your book reads like a thriller. How much have you exaggerated? How much have you novelized in order to hold our attention?

Everything in the book is based in science fact, meaning all of the facts, all of the figures. I write a hundred or so pages of notes in the back of the book for readers to be able to answer the question that you are asking me. ... In the notes, you can find that answer.

Did any of those people give you good recommendations for how to avoid a disaster scenario, or at least how to avoid these things proliferating?

Well, you know, the ticking clock scenario that I write has an even more urgent ticking clock, which is the public’s pressure on lawmakers to absolutely do something about this nightmare scenario before it happens. Look, we have a world right now where you have the CEOs of the largest AI companies in the world admitting publicly that the lane of bio mixed with AI is of their top concern. You don’t hear that about nuclear. You hear that about bio.

How do you sleep through the night?

Anyone who knows me personally can vouch for the fact that I am an optimist at heart. I really believe that information is king. Once you know things, it gives you a lot of power. Perhaps that’s whistling by the graveyard, but that’s what works for me.

Do you have a biohazard suit?

I do not. I do not. But I do have a few gas masks. I must tell the truth.

factcheck_even-girlbosses-cant-stand-the:
How ironic that the feminist labor movement that promised to liberate women may actually vitiate their happiness and undercut the successful work they hoped to find.

“The share of women in heterosexual marriages who make as much or more than their husbands has nearly tripled over the past five decades, according to the Pew Research Center,” The Washington Post notes this week. Another report from last year found that women now comprise almost half of managers in the United States, an increase of more than 50 percent from 1980, and one that is occurring across a host of professional categories. And, as was reported last month, women accounted for almost all new job hires in August.

Feminists laud this as an unqualified victory in the march toward equality in all things. But is it good for work? What we know about female leadership, and my own experiences as a manager, would suggest perhaps not so much.

“This has been beyond a doubt the best office I have ever worked in.” As a supervisor, the comment was an honor, but it was particularly remarkable coming from a woman in an office culture that was almost entirely male. My employee was a hard-charging, demonstrably successful young woman with a graduate degree from one of the most left-wing private universities in the country. She was not the only woman (or man) to express such a sentiment during my time as a supervisor in that particular position.

When I was part of an office leadership team that was almost exclusively male, the dynamics were about as antithetical to the stereotypes as you can get; indeed, a significant body of research shows there is little-to-no difference in abusive male versus female supervision. There was no “toxic masculine” chest-thumping, nor was there any sexual harassment or innuendo. There was no observable favoritism toward certain men. All the male managers were family men, though apart from me, none of them were particularly religious. All of us had served in either Afghanistan or Iraq.

Without a doubt, this male-dominated leadership fostered a result-oriented, assertive, competitive, and risk-tolerant environment whose successes made it the envy of other teams in the organization. As Doug Barry and Daniel O’Connor observe in their recent book First Line of Defense, “Men are fighters. … [They] were made for risk and adventure.”

That work environment was also, no surprise, not a particularly emotive or “chatty” work culture. Meetings were comparatively few and short, and managers voiced their annoyance with those incapable of getting to the damn point. Yet, also contrary to the stereotype, it was famously accommodating to those with family responsibilities. As long as the female employees did good work, no (male) manager ever questioned pregnant or nursing mothers who required time for medical appointments, pumping, or other maternal necessities.

So why did so many female employees — who, so the feminist narrative tells us, are suffering under patriarchal societal structures — tell my fellow male managers and me how grateful they were for what they acknowledged was a superior professional structure? Some of the reason was simply that my fellow male managers were decent men, the kind who recognize that while employees need professional challenges to keep them engaged, they also need to feel appreciated, respected, and free to have a fulfilled personal life. And, as many female employees told me, they were quite surprisingly not getting this when they were led by female supervisors.

Women, so the research tells us, are more nurturing, empathic, and communicative. One would think these would be unmitigated benefits in professional environments. In many cases, they are. But these qualities can also be a double-edged sword for the workforce, as qualities typically associated with women — including agreeableness, conflict avoidance, and risk aversion — are disadvantages for supervisors.

I certainly heard complaints from male employees about previous work cultures that were female-dominated, in which they felt excluded or bullied, feminist bosses seemingly having decided to direct all of their anger over supposedly centuries of patriarchal oppression on some hapless new male hire. But by far the most complaints I heard about female-dominated work came from women I managed. Women who had been pregnant or had little children told me their female bosses were less sympathetic to the various needs related to motherhood than male counterparts who seemed more willing to grant mothers some slack. They told me how they tired of cattish work cultures defined by inscrutably complex cliques.

The reason for this, as even recent research supports, has as much to do with a feminine overreaction to the “evil patriarchy” as it does with certain feminine qualities that prioritize personality and communication style and thus ostracize those who fail to navigate female-dominated social structures. Women who, for the sake of their careers, never had children or placed careers over their kids — research refers to them as “queen bees” — not only lack sympathy for those colleagues who do, but seem to punish them, perhaps because they feel the loss of not having kids of their own. This is likely aggravated by female leaders thinking they need to manifest male qualities such as assertiveness or hiding their emotions. One first-time nursing mother told me a previous female boss told her that if she wanted to have a successful career, she shouldn’t have any more children.

I have no desire to apply rose-colored glasses to a past, male-dominated work environment in which women were routinely subjected to derision and sexual harassment, nor to the obvious fact that men today remain just as capable of doing such terrible misdeeds when given the reins of power. Rather, my point is that men, because of various qualities more common to their sex, also possess the capacity for transformative, self-sacrificing leadership. As a sex, they are generally more able to overcome resentment and bitterness, to overlook slights, and to exemplify physical, mental, and emotional resilience. When properly formed, they can be inspired to what Teddy Roosevelt in 1899 called “the doctrine of the strenuous life, the life of toil and effort, of labor and strife,” willing to risk failure to avoid being labeled a “man of timid peace.”

As men’s influence over work wanes — especially as woke ideologues claim that “historic wrongs” demand a reverse, female-dominant workplace — I suspect we will see less of a utopia of so-called gender equality and more of a feminist dystopia, as essayist Helen Andrews last year provocatively warned us. Those workplaces will be more cliquish and more beholden to gossip and personal grudges. They will be defined by micromanagement, indecision, and an aversion to risk. And, counterintuitively, the attempt to exhibit masculine traits will make them less welcoming to women seeking a balanced family life and the freedom to be engaged, devoted mothers.

How ironic that the feminist labor movement that promised to liberate women to discover fulfillment and flourishing in a competitive career may actually vitiate their happiness and undercut the successful work they hoped to find.

mark-carney-turkey-values-realism:
Leftist Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney insisted during a press conference in Istanbul, Turkey, on Friday that expanding economic and defense ties with the Islamist state was not a violation of his progressive values, declaring, “Engagement is not approval.”

He told reporters that “values-based realism,” which is what he calls his foreign policy, means that Canada can do business with nations whose behavior it doesn’t approve of.

Carney traveled to Turkey, a fellow NATO ally nation, on Wednesday to discuss expanding trade volume and other bilateral cooperation. His visit is unprecedented in the history of the two countries and raised eyebrows at home given strongman Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s repression of a variety of communities in his country, including the LGBTQ2A+ community, non-Sunni Muslims, Kurds, and anti-Islamists in general. Erdogan is arguably the most vocal head of state supporting the genocidal jihadist terrorist organization Hamas and has used state repression to suppress the opposition and stay in power during the past three rounds of national elections.

Carney insisted when challenged by reporters on Friday that doing business with a government with such a poor human rights track record did not undermine Canada’s own values or legitimize Erdogan.

“There are very few countries in this world that have the standards of Canada, the rights of Canada, the conviction of Canada, the constant reinforcement of those rights, so that all Canadians can live their lives as they choose,” he asserted, according to the Globe and Mail.

“Our first and foremost job is protecting, not just protecting LGBTQI rights and two-spirited rights in Canada, but promoting those rights and ensuring that all Canadians can live their full selves in Canada. So first and foremost, that’s our responsibility,” he said. “Two-spirit” is a uniquely Native American/First Nation concept in which someone identifies as both male and female simultaneously, or a third “gender.” There is no significant documentation of the presence of two-spirit people in Turkey.

In addition to insisting that he was not legitimizing Erdogan and did not approve of his government, Carney insisted that it was necessary to engage Turkey to become a “truly sovereign nation,” hinting at Carney’s campaign to distance Canada from the United States. Carney’s term as prime minister has been defined by antagonism towards America and the declaration that the “old relationship” with Canada’s closest ally was “over.”

“Part of the way we discharge that is to be a truly sovereign nation. Part of the way we become a truly sovereign nation and reinforce our sovereignty is to have a broad range of partnerships around the world,” he reportedly said.

Both Canadian and Turkish media reported that the meeting between Carney and Erdogan on Thursday yielded significant advances in bilateral trade and development.

“We are now starting a new era between Türkiye and Canada,” Erdoğan declared triumphantly on Thursday.

The two leaders signed a “three-year action plan” to expand trade, focusing on defense and energy. The Turkish president said that he aspired to raise the two countries’ bilateral trade volume, currently standing at $3 billion a year, to $10 billion, with a short-term boost to $5 billion.

“Today, we have overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkey and Canada for many years. Now we are launching a new era between Turkey and Canada,” Erdogan explained, according to the Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency. “Our decision on a strategic partnership will not be merely a symbolic step on paper.”

Among the major deals pursued will be trade in liquefied natural gas, nuclear power, mining and critical minerals. Carney touted in particular the potential that the Canadian company AtkinsRéalis could secure an agreement to build nuclear reactors for Turkey, which has traditionally relied on Russia for nuclear development. Carney stated that the deal was not set, however, only that the chances of securing one on nuclear energy were “good,” compared to barely existent a year ago.

The two nations, Erdogan and Carney stated on Thursday, would also pursue development projects in poorer, third-world countries, Anadolu added.

Among the biggest announcements was the confirmation that Turkey and Canada would also pursue negotiations towards a free trade deal. This agreement, Carney said, would be based on negotiations expected to begin in November. Such a deal would dramatically expand Turkish access to the Canadian market and its substantial fossil fuel resources, as well as grant Canada an opening to importing a much higher volume of Turkish goods.

Human rights observers have expressed much more limited enthusiasm for expanding business with Turkey than Carney has. The Globe and Mail quoted University of Ottawa Professor Roland Paris lamenting that Carney was “not getting the balance right” between trade and human rights concerns, stating he was “decidedly on the side of pursuing commercial goals while downplaying other questions of human rights and democracy and the rule of law.”

By

Eric McDaniel

,

Joel Rose

,

Henry Larson

,

Sarah Handel

,

Dana Farrington

NPR's Eric McDaniel reports on how Congress has reacted to President Trump's executive order exempting Russia from economic sanctions.

JOEL ROSE, HOST:  Ukrainian drones attacked two major Russian cities this weekend, launching one of their largest strikes this year at targets in Moscow and St. Petersburg. But as Ukraine staged its latest attack, the U.S. has been tipping the scales for Russia. Last weekend, President Trump announced an oil deal with the Russian government, bypassing existing U.S. sanctions on Moscow. The president next called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal.ROSE: All this, and then late in the day on Friday, Trump signed an executive order exempting Russia from sweeping economic sanctions passed by Congress.(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "MEET THE PRESS")PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: But if United States will support Putin, I mean, it's unbelievable. It's tragedy. It's historic mistake and big tragedy.ROSE: Asked this morning in an interview on NBC's "Meet The Press" whether Ukraine can win the war without the U.S., Zelenskyy was unequivocal.(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "MEET THE PRESS")VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We hope that president, his team will be on our side - minimum, in the middle.ROSE: For more on the evolving relationship between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine, I'm joined now by NPR congressional reporter Eric McDaniel. Hey, Eric.ERIC MCDANIEL, BYLINE: Hey.ROSE: So the White House says it is in the national security interest of the United States to waive these sanctions. What's the argument there? Why is it in the national interest?MCDANIEL: I mean, I think what's important to know is that it's coming on the back of a diesel sales deal that the U.S. struck with Russia earlier in the week. The president is deeply concerned about energy prices. It is a huge issue in the midterm elections. But I should just note, analysts with the International Energy Agency, which tracks all of this stuff, said it isn't really likely this diesel sales deal to nudge the extremely high price of diesel fuel, which is used in all transport of goods, basically any lower.But these sanctions are maybe another lever that Trump can pull on energy prices, say, the only one he's got outside of winding down the Iran war to try and lower costs. And these prices, like I said, are at the top of voters' minds during this final stretch of the midterm elections. And when Congress passed the sanctions law in the first place, it did give Trump the power to temporarily waive sanctions if needed, and of course, he now has.Trump has expressed frustration, too, at Ukraine for its strikes against Russia's energy infrastructure, even as Russia continues its own strikes, saying that the strikes are all driving the cost of fuel higher. And the IEA says supply disruption due to ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, including the U.S.-Iran war, is the primary driver of costs here. So we'll see if really any of this can nudge things down.ROSE: So while the president seems to have his eye on energy prices, this sanctions package was designed to bolster Ukraine's war effort, and it passed - we should say - on a robust, bipartisan basis through Congress. How are lawmakers reacting?MCDANIEL: Let's start in the spot that's most interesting to me, which I will say is South Carolina. Senator Darline Graham - you might remember that name - her late brother, Lindsey, was this law's primary champion. He was the senator for South Carolina. She's now running for a full term there. Graham told Meg Kinnard of the AP that she understood that the president is concerned about costs but that she backs the sanctions to put pressure on Russia. Other Republicans have voiced their own concerns in much stronger terms.He does have some support in the party. Senator James Lankford, Republican of Oklahoma, told NBC's "Meet The Press" that the president is trying to balance America's needs while also considering how best to support Ukraine. And Democrats, of course, are mad. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that, quote, "by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier."ROSE: So what happens now? Does Congress have any recourse here?MCDANIEL: I'll bring you into a congressional term of art - they can do basically diddly-squat. And that's on a couple of levels. As I mentioned, the law gives the president power to waive these as long as he provides a national security justification, which he has. And also relevant here, Congress isn't even here in Washington with us. They won't be for weeks and weeks. They're out campaigning until midterm voting ends, and the environment when they come back, sure, maybe they revisit the issue. Republicans, though, who are going to be finishing their terms, would have more space to oppose the president if they so desire.ROSE: But presumably, this is not the only thing that's going to be on their agenda after the midterms, right?MCDANIEL: Right. That's no secret. They already have a lot of things they've got to handle, among them, government funding. They were loath to let government funding expire before midterm elections. They kicked the can from the end of September to the beginning of December. And there's also going to be separate fights. There's a farm aid bill. There's war funding. There's the debt ceiling, which is basically the U.S. government upping its own credit card limit. And if Republicans do lose control of the Senate, they'll also have to rush through as many Trump appointees as possible before Democrats get the upper hand in January, which could really clog up their legislative calendar. Candidly, I don't see them coming back to sanctions.ROSE: All right. That is NPR's Eric McDaniel. Thank you very much.MCDANIEL: Thank you.
